POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Sat, 31 Oct 2026 14:20:54 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 Merz ‘surprised’ by Asian pushback to ‘Made in Europe’ plan for car industry https://www.politico.eu/article/friedrich-merz-surprised-by-asian-pushback-over-made-in-europe-car-industry/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 14:19:53 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9250563 German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was “surprised” by the intensity of the pushback from East Asian countries against planned “Made in Europe” rules for the bloc’s car sector.

Asian countries strongly protested a plan agreed by Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, under which Brussels would restrict car subsidies to vehicles produced inside the EU, Switzerland and the U.K.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung told reporters that he had “asked Merz for support so that Korea would be treated like the EU member states.” A similar complaint was voiced in Japan.

“That was, in fact, a topic that surprised me a bit, given the intensity with which it was presented,” Merz told reporters before returning from his five-day tour of East Asian countries on Friday evening.

Merz admitted the Franco-German proposal had “sparked considerable concern in the region — in Singapore, Japan, and Korea — that we may be facing a new wave of protectionism in Europe, that we are closing ourselves off from other countries.”

The chancellor vowed to take those complaints “very seriously” and to raise them at the next EU leaders’ summit. The bloc’s leaders are set to meet in Dublin on Nov. 13 for an informal gathering.

Merz proposed a “global political alliance for rules-based trade” between so-called middle powers in speeches in Seoul and Tokyo. The EU, Asian nations, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the South American Mercosur trade bloc should “coordinate” and “act together” if others challenged the international rules “or if economic pressure were to be exerted” — a thinly veiled reference to Chinese threats to restrict access to rare earth metals or the tariff threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.

But the pushback from South Korea and Japan are a sharp reminder of how industry-specific frictions can hamper the implementation of the larger alliance proposed by Merz.

]]> en Burnham ‘open’ to formal apology for Britain’s slave trade https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-burnham-open-to-formal-apology-for-britain-slave-trade/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:55:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9250317 U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was “open” to calls for the British state to formally apologize for its role in the transatlantic slave trade.

Burnham offered a “structured dialogue with those affected” by the slave trade in an opinion piece for the Guardian, published ahead of a summit of Commonwealth countries starting Sunday.

“Having these difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future is the right thing to do. It is also the patriotic thing to do,” Burnham wrote.

However, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries for Britain to pay financial reparations for the slave trade, saying that they would be the wrong solution.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part,” the prime minister argued.

Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced in June a manifesto by Caribbean leaders setting out the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations from former colonial powers.

Burnham will attend the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, which runs through Wednesday. It will be his first foreign trip with King Charles.

It will be a crucial test for the prime minister, who will try to avoid a fight over slavery reparations that marred his predecessor Keir Starmer’s visit at the last summit in 2024.

]]> en Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymyr-zelenskyy-urges-us-speed-up-patriot-deliveries/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:41:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9250149 Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for approving the sale of Patriot interceptors but urged Washington to fast-track the delivery of the defensive missiles.

Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision” by the U.S. to approve the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missiles — but said the years-long wait to deliver them was too long for Ukraine’s urgent needs.

“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote in a Facebook post on Friday night.

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.

Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.

In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

“Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said.

The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months.

However, the White House said that it won’t pay for the Patriot interceptors. “The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies,” a statement from the State Department said.

]]> en Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-president-karol-nawrocki-rule-of-law-crisis/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 10:03:04 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9250146 WARSAW — Polish President Karol Nawrocki forced his way into the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw shortly after midnight on Saturday, in the latest escalation of the rule-of-law tussle between the PiS-allied president and Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

A video published overnight showed Nawrocki pushing through people gathered at the court’s entrance, including Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge whose disputed nomination as the court’s acting president triggered the crisis on Friday.

Another judge of the top court, Maciej Berek, accused the president of physically confronting Korwin-Piotrowska. Presidential aide Rafał Leśkiewicz claimed it was the judges, whom he called “usurpers,” who had obstructed and manhandled Nawrocki.

Inside, Nawrocki told Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges that were recently elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority: “You are not judges [of the Tribunal].”

The confrontation marked a dramatic escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the court’s president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański — both named by PiS and seen as loyalists — claiming authority to take over the court’s management. Święczkowski rejected the move.

In a statement issued around 5 a.m., Nawrocki accused the government of “forcibly seizing a constitutional institution”, demanded that police leave the court grounds and summoned emergency consultations with parliamentary parties for Saturday, citing a “threat to Poland’s internal security.”

Police remain deployed outside the tribunal, where PiS supporters had staged an anti-government protest camp for weeks.

The broader dispute stems from Tusk’s efforts to reverse controversial moves by former PiS governments to fill the court with judges aligned with the nationalist party. These efforts have met stiff resistance from PiS and Nawrocki, who refused to swear in some judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority.

The judges subsequently took oaths in parliament, in a ceremony Nawrocki considers null and void, while Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

]]> en Funding deadlock derails global effort to save nature https://www.politico.eu/article/funding-deadlock-derails-global-effort-to-save-nature/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 31 Oct 2026 07:35:24 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9246771 YEREVAN, Armenia — Scorching wildfires, disastrous floods and the looming mass extinction of species weren’t enough to convince wealthy nations to unlock crucial funds needed to halt biodiversity loss at a global nature summit this week.  

As countries around the world race against the clock to protect what’s left of the Earth’s collapsing ecosystems, global talks aimed at speeding up nature protection efforts yielded underwhelming results.  

The United Nations COP17 on biodiversity ended on Saturday with a renewed promise from countries to speed up global efforts to protect nature and restore depleted ecosystems by 2030.   

But behind that grand gesture, governments are still struggling to unlock the hundreds of billions needed to meet global biodiversity protection targets. The reason? A profound and unresolved disagreement over where that money should come from. 

“If we’re mutually unhappy that’s probably the closest we can get to on these very delicate compromises,” said a member of the Swiss delegation just before the text was adopted.

After two weeks of negotiations over how to speed up efforts to protect ecosystems, nearly 200 countries secured a hard-fought agreement to “accelerate the implementation” of the global biodiversity framework  “including by increased ambition in addressing the gaps, challenges and barriers related to implementation,” according to a draft of the text, the final version of which was not immediately available.

Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan, who presided over the summit, said negotiators had “achieved more than we could have expected.”

But in the end, governments could not agree on how to increase the number of countries currently contributing to biodiversity finance, instead only stating the obvious: that more funds would be better.

The summit exposed a growing chasm between nations over who should be held financially responsible for funding conservation measures worldwide: historically wealthy countries whose economies have caused immense damage to the environment, or newly rich states whose economies have grown exponentially in the last three decades. 

“This COP was always going to be difficult,” said Steven Guilbeault, former environment minister for Canada, adding that “COP17’s real legacy will be decided far beyond these walls, when words need to translate to action.”

Negotiators are leaving Yerevan with many issues left to resolve between now and the next COP in 2028 in Ecuador, including on how to attract more companies that benefit from nature to fund conservation projects via the Cali Fund, a landmark vehicle aimed at mobilizing private finance into nature established in 2024.

Governments know they are running out of time. At COP17, scientific experts reiterated that a million species are at risk of extinction, and the U.N. has identified an annual biodiversity financing gap of $700 billion.  

“We’re not on track to stop and reverse the biodiversity loss by 2030,” said Monique Barbut, France’s environment minister, during a COP17 plenary session on Wednesday. The world needs to “mobilize all international funding sources” to make it happen, she insisted.

The talks also ran long due to disagreements over language related to the involvement of Indigenous peoples in a key decision-making body of the Convention.

The dispute 

The U.N. Convention on Biological Diversity relies on the consensus that rich countries should pay more to protect nature because of the pressure their societies and economies exert on global ecosystems. 

Since its ratification in the 1990s, a group of wealthy countries including Canada, Australia, Japan, the U.K., Switzerland, Norway and some EU members have been funding efforts to implement the Convention.

Now, those countries want other high-income nations to chip in more. “We all know that we need more resources to ensure the effective implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework,” said Jessika Roswall, the EU’s environment commissioner.

But during the negotiations, non-donor countries — which include China, Saudi Arabia, Russia and Argentina — pushed back against any kind of income-related criteria to determine who should or shouldn’t be paying. 

The deadlock angered some nations set to benefit from a larger donor base. “Are you telling me that rich petro-states who are in many cases wealthier than some of the original list of donors and responsible for a ton of emissions and harmful practices that directly affect biodiversity shouldn’t contribute to the fund?” said Juan Carlos Navarro, Environment Minister for Panama on Wednesday, as negotiations were ongoing. 

The countries “don’t want to have the same obligations as developed countries on this issue [and] bring up the argument of ecological responsibilities,” said Juliette Landry, a senior research fellow at the think tank IDDRI. 

In the end, countries agreed simply to state that “contributions from more Parties
would improve the mobilization of biodiversity finance” and invited others to contribute voluntarily, the draft text shows.

Some successes 

Despite the divisions, many hailed the final agreement as a win for green multilateralism as governments remain committed to the overarching goal of protecting 30% of Earth’s land and sea areas and increase financing for biodiversity to $200 billion annually by 2030. 

“In Yerevan, we saw environmental multilateralism prevail once again. Countries came together, found the spirit of compromise and allowed us to agree important decisions that will support real progress for people and for planet,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UN Environment Programme.

After two weeks of endless meetings, panels and plenary sessions, negotiators agreed to strengthen the role of cities and local governments in implementing biodiversity goals, and improve how biodiversity funding reaches them. They also adopted decisions to support capacity-building and scientific cooperation, and agreed that more needs to be done to protect marine ecosystems.

Countries also recognized the need to reduce subsidies funding economic activities that harm nature and create incentives for activities that protect it. “Incentive reform has moved from the margins to the mainstream of the biodiversity agenda,” said Eva zabey, CEO of the Business for Nature coalition.

Some governments including Germany, Iceland, Uzbekistan and Spain made fresh financial commitments totalling $1.8 billion to the Global Biodiversity Framework Fund and the Global Environment Facility, the funding structures set up to implement the Convention. Under the GBF, countries have pledged to mobilize $200 billion annually by 2030.  

The U.N. Environment Programme also published a report showing that nature restoration is underway at an “unprecedented scale” with over 250 million hectares of land under restoration worldwide.

Still, countries remain off track on meeting their 2030 targets.

In Yerevan, green groups welcomed the agreement but criticized its lack of ambition key issues.

“Political promises made in Yerevan set good intentions, but won’t remove major roadblocks to implementation such as insufficient finance, fiscal and debt constraints, the nearly empty coffers of the Cali Fund and urgent reform of harmful subsidies,” said An Lambrechts, a biodiversity politics expert with Greenpeace International.

Governments have struggled to stay the course since inking the Global Biodiversity Framework in 2022. Though many countries have adopted national biodiversity strategies, financial flows to conservation projects are nowhere near where they ought to be. Geopolitical shifts and economic crises have also made it harder for governments — including the 27 EU member countries — to prioritize environmental protection. 

Countries agreed to renew talks to implement the objectives of the convention in Ecuador.

]]> en 8 things we learned at the EU-Canada summit https://www.politico.eu/article/8-things-we-learned-eu-canada-summit/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 21:43:34 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9249804 MONTREAL — Prime Minister Mark Carney wanted the landmark EU-Canada summit to be about much more than “nomenclature.” He got what he craved. 

Over a whirlwind 48 hours in Montreal, top officials from Brussels and Ottawa huddled to pursue agreements on critical minerals, super computers and defense cooperation.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Carney gathered as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to upend the global order and Chinese dominance of critical markets squeezes middle powers. 

Those challenges have pushed the EU and Canada into a rapidly developing partnership that eclipses anything attempted by Brussels with a non-member country since the bloc was formed. 

Here are all the key things POLITICO learned during the EU-Canada meetings. 

Carney finally embraced ‘associate membership’

Initially reluctant, the Canadian prime minister came around by the end of the summit to endorse von der Leyen’s controversial label for the global alliance the EU and Canada are building. 

Carney set a six-month deadline to firm up the ground rules of what “associate membership” is, trialing an induction process that could be a model for other non-European countries.

“With Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member, in the coming months we will determine the full substance, scale and scope of this new form of membership,” he said Friday. 

Carney added he will meet periodically with von der Leyen to track progress, including a return trip for the College of European Commissioners to meet with their Canadian counterparts in March.

Got minerals

Both Canadian and EU officials are walking away from the summit with at least one major win: the framework agreement signed between the European Investment Bank and Canada that will open up the bloc’s lending arm to Canadian critical minerals crucial for future tech. 

That means batteries, circuit boards and semiconductors, which all require lithium, nickel, cobalt and other critical raw materials that, as of now, the EU is largely dependent on China to score.

The deal helps wean the Europeans off a politically volatile critical minerals dealer, for a more reliable Canadian supplier. 

The agreement does not immediately unlock funding for specific projects, but it supports pathways for future investments in Canadian mining and helps link the bloc’s supply chains with Canada’s.

Canada’s energy ambitions still point east

Critical minerals aren’t the only Canadian natural resource on the menu for Europeans. 

Carney has said he wants to make Canada an “energy superpower” and leverage huge stores of oil and liquefied natural gas in his country for export. The only problem: Most of it is in the western province of Alberta, far from Europe.

But the summit concluded with a commitment by both sides to a “long-term feasibility study” on exporting LNG to Europe via the east coast or Arctic ports closer to the bloc. 

“There’s also a huge opportunity in terms of bringing some of the fossils and gas from Canada to the EU,” said a Commission official, who was granted anonymity to talk about sensitive diplomatic negotiations. “The old infrastructure in Canada was built north-south for historical reasons, but now there is talk of starting to build east-west.”

Making nice with Washington? Don’t hold your breath.

As Europeans and Canadians preached deeper ties, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) was there doing damage control.

Welch, whose state is a little over an hour’s drive south of Montreal, spent Thursday reassuring business leaders that U.S. relations with Canada and beyond can, some day, get back to normal. When exactly, he couldn’t say for sure.

During his trip, Welch met with Quebec Chief Trade Negotiator Pascal Paradis, tourism industry leaders, businesses and manufacturers nailed by tariffs, and hit up a Eurasia Group lunch.

Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections could offer a waypoint to warmer relations. But Welch loaded his optimism about Democratic Party fortunes with caveats.

“I think we’ll be successful, but you’ll still have a president who abuses his authority and acts in arbitrary ways,” he said. “It’s not like I can give any assurance that things are going to change.” 

Unspoken in the communiqué: China

Canada and the EU pledged deeper cooperation on pumping more European money into the mining, production and refining of critical minerals, a response to China’s dominance of the global market for those minerals. But the final summit communiqué steers clear of naming specific countries. 

Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty was more candid.

“China has been vacuuming up as many critical minerals as they can throughout the world, particularly in the African continent, cutting deals, usually infrastructure for critical mineral deals. That could be a soccer stadium, for example. It could be a light rail system,” McGuinty told POLITICO at the summit Friday.

“It turns out that Canada’s got a huge amount of critical minerals, and basically all 10 of the 10 critical minerals on the short list for NATO, which the United States is also aware of. We’re going to not only exploit, but we intend to move to transform,” he said.

The common language: Sovereignty

Outside the summit, many Montrealers were oblivious to the landmark meeting taking place in the city. Inside, the vibe was existential.

The trio of leaders — Carney, von der Leyen and Costa — invoked individual and collective sovereignty as reasons to pursue a closer alliance to weather “new storms” stoked by climate change, challenges to democratic norms and the weaponization of trade. Carney has notably claimed concerns about encroachment on Canada’s sovereignty as a reason to walk away from trade talks with the Trump administration. 

“Today is about sovereignty,” Carney said. “We’re building the industries and infrastructure that underwrite our collective security.”

Quebec wanted a seat at the table

The summit came to Montreal weeks after Quebec — the French-speaking province in Canada that hosted the summit — elected a separatist government. Quebec shares powers with Ottawa and had its own seat in the CETA trade talks with the EU over a decade ago; and it had sought a similar role at this summit. 

But Ottawa refused to let new Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon address the summit, so he boycotted it, complaining he was being asked to “serve shrimp cocktail.” 

Carney accused him of leaving “an empty chair.” It stayed empty, even though six former Quebec premiers came to dinner.

The Europeans did not escape unscathed. The Quebec press panned von der Leyen’s English-only speech on the opening day as a faux pas in Canada’s largest francophone metropolis. Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera did little better, telling Radio-Canada in French that, for Brussels, summits like this are between national governments.

Bagel diplomacy

In a town where the original heated rivalry persists between two bagel shops, von der Leyen couldn’t resist picking a side with a photo-op at St-Viateur. 

Sorry Fairmount. 

]]> en Tusk-Nawrocki battle escalates as chief judge is ousted from Poland’s top court https://www.politico.eu/article/tusk-nawrocki-battle-escalates-chief-judge-ousted-from-polands-top-court/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 21:12:50 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9249705 Poland’s constitutional court descended into turmoil Friday evening as judges barred from hearing cases moved to oust the institution’s nationalist-linked leadership, sparking accusations of a coup and tense protests.

Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge with the court, ordered its president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy to be suspended for a month and announced she was taking charge. Święczkowski rejected her authority, accusing those involved of a “coup d’état,” while his deputy was turned away at the building’s gates.

The showdown marks an escalation in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s struggle to undo the judicial overhaul carried out by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) former government. During its eight years in power, PiS filled the Constitutional Tribunal with its appointees, including Święczkowski and his deputy, placing it at the heart of Poland’s confrontation with Brussels over the rule of law.

Outside the tribunal, protesters clashed with police, who said objects had been thrown at officers and three people detained after climbing over the court’s fence. Police said they had deployed to maintain security following warnings of threats to judges and staff, but had not entered the building.

PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński took part in the protest and tried to force his way into the court building. He accused Tusk of staging a “coup” against the court and turning Poland into a “police state,” and demanded presidential intervention.

President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally and rival of Tusk, interrupted his official trip to Senegal, declaring, “At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.”

Tusk was defiant. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote on X. “After years of PiS lawlessness, it’s a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.”

The tribunal, which can strike down legislation, helped impose a near-total abortion ban under PiS and challenged the supremacy of EU law. Last December, the EU’s top court ruled that it failed to meet European standards of judicial independence.

But efforts to change the court’s makeup have met resistance. Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority. They took their oaths in parliament instead, but Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek blamed the turmoil on Święczkowski, who he accused of turning the institution into his “private fiefdom” and preventing newly elected judges from doing their jobs.

“And now the judges have spoken,” Żurek told POLITICO.

Żurek, who also serves as Poland’s prosecutor general, said he submitted five requests to lift the immunity of Święczkowski and his deputy, backed by 50 volumes of case files. He defended Korwin-Piotrowska’s move as a decision by a legally appointed judge, insisting that the government had nothing to do with it.

]]> en Mark Carney puts deadline on EU ‘associate membership’ push https://www.politico.eu/article/mark-carney-puts-deadline-on-eu-associate-membership-push/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 30 Oct 2026 19:11:14 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9247929 MONTREAL — Canada embraced the European Union’s offer of “associate membership” after a two-day summit at which Brussels and Ottawa gave themselves until next June to work out what their new relationship will look like.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s endorsement of the proposal by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen followed weeks of hesitation, a hostile response from U.S. President Donald Trump and pushback from EU heavyweight Germany.

“In the coming months, we will determine the full substance, scale, and scope of this new form of membership,” Carney told a press conference on Friday at the end of the two-day summit at the Port of Montreal. 

“Today, we move towards associate membership for Canada,” Carney said, describing it as “the deepest possible partnership short of accession.”

The two sides have set a June 2027 deadline to determine the terms and boundaries of their intensifying relationship — an alliance that comes with a payment schedule. Carney danced around a question pressing him on how much associate membership will cost the Canadian public.

“We don’t view this as paying, personally,” Carney said, stressing the alliance as a “positive” project.

Von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa, standing either side of Carney, presented the experiment as a necessary survival strategy to thrive in an increasingly dangerous world.

“The concept of an associate member is uncharted territory but we have the ambition, trust and creativity to shape it together,” Von der Leyen told reporters. “To be crystal clear, this is not a partnership against anybody, but for our common strength.”

Canadian government officials who spoke to reporters after the press conference confirmed legislation won’t be necessary to legitimize Canada’s EU associate membership status.

“Our relationship is so special that we want to create something new — to go beyond a simple association, everything short of a full EU membership,” said Costa, pitching a new model for non-European countries to integrate more closely with the bloc. “Our association will be the closest, deepest and most unique of its kind.”

Irritants persist

Despite the upbeat rhetoric, some longstanding trade disputes remained unresolved after the summit.

Carney told reporters the two sides had reached an agreement on carveouts from a landmark EU anti-deforestation law, but Canadian government officials subsequently walked back his assertion.

The issue remains part of ongoing trade discussions, one official said, noting progress in addressing what Canada views as flaws in the legislation. The officials were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic and trade negotiations.

Another irritant has been whether Canada would qualify for “Made in Europe” status under the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act, a landmark measure that would seek to channel public procurement spending in sectors ranging from green energy to automotive toward locally produced goods. 

Von der Leyen said the regulation proposed earlier this year by the Commission foresaw including Canada as a free-trade partner, but added that it was now subject to review by EU lawmakers and governments.

“The Industrial Accelerator Act has been proposed by the Commission to include all countries with whom we have free-trade agreements. So automatically Canada would be in,” she said in response to a question. 

“Of course now the proposal has to go through the co-legislative process. But our proposal is very clear in including Canada.”

Despite months of preparations, the summit itself was chaotic, with agenda details confirmed at short notice and bilateral meetings split between two locations. The informal arrangements were intended to encourage more face time between EU commissioners and Canadian ministers, who are set to see much more of each other.

Canadian ministers have been invited to attend more meetings with their EU counterparts as part of a plan to deepen political alignment. Recent participation by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu in informal EU meetings has served as a trial run.

Carney himself is expected in Dublin in two weeks, having accepted Costa’s invitation to join an informal European Council meeting.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sat, 31 Oct 2026 01:09:52 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 [Interview] Canadian scholar Henry Giroux on ‘gangster capitalism’ and why he supports Europe’s student revolts https://euobserver.com/245348/interview-canadian-scholar-henry-giroux-on-why-europes-student-protests-are-a-revolt-against-gangster-capitalism/ Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245348 Dr Henry Giroux has watched student revolts in Europe and is cheering them on. The scholar of critical pedagogy says ‘gangster capitalism’ is allowing the far-right to thrive and that culture is threatening democracy itself.]]> Across Europe, young people have taken to the streets to demand improved education and voice frustration at generational and structural inequalities.

From Canada, Dr Henry Giroux has watched protests unfold and is cheering them on. Speaking with EUobserver, the scholar of critical pedagogy analyses the root causes of mass discontent. He discussed the global fight for democracy and warns ‘gangster capitalism’ has enabled the far-right to thrive.

You gave a speech in which you said widening inequalities are hollowing out democracy, as well as rising authoritarianism and assaults on public institutions. At what point does a society stop being a democracy?

I think a democracy dies when you no longer have the apparatuses available to take seriously the fact that you can’t have a democracy without informed citizens.

You start seeing inequality translate itself into the criminalisation of culture itself: not simply an attempt to spread ideologies that depoliticise people, but ideologies that are geared at creating a fascist subject – somebody who’s unthinking, doesn’t really understand context or the problems their lives are basically engaged in. Such a person turns to educational institutions – what I call pedagogical regimes of terror – and to communities of hate and bigotry.

Read more

One-in-three European voters now support an authoritarian or populist party, new research reveals

But where the left has really failed around this question is that education is central to politics – it’s not just about schooling, it’s embedded. The most powerful educational institutions today are cultural apparatuses like podcasts, X, or other social media. These are powerful regimes for telling stories that normalise inequality, attack the welfare state, unions, and all those things that make a democracy viable.

When I talk about democracy and education, I don’t ask: ‘What is good educational policy?’. I think the real question is: ‘What kind of education does a democracy require?’

It’s a conversation about power. Who controls the apparatuses of education? What kind of agents are they trying to create? What kind of values are they justifying?

All we have to do is look at what’s happening all over Europe, with respect to these student revolts. There are differences in these revolts, but the overarching connection is that young people are saying, ‘We’ve had enough of gangster capitalism. It’s destroying our lives.’

You can’t have a democracy when it goes after the welfare state. I listen to the French leaders saying things like, ‘Oh, the debt is terrible now. It’s off the charts.’ Well, you know what isn’t off the charts? The growth of money concentrated in the hands of relatively few people. And at the same time, it’s off the charts at the expense of the welfare of students, and others struggling to pay their bills. 

Read more

French school protests to continue, after prime minister ignores demands

You often use the term ‘gangster capitalism’, which is quite strong. Can you define it?

Gangster capitalism concentrates wealth in relatively few hands at the expense of any institution that would make democracy possible because it’s more concerned about the belief in the ability of markets to solve all problems. And it seems to me that it does a few things that we need to talk about.

]]> No extra funds for biodiversity at UN meeting, as vast majority of EU natural treasures left unprotected https://euobserver.com/246078/no-extra-funds-for-biodiversity-at-un-meeting-as-vast-majority-of-eu-natural-treasures-left-unprotected/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:03:39 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246078 Spending on repairing damaged ecosystems would need to rise fourfould, to almost $300bn to meet the natural protection goal countries set in 2022, a recent UN report found.]]> Spending on repairing damaged ecosystems would need to rise fourfold to almost $300bn (€269m) to meet the natural protection goal which UN countries set in 2022, a new report has found.

Some 250m hectares of natural ecosystems, or an area the size of Kazakhstan, is currently under protection to let it regenerate, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) study.

Presented at the biodiversity conference in Yerevan on Thursday (29 October), the authors said the result was “encouraging,” though it still amounted to only 34 percent of the goal environment ministers from across the world had set themselves for 2030.

At sea and in freshwater ecosystems, the situation was very different, with only 11m hectares protected.

Read more

Europe can’t lead on nature at COP17 while cutting biodiversity cash at home

Protecting natural areas degraded by human activity, such as pollution or overfishing, is key to preserving local species and biodiversity.

UNEP says restoring even 15 percent of priority areas would mean six in 10 species projected to go extinct could be spared.

And while nature restoration is key for food and water security, it is also important for climate resilience, the European Environment Agency (EEA) spokesperson told EUobserver.

The UN agency’s report is the first to gather data for land and water environments and evaluate progress in biodiversity conservation targets there, just as two weeks of negotiations at the biannual ‘COP 17’ meeting close on Friday.

Read more

‘Cementing over our own future’: Europe’s nature loss is 600 football pitches daily

We are “still not restoring nature at the scale or speed required,” said Inger Andersen, UNEP’s executive director, in a statement, urging countries to step up their efforts by the 2030 deadline.

The summit is to conclude with plans for the next four years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway, but significant financial commitments remain unlikely.

Jutta Paulus, a German Greens MEP representing the European Parliament at the conference, said “chronic underfunding” of biodiversity protection is the “main obstacle on our way to food security, a functioning economy and prosperity.”

In terms of ocean restoration, the EU needs “significantly greater investment in restoration, monitoring, and enforcement” to ensure real effects, saaid Nicolas Fournier, campaign director at Oceana in Europe, a marine protection NGO.

“Restoring an area with public money only to allow destructive activities to continue is not restoration – it is a waste of public resources,” he told EUobserver.

In the EU, protected areas amounted to 26 percent of land in 2024, and less than 14 percent of the sea area in 2023, according to EEA data.

To reach the 30 percent target by 2030, member states have to develop national plans, reviewed by the commission and the EEA.

]]> Belgian parliament to vote on divisive new law allowing police raids on people’s homes, if they are suspected of harbouring an undocumented migrant https://euobserver.com/246021/belgian-parliament-to-vote-on-divisive-new-law-allowing-police-raids-on-peoples-homes-if-they-are-suspected-of-harbouring-an-undocumented-migrant/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 15:45:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246021 “The Belgian government may call them ‘home visits’, but that doesn’t change what they are: police forcibly entering private homes and traumatising families and children to arrest people", said one critic of the bill. ]]> Belgium is pressing ahead with a new bill allowing police to potentially raid a person’s home suspected of harbouring an undocumented migrant.

Set for a vote next Thursday (4 November) in Belgium’s parliament, the law paves the wave for similar provisions in the EU’s deportation regulation.

Although Belgium abstained in the vote on the EU-level law given internal objections over possible EU deportation facilities abroad, Belgium’s coalition government appears determined to allow authorities to force their way into homes.

Read more

Police will get powers to raid homes in new EU deportation bill

The new law, championed by Belgium’s rightwing migration minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt of the N-VA, has triggered widespread criticism.

A spectrum form human rights defenders to Belgian judges have issued multiple warnings that the law would potentially violate constitutional rights of those who host undocumented immigrants.

If a person is suspected of hosting an undocumented migrant deemed a security threat, then the police can enter their home between 5AM and 9PM and search through their documents and personal belongings even if children are present.

  • Confirmed Ukrainian military losses have exceeded 220,000, while the share of missing personnel is rising.
  • Ukraine lost thousands of personnel both during the Kursk region operation and in the battle for Krynky.
  • Following an unofficial pause, Ukraine has resumed attacks on Russian refineries — and with considerable success.
  • Ukraine claims to have hit another two Russian Su-34 aircraft. Russia has suffered too many such losses over the past two months.
  • Videos of the day: a report on a soldier who operates drones with his chin; a welcome for Ukraine’s ombudsman in Oleshky.

    • In Ukraine Battlefield update, we report fairly regularly on the enormous losses suffered by Russian soldiers. The Ukrainian command publishes them daily. This figure is probably inflated, but it shows a trend. And that trend shows that October is already the bloodiest month since the start of the full-scale invasion.

    Verified figures are also published by the independent Russian outlets Mediazona and the Russian BBC. The problem is that they can only verify these figures retrospectively, while the Russian state is placing ever more obstacles in their way as they seek information about deaths.

    As Dima Treshchanin wrote, the author of the project, they are currently working on deaths from the summer of 2025.

    However, we devote less attention to Ukrainian military losses. Unfortunately, these are also high.

    However, when independent analysts examined its data, they found it credible. Each entry links to a source of information on a Ukrainian website, mostly an obituary, and the analysts did not find many duplicates either.

    Ukrainian losses are tracked by the UA Losses project. It is an anonymous website and its background is a mystery. Ukrainian authorities describe it as propaganda and have blocked access to its website in Ukraine.

    UA Losses has updated its data in recent days.

    ]]>         Culture groups ‘on their knees’ after 30% funding cut proposed in EU’s next budget https://euobserver.com/245996/culture-groups-on-their-knees-after-30-funding-cut-proposed-in-next-eus-budget/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:05:12 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245996 Culture, media and rights groups demand that European capitals oppose a 30 percent cut to €8.6bn proposed for AgoraEU in the EU's next long-term budget. “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP.]]> “Thirty percent, we won’t consent” chants echoed across Schuman roundabout in the Brussels European quarter this week, as culture, media and journalist workers demanded that national leaders halt plans to reduce cash for culture in a protest on Thursday (29 October).

    Representatives from European rights forums, culture groups and a journalism federation gathered in a bid to keep enough money flowing to their organisations.

    “There’s a very grim future if we continue with these cuts,” said Rhys Nugent of Culture Action Europe, one of the protest’s organisers. “These sectors are already on their knees.”

    The demonstration came after EU leaders discussed giving less money than previously proposed to AgoraEU, an umbrella for culture, media, democracy and rights initiatives, within the EU’s 2028-2034 budget.

    30% less for culture

    Reacting to the EU Commission’s proposal to give AgoraEU €8.6bn under the long-term budget, the EU parliament’s budget committee asked to ramp this up to €10.7bn.

    But national capitals have not agreed to either proposal.

    Instead, the Irish presidency of Council presented a plan earlier this month (October 10) to allocate €5.3bn for AgoraEU –  representing a 30 percent cut to the commission’s proposal. It was responding to pressures for frugality from some member states.

    National capitals are yet to finalise a budget agreement.

    Read more

    Pressure mounts on EU leaders to strike a budget deal by December

    “They picked culture because they think it’s an easy target, but it will affect journalists, artists and NGOs who are the backbone of our democratic society” said Nela Reihl, a German Green MEP and chair of parliament’s culture and education committee.

    “If this goes through, people will wake up one day and ask: why are my rights not protected? Why has that film festival disappeared? Where has my local publisher gone?” she said.

    “These cuts will save only a tiny percent of the EU budget but cause massive damage to these sectors,” added the German lawmaker. 

    What could be chopped?

    AgoraEU is a new umbrella for Creative Europe and Citizens, Equality, Rights and Values (CERV).

    Protest organiser Nugent said Creative Europe “funds everything from small theatrical productions to large cooperation around Europe.”

    He pointed to Flow, an Oscar-winning film, Europa Cinemas, and Culture Moves Europe as examples of the types of bodies that could be affected by a lack of EU funding.

What's in them?]]> One could ask, what might politicians from a far-right party — as the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution describes Alternative for Germany (AfD), write to one another?

    More than 400,000 emails exchanged by AfD members between March 2013 and September 2026, effectively covering the party’s entire history, have appeared online.

    They were published by hackers from the Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets) organisation, who obtained 284 gigabytes of data, including minutes from meetings of the party leadership, payslips, strategic documents, membership lists and donors’ names.

    AfD and its enemies

    According to the Correctiv website, the material also includes election campaign plans, for example for the 2025 parliamentary election. Their authors describe how to reach potential voter groups. They describe the governing parties at the time as enemies.

    It is unclear yet whether all the emails are genuine, but the party has confirmed the leak. German media outlets with access to them estimate that assessing the information could take months.

    It is already clear that the emails offer an insight into how Germany’s currently strongest political party operates and how it approaches certain issues, including neo-Nazism.

    The media are gradually uncovering messages that are uncomfortable for AfD’s leading figures, including its co-chair Alice Weidel.

    One of the most striking findings is that in private she was not as radical as she liked to portray herself in public. And, according to German media, the difference is considerable.

    The leaked emails also suggest how the German party sought to forge closer ties with the US conservative Maga movement and president Donald Trump, whom it saw as a potential ally.

    In foreign policy, they also point to deeper links with Russia than had previously been known.

    Thousands of emails could also play a role in a potential ban on the party, which is not yet decided upon but is being debated in Berlin.

    So what have they revealed?

    What had not previously been known about relations with Russia

Survivors onboard an NGO rescue ship recount what they lived through, while Brussels sets its eye on a new migration facility in authoritarian-led eastern Libya.]]> When Sulaiman saw the Humanity 1 approaching, he thought to himself: “if they are Libyans, let me die. I will not go back there.”

    The 25 year old Nigerian man is one of many rescued by the German NGO SOS Humanity on Tuesday (27 October) to have escaped living hell in Libya, at the hands of a regime paid by the EU to keep migrants away from its borders.

    “I was in prison for one year, for no reason,” said Sulaiman, whose name has been changed to preserve his anonymity. “Any time in the morning they come to distribute food, there are beatings. No one lets you go without a beating,” he told EUobserver.

    Every day he’d subsist on one small slice of bread in “a cage for 100 people, where there are all skeletons,” he described with tears in his eyes. 

    Sulaiman had tried to leave Libya twice before on small boats, but each time he’d been pulled back to land by violent militias, one of whom he described to be an ‘official’ authority. 

    Data from the International Organisation for migration (IOM) and the UN found over 200,000 people to have been illegally intercepted in the central Mediterranean and returned to Libya since 2016. 

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    And like many other search and rescue organisations, SOS Humanity’s own work has been significantly impeded by Libyan groups – whether they be the so-called Libyan coast guard or paramilitary groups known for hijacking small migrant boats in open sea to rob everyone on board and pull them back to illegal detention facilities.

    Men, women, families with children, and unaccompanied minors alike are kept in prisons until they can pay their way out.

    “I lied, and told my family I was in Tunisia,” a young boy from Sudan told EUobserver. 

    “I knew my mother couldn’t take it, knowing what would be happening to me in Libya,” he said, after having been rescued by SOS Humanity alongside 27 others in the early hours of Tuesday. He is one of 10 children aboard traveling alone.

    ]]>         Listen: Why is the EU introducing a new €2 charge on parcels? https://euobserver.com/245922/listen-why-is-the-eu-introducing-a-new-e2-charge-on-parcels/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:36:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245922 From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below:

    From this Sunday, the EU is imposing a new €2 charge on parcels coming from outside the bloc. It comes on top of the €3 charge on small parcels announced in June.

    So why is the EU doing this, and what difference will it make? Let’s start with what’s changing.

    From this Sunday, there will be a €2 tax on each product category contained in a parcel coming from outside the EU. This ads up to the €3 tax on small parcels introduced in June this year. So for a parcel of less than €150, you can already count a €5 charge, and that’s if your parcel contains just one category of item.

    Say you order four different garments from the Chinese platform Shein. The total charge comes to €20.

    Officially, it’s the sellers who are supposed to pay, not consumers. But in practice, they pass the cost on to customers one way or another.

    So why this second charge? The €3 charge adopted in June was meant to tackle the flood of small parcels coming from companies like Temu and Shein.

    Parcels of very low value, often just a few euros. And that’s not an exaggeration. According to Kristian Vanderwaeren, Belgium’s head of customs, the average value of a parcel before the charge was around €5. And that’s an average, so imagine the number of parcels worth less than €5 that literally come from the other side of the world.

    Read more

    Listen: Who will benefit from the new €3 tax on small parcels?

    Until now, parcels worth less than €150 were exempt from customs duties. That was a big hole in customs revenue. And at the same time, customs officers had more and more parcels to process. Hence the €3 levy.

    Now the new charge is different. It applies to all parcels, not just the smallest ones. Its goal is to raise revenue to cover the cost of checks. Because if the EU wants to fight fraud and make sure products on the market are safe, customs controls have to increase. And that takes time, and therefore money.

    We don’t know yet exactly how much the new tax will bring in revenues. What we know, even if the situation is not comparable, is what the €3 tax is starting to bring.

    Between June and September, the €3 charge brought in €364mln for Belgian customs. In just three months.

    Belgium is a major entry point for parcels bound for the EU, through the port of Antwerp and Liège airport. So we cannot duplicate that figure for other EU countries.

    Read more

    EU ‘open’ to curbs on imports of Chinese chemicals and machinery, after hybrid-car deal

    Still, over a full year, the two charges combined, on top of standard customs duties, should raise a significant amount. We can therefore imagine that countries outside the EU are not happy, especially China.

    Beijing describes the measure as protectionist. It also argues that the cost will largely be passed on to European consumers, which means, in its view, that the EU is shooting itself in the foot.

    But that is, to some extent, exactly what Europeans are hoping for. If Chinese products become more expensive, they become less attractive.

    Business groups agree. Comeos, the Belgian federation for trade and services, welcomed the charge as a response to unfair competition.

    Think about an everyday product worth less than €100. There is usually a big price gap between the Chinese version and the one made in Europe. When that gap is somewhere between €5 and €20, the charge can tip the balance. It may push you to buy local, or not to buy at all. In both case, this means less money getting out of the EU.

    And there are already signs it’s working. Since the €3 charge came in in June, the volume of small parcels arriving at Liège airport has dropped by 60 percent.

    The European consumer organisation BEUC has also welcomed the move, saying more border controls mean safer products.

    Something that is not immediately visible for citizens, but which has its importance.

    CIB is a manipulative communication tactic that uses a combination of authentic, fake and duplicated social media accounts to operate as an adversarial network across platforms such as X, Facebook or Bluesky.

    By coordinating their activity, these accounts can amplify particular messages and create an online impression that may not reflect the reality of public opinion.

    The tactic spread massively during Covid.

    In a paper entitled ‘Coordinated inauthentic behavior: An innovative manipulation tactic to amplify Covid-19 anti-vaccine communication outreach via social media’, Monica Murero wrote that such operations could be “one of the greatest threats to freedom of expression and democracy in our society”.

    But this distortion becomes particularly visible during elections.

    Indeed, with political momentum, spreading messages and content online can influence how voters perceive the strength of an incumbent government and the prospects of its opposition.

    Manufacturing political dominance

    The latest example is Serbia.

    Ahead of parliamentary elections in Serbia, the Balkan Free Media Initiative (BFMI), in collaboration with Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub, investigated how coordinated networks promoted former Serbian PM and president Aleksandar Vučić while undermining independent media.

    “CIB corrupts the public signal that democracies rely on to understand themselves,” head of research at BFMI Vanesa Valcheva told EUobserver.

    The findings point to a broader problem for democratic debate: online visibility can be manipulated to sustain an image of political dominance, even when the picture on the ground appears different.

    “Incumbents often try to look unbeatable to discourage opposition voters, reassure their supporters, and show outside partners that things are unlikely to change,” Valcheva said.

    Before the rise of these coordinated online operations, the digital space offered dissent more room to breathe.

    But nowadays, CIB networks can undermine the online space by repeatedly circulating messages that support a particular political interest and make it appear more widely shared than it is.

    And indeed, Vučić dominated the space on X and Facebook while the streets suggested otherwise.

The question that will outlast the result is not who wins, but whether the winner is willing to say no to prime minister Rumen Radev.

    Radev spent nine years as president with Iliana Yotova as his vice-president.

    He resigned in January to enter party politics and the office passed to her automatically; she has never been elected to it.

    In April his Progressive Bulgaria coalition won 131 of parliament’s 240 seats, and it now backs her for a full term.

    In the first round she led Andrey Gyurov, a former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition, by fewer than three points. Turnout was 22 percent – the lowest on record.

    Read more

    [Interview] Bulgaria’s presidential election becomes a test of Rumen Radev’s grip on power

    The presidency’s power to say no

    An elected majority is legitimate; so is cooperation between government and president. The constitutional risk begins where cooperation becomes an expectation of loyalty. An institution can keep every legal power and still lose the will to use it against political allies.

    In Bulgaria those powers are modest but real.

    A president can send a law back, and parliament must debate and vote on it again in public. Radev’s majority can pass it a second time with 121 votes, but the second vote is on the record.

    A president can also refer a law to the Constitutional Court, commands the armed forces, and chairs the Consultative Council on National Security, where the state assesses threats to itself.

    None of this can stop a determined majority. All of it can force one to explain itself.

    Black Sea test came late

    Meanwhile, since the start of October, at least seven merchant ships have been hit by drones off the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts.

    Both governments suspect Russian involvement, although responsibility has not been conclusively established; more than two dozen sailors are dead or missing.

    Read more

    EU unlikely to send Black Sea naval mission to repel Russian drone attacks on Ukrainian grain ships, despite Kallas’ support

    The first strike in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone came on 6 October. By then Yotova had been president for nine months without once convening the security council. She convened it the next day, after the opposition demanded it in public.

    It condemned the attacks and endorsed better surveillance and counter-drone defences: the right decisions, taken after the pressure rather than before the risk.

    Her legislative record points the same way.

    Yotova knows how to use a veto: in February she returned an Electoral Code amendment that limited the number of polling stations in countries outside the EU, calling it unconstitutional.

    That parliament was not Radev’s. Against his majority the test came in July, with the 2026 budget. The reformist and conservative opposition, the Podkrepa trade union and a petition with more than 32,000 signatures asked her to return it. Y

    Yotova argued that a veto would deepen financial uncertainty and promulgated the budget. On 20 October, the Constitutional Court upheld the budget as a whole but struck down two provisions inserted through it. The challenge came from MPs and the ombudsman, not the presidency.

    Nato dispute

    One policy dispute between the candidates concerns Article 4 of the Nato treaty. Gyurov wants Bulgaria to request consultations with its allies. Yotova initially opposed invoking it, but later acknowledged that coordinated action with other allies remained an option.

    Radev ruled it out on the day of the first attack because the ships were struck outside Bulgarian territorial waters. Yet Article 4 does not require an attack on national territory; it applies whenever an ally considers its security threatened. Whether to invoke it is a political choice. Territorial eligibility is not the obstacle.

    The test of an independent presidency is not whether it agrees with the government on Article 4. It is whether it would demand a public account of what the state knew, what it did and what went wrong, and publish it even when it embarrasses the people who put it in office.

    The European Commission’s rule-of-law report in July noted that most of Bulgaria’s regulators had their mandates renewed without becoming any more independent. A renewed mandate is not proof of oversight. Neither is a convened council.

    The same test applies to Gyurov, an independent nominated by the reformist parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, who told CNN on 23 October that Bulgaria needs a counterweight to its government. A counterweight that only ever pushes against Radev is a faction, not an institution. A president elected by the opposition would have to challenge the opposition too.

    EU leaders condemned the attacks at their 15–16 October summit, and Nato has announced additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones.

    Both are entitled to a clear account of what Bulgaria saw, when it acted and what failed.

    Brussels, for its part, should judge institutional independence not by formal procedures, but by whether those institutions are willing to challenge those in power. The question to ask is simpler: when did it last contradict the government?

    Radev has a mandate to govern. The next president will hold a separate one: to question, to return, to refer and, when necessary, to refuse.

    Europe does not need a Bulgaria that pretends it never makes mistakes. It needs one that can find and correct them before its sailors, its neighbours and its allies pay for them.

    The word “member” is already a problem, because it implies some form of participation in the EU. And the treaties limit that to a certain geographical area, which, as you can imagine, doesn’t stretch across the Atlantic.

    So what does the Commission actually have in mind? According to an EU official, associate member status would mean consulting each other even more on a number of policies: climate, energy, AI, security and so on.

    Canada could also join some EU programmes more automatically. Although in reality, it already takes part in several of them, such as Horizon, the research programme, or SAFE, the defence loan instrument. The same official says there would also be more regular meetings to coordinate positions.

    But all of this remains very vague. For many observers, von der Leyen’s proposal was above all a way to show the friendship between the EU and Canada, at a time when the United States is behaving in a threatening way.

    Now, what does Canada think of this? When von der Leyen made her proposal in her speech, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed it, as diplomacy and politeness require.

    Read more

    THIS WEEK: the EU’s new Canada offer, cash for farmers and Russia’s Lavrov returns to G20?

    Since then, according to Canadian media, he has avoided using the expression “associate member”. And in any case, Canada has no intention of joining the EU. It simply isn’t something it is interested in.

    So whether there are ways to deepen cooperation is, once again, still to be seen.

    The summit, will surely not bring answers or decisions on such a relationship.
    More time will be needed to discuss a new status, or leave it completely.

    In the meantime, the two blocs will sign what they call an “alliance for the future”. It is less binding and more consensual.

    That’s what bilateral summits like this are for: reminding everyone of existing alliances, or clarifying them in some cases. Both sides adopt a joint declaration, a document in which they try to announce shared projects and take common positions on major international issues.

    But as for associate membership, that will have to wait. 

    ]]>         Tinned food and three days of bottled water? Fine. But European citizens stockpiling ignores a grim factor: your neighbours will become your enemies https://euobserver.com/245385/tinned-food-and-three-days-of-bottled-water-fine-but-european-citizens-stockpiling-ignores-a-grim-factor-your-neighbours-will-become-your-enemies/ Wed, 28 Oct 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=245385 A friend of mine recently proudly showed me her cellar, stocked with three to four weeks of water and food. “Of course, we’ll be sharing it with the neighbours” she said.But the only thought in my head was “After three to four weeks of no food, no electricity, no internet and no water, you’ll be fighting your neighbours off, no inviting them in.”]]> My home government, the UK, last week somewhat belatedly joined the growing list of EU and European nations advising its citizens to stockpile essential supplies for a minimum of three days, in case of unforeseen (or initially unsolvable) crises.

    In doing so, London helped bring into the mainstream what until around a decade ago had been the preserve of nutty survivalist US “preppers” (colloquial abbreviation for the conspiracy loons in woodshacks in backwoods America, preparing for the return of Jesus Christ or a ‘commie invasion’).

    Instead, the topic has now become a nervously jokey staple of middle-class dinner parties.

    As the conversation wanders from what horrible disaster might befall society, from freak flooding, to nuclear war, to an internet blackout or poisoned water supplies, the talk rapidly becomes one of ‘so what’s in your box’?

    The UK list was a ‘success’ in that – unlike the early days of Covid – it didn’t result in mass panic buying, and empty shelves. But the mass panic is a point we’ll come back to.

      <title>The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/31/elon-musk-midterms-spending-visualized</link>
      <description><p>The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history</p><p>Elon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/jan/03/tesla-diner-elon-musk-los-angeles">Tesla Diner in Los Angeles</a>, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.</p><p>Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/31/elon-musk-midterms-spending-visualized">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Binance exchange says it will cover customer losses as it scrambles to freeze affected assets, with about $3bn located so far</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/30/crypto-heist-binance-who-did-it-are-investments-safe">Q&amp;A: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist?</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/30/tell-us-have-you-been-affected-by-the-binance-hack">Tell us: have you been affected by the Binance hack?</a></p></li></ul><p>The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.</p><p>Binance said it would cover all customer losses as it froze $3bn of the affected assets.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/29/binance-crypto-exchange-hack">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Tech sell-off drives US markets down by nearly $1tn after subpar earnings reports</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/30/tech-stocks-drop-earnings-report</link>
      <description><p>Big tech stocks falter as investors question whether billions being poured into AI can generate returns quickly enough</p><p>A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings from leading tech companies drove US markets down by hundreds of billions of dollars Friday. In total, the decline has knocked nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.</p><p>The S&amp;P 500, the index of the 500 most valuable companies in the US, fell by more than 1% Friday, losing hundreds of billions of dollars in market value. It was on track to erase its gain for October, even though it set its all-time high during the same month. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down even further, more than 3%, also erasing hundreds of billions in value. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell less.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/30/tech-stocks-drop-earnings-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US economy grows faster than expected but inflation rises to 3.7%</title>

      <description><p>Commerce department data contrasts with sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment as midterms loom</p><p>The US economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter while inflation accelerated in September, according to new commerce department data released on Thursday, less than a week before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.</p><p>Gross domestic product (GDP) increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the commerce department’s ⁠bureau of economic analysis said in its advance estimate of the third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/29/economy-growth-third-quarter">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Regulator demands companies explain how and why they charge different prices for the same product or service </p><p>The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is demanding some of the US’s biggest airlines, ride-share companies and retailers divulge how they are using algorithms and loyalty programs to target customers and drivers with different prices and wages.</p><p>Nine companies – Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart – were named in the inquiry, which comes after <a href="https://www.consumerreports.org/money/questionable-business-practices/instacart-ai-pricing-experiment-inflating-grocery-bills-a1142182490/">investigations</a> and lawsuits alleging consumers are charged different prices based on their buying histories and drivers <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/uber-drivers-claim-personal-data-used-to-manipulate-fares/">paid different fares</a> based on their personal histories.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/29/delta-uber-ftc-pricing">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/european-central-bank-chief-christine-lagarde-to-step-down-nine-months-early</link>
      <description><p>Possible candidate to run World Economic Forum departs ECB nine months early, saying she wants to speak her mind about world affairs</p><p>Christine Lagarde, the eurozone’s top central banker, has said she is stepping down nine months early to speak her mind about world affairs and confront the “misrepresentation of the truth”.</p><p>Ending months of speculation about her future at the European Central Bank, Lagarde said she would quit her role as president next February rather than October next year because the rules of neutrality that governed her job prevented her from influencing debate about financial and economics affairs.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/29/european-central-bank-chief-christine-lagarde-to-step-down-nine-months-early">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word.
