<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSat, 31 Oct 2026 15:26:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Jack Chambers ‘disappointed’ as WRC says public sector pay talks at ‘an impasse’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/31/talks-between-unions-and-government-over-new-pay-deal-finish-without-agreement/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/31/talks-between-unions-and-government-over-new-pay-deal-finish-without-agreement/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:52:29 +0000Talks between the public sector unions and the Government on certain aspects of a new pay deal have reached “an impasse”, the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) said on Saturday.

The prospect of a second national public service strike grew on Friday evening as talks between Government representatives and union leaders at concluded without agreement.

In a statement on Saturday morning, the WRC said it was requesting that the Government-appointed group led by Kevin Foley consider certain issues and “put forward a means of resolution”.

“Having engaged in intensive talks for 10 days, under the auspices of the WRC the commission is of the view that certain matters have reached an impasse and is requesting that the Government-appointed group consider those issues and put forward a means of resolution,” it said.

“All other matters under discussion shall remain with the WRC. As talks have yet to conclude, all discussions will continue to remain confidential to the parties.”

Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said he was disappointed by the progress.

“I am disappointed that, despite intensive negotiations over the last 10 days public service pay discussions have not yet delivered an agreed outcome,” he said.

“I recognise the efforts of all parties over recent weeks and thank the WRC for its role in supporting these discussions.

“Government remains committed to agreeing a fair and credible pay deal for workers across the public service that is also affordable and sustainable for the country.”

Speaking as the talks ended at about 11.30pm, Kevin Callinan, general secretary of Fórsa, said it had become clear that the gap between the two sides was too great to close at this stage and, with no further talks planned for over the weekend, he and the other trade union participants in the process would now brief the other public service unions on Monday.

“It doesn’t seem possible at this moment that we’re going to be able to reach an agreement that we could confidently put to our members in a ballot so our next step is to meet with our affiliate unions on Monday morning, where we’ll brief them on the negotiations, and decide on what comes next,” he said.

How can the public sector pay deal get over the line?

Asked if it was possible the two sides would be brought back together under the auspices of the Kevin Foley-led committee appointed to help resolve the outstanding difficulties that had originally prevented the talks getting started, Callinan said that was a matter for the WRC but that the unions would remain available and would attend any process initiated.

“But we really need to be confident that any proposals would be likely to be accepted by members of the ballot, and we’re a long way from that,” he said.

He said the union side had been consistent from the outset with regard to the issues that needed to be addressed by Government in terms of the gap between pay increases and inflation over the past five years, an increase for the second half of this year and measures to ensure members were protected against spikes in inflation over the course of any new deal and agreement.

A second national public services strike will be scheduled for Wednesday, November 11th, if no deal between the Government and trade unions on a new pay agreement is reached over the weekend, Callinan said earlier.

Callinan, who is also chair of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions’ public services committee, said the 19 unions it encompasses should meet on Monday to get an update on the talks and, if no agreement has been reached by then, to discuss taking further action.

He said the strike, which would again close the State’s schools and severely affect health, local authority and other services, would allow for demonstrations in Dublin and other big urban centres by more than 300,000 staff affected.

In an earlier update to the 100,000 members of his own union, Callinan said the talks had been “lengthy and at times heated” and that while a deal remains possible “the Government has yet to put forward a credible offer, and it remains to be seen whether it will do so”.

John FitzGerald: Across-the-board pay rise will do little to help fill key public sector posts

He said it remains unclear whether an agreement can be reached over the coming days.

Referencing the prospect of another one-day stoppage, Callinan told members: “If we fail to reach an acceptable agreement by the weekend, it leaves unions with no alternative but to escalate the action.”

Senior officials from the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform as well as the four union leaders participating in the main negotiations arrived for the latest session at 10am on Friday.

There had been some optimism that an agreement could be reached if the two sides pushed through the night on Thursday, but in the end it was concluded that their respective conditions were not close enough to continue past about 10pm.

Arrangements for a second national strike on November 11th have to be put in place early next week as seven days’ notice must be given.

In health, the required notice period is generally three weeks but the unions believe they are covered by the original notice of action served last month and the continuing work-to-rule.

The potential for another national stoppage may be viewed by the Government side as an attempt by the unions to leverage their power as the talks enter what one source described as their “crunch period”.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Cricut Maker 5 review: Home crafting levels up ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/31/cricut-maker-5-review-home-crafting-levels-up/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/consumer-tech/review/2026/10/31/cricut-maker-5-review-home-crafting-levels-up/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 05:55:00 +0000I am a serial hobby offender. It started off with knitting and crochet, then sewing and embroidery. Clay crafts, latch hook cushions, macramé kits - I have an unearned confidence that I can master any task and an unhealthy dependence on the Lidl middle aisle, which feeds the appetite for new materials and kits to try.

Some didn’t take. I made one lot of home-made bath bombs before sneezing into the ingredients. The soap-making kit has also remained unused, despite my best intentions and a social media algorithm that tries to steer me towards beautifully made creations. Some things are worth paying someone else to tackle.

But one thing that has stuck is the Cricut machine. If you aren’t familiar with the brand, Cricut has a range of digital cutting machines that help you create home-made cards or fabric hair accessories. You can slap a logo on a canvas bag (with a heat press) or customise some T-shirts with slogans and graphics. All you need is access to a laptop, tablet or smartphone that can run the Cricut Design Space software, and a bit of imagination.

The gateway drug is the Cricut Joy, the mini-machine that will tackle small projects and is compact enough to tuck away. But before long you progress to the Maker, which will take on all sorts of projects, whether you want to make personalised gift boxes, create your own stickers, personalise your clothing or create signs.

It cuts a wide range of materials, from fabric and paper to vinyl and wood. Add in a few extra tools, and you can engrave metal with it – once it fits through the machine – or deboss leather. Before you know it, you are fully kitted out with the complete range of tools, the heat presses for hats and mugs, and Cricut has officially taken over your life.

Cricut Joy 2 review: updated machine is a mini crafting powerhouse

The Maker 5 is the latest machine to hit the market. The updated Cricut will cut thicker material than before, which makes it more versatile and less frustrating to use. Despite that, it is more compact than its predecessors, which makes it easier to stash away. Cricut has ditched the lid and the small holder for tools on the left side of the machine to trim down the size, which is no real loss.

The first thing you notice about the Maker 5 is that there is no power button. You plug it in, and it switches on. On one hand, there is one less thing to mess around with; on the other, I now need to unplug the machine every time I use it to turn it off, which is awkward to get to. If you encounter a problem – a material gets stuck, for example – and the machine needs to be rebooted, you also have to unplug the power supply to restart it.

Getting started, though, is easy enough. Cricut’s Design Space software guides you through the entire process, registering the machine to your account and performing a test cut before unleashing you on the crafting world.

The first problem you might encounter is the sheer choice of things you can make. Home-made cards, cake toppers, decals for walls and windows, leather keyrings, hair bows – Cricut has a range of projects ready to make. Some of these are locked away behind Cricut’s Access subscription service, which will cost you an extra €125 a year but gives you access to images, fonts and thousands of ready-to-make projects, and gets you a discount on Cricut’s store.

Cricut Joy Xtra: The perfect introduction to craft cutting machines

You can also create your own project from scratch, either by designing it yourselfor through Cricut’s AI helper. You come up with the idea, and Cricut helps you make it.

Of course, the success of that will entirely depend on your idea. If you are a complete beginner, then you might want to temper your expectations about what you can achieve with a little imagination and some paper and glue. Start with something a bit easier than an elaborate gift box, for example.

You can use Cricut’s own smart materials – vinyl, cardstock, paper and so on – that don’t require a cutting mat to run through the machine. But to be more flexible and to keep costs down, having some compatible cutting mats on hand is a good idea. That way you can buy materials in your local craft shop (or Lidl) and it opens up a wider range.

As it is Halloween, the obvious choice was some spooky decor and accessories. Some window cling vinyl ghosts, a few Halloween-themed treat boxes; you get the general idea. It tackled all of them with ease.

The second important thing to know about the Maker 5 is that it is faster than its predecessors. I spend more time waiting for the machines to cut than I do assembling the final projects, so the difference was noticeable. It was also more reliable than my ageing Maker 3, with fewer jams and errors.

Good

The Maker 5 is fast, reliable, and more versatile than its predecessors. It cuts thicker materials, runs quicker, and if you are a beginner, it will hold your hand through the difficult early days of getting started. An AI assistant, powered by ChatGPT, will also help you with project assembly, helping you troubleshoot if something goes wrong.

Bad

If you are already a Cricut user, be aware that some accessories are not compatible with the Maker 5. For example, the scoring stylus is no longer an option; you can only use the scoring tool or wheel.

The pens that worked with older Cricut machines are also not compatible with the Maker 5, although the Joy pens are. Cricut includes an adaptor in the box now to make the pens work with older machines.

Everything else

Cricut Access is included for a month free of charge; after that you have to pay for the monthly or yearly subscription. I found it helpful when getting started, but if you are confident of designing your own projects, you may not need the extra expense.

Go for the Essential Bundle (€450, Harvey Norman) to make sure you have enough materials and tools to get started.

Verdict: Four stars

The Maker 5 is a versatile machine that helps you unlock your creativity. Christmas looks like it might be levelling up.

]]><![CDATA[Cork group linked to emergency accommodation centres doubles profit to €15m]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/31/cork-group-linked-to-emergency-accommodation-centres-doubles-profit-to-15m/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/31/cork-group-linked-to-emergency-accommodation-centres-doubles-profit-to-15m/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:01 +0000John Crean and Tony O’Neill’s Peppard Investments, which is involved in the provision of emergency accommodation, more than doubled its profit to €15 million last year.

The Cork-based group led by Crean and O’Neill has interests spanning property development, nursing homes and emergency accommodation centres.

Newly filed consolidated accounts for their group by Peppard Investment Holdings Limited showed their network of 23 Irish companies reported combined turnover of €29.2 million last year, an increase of 17 per cent compared with 2024.

The group’s pretax profits more than doubled to €16.5 million in the year after it received an additional €9 million of income from a joint venture involved in emergency accommodation in 2025 called Kintrona Limited.

Following a tax expense of almost €1.2 million, Crean and O’Neill’s group booked a final after-tax profit of €15.2 million, up from €6.1 million the year previous.

The pair behind the property development company elected not to pay a dividend during the year, but shared a remuneration package of €500,000.

The accounts showed that Peppard Investments expanded its Irish operation last year through the acquisition of controlling stakes in some companies involved in the nursing home sector, including BMC (Nursing Home) Limited, a firm linked to the Padre Pio Nursing Home in Holycross, Co Tipperary.

Peppard Investments also ramped up its construction project activity in the year, with work in progress by the firm rising from €11.6 million at the end of 2024 to €45.2 million by the end of last year. The firm’s net assets also rose to €37.1 million from €21.8 million.

The financial accounts did not provide details on what construction projects led to the firm’s work in progress rising to more than €45 million. Based on planning records, the company has permission to develop a number of residential projects in Macroom and Kilbrittain in Co Cork.

In recent years, several of the company’s subsidiaries have earned large sums from the provision of accommodation and services to the State’s International Protection Accommodation Services and housing for those who left Ukraine following Russia’s invasion.

Crean and O’Neill’s firm Next Week and Co Limited has operated the 108-bedroom Riverside Park hotel in Macroom and also ran the 230-bed property called Abbeyfield Hotel in Ballaghaderreen, Co Roscommon.

The latest accounts for the firm said it faces a risk that contracts it has signed to provide emergency reception, orientation and accommodation centres may not be renewed, which would lead to “a reduction in sales, margin and profitability”.

Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan, who now oversees the State’s efforts to provide emergency accommodation through IPAS, has previously said he would probe the value for money the State has received from private firms providing emergency services.

He said the Government’s approach would pivot towards State-run solutions in a bid to reduce the country’s reliance on private providers.

]]><![CDATA[Is Anthropic’s $100bn IPO a warning sign for investors?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/31/is-anthropics-100bn-ipo-a-warning-sign-for-investors/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/31/is-anthropics-100bn-ipo-a-warning-sign-for-investors/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000The biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history is coming, with Anthropic’s stock market debut on the way. Could it be a warning sign for investors?

Comparisons with 1999’s dotcom mania, when a flood of new listings hit the market, are common. The obvious counterpoint is that, unlike most dotcom-era hopefuls, companies such as Anthropic already generate billions in revenue, with soaring demand for their products.

However, 2026 leaves 1999 in the dust in one respect – the amount of money raised in public listings.

DataTrek Research’s Nicholas Colas notes 476 companies went public in 1999, raising $65 billion, or just over $130 billion (€116 billion) in today’s prices. Contrast that with SpaceX alone raising $85.7 billion when it went public in June. Anthropic’s IPO is expected to raise $100 billion.

All too many of 1999’s IPOs were duds, but it also included companies such as Goldman Sachs, UPS, BlackRock and Nvidia.

SpaceX falls back to Earth after IPO frenzy

Indeed, Nvidia’s subsequent success more than compensated for the many failures; one spectacular winner can more than make up for a multitude of Pets.coms.

Things were crazy in 1999 but the sheer number of offerings gave investors more chances to find long-term winners, says Colas. In contrast, today’s market “puts a lot of eggs in a limited number of baskets”.

And even if SpaceX and Anthropic – and perhaps OpenAI in 2027 – live up to the hype, enormous starting valuations leave less room for investors to hit the jackpot.

Additionally, mega-IPOs tend to be disappointing affairs, with JPMorgan data showing that shares in the 18 largest US IPOs underperformed the S&P 500 by a median 30 percentage points in their first year.

Anthropic says its AI technology ‘could pose catastrophic or existential risk to humanity’

Ominously, the S&P 500 itself returned a median of just 3 per cent in the year following these mega-IPOs, compared with a long-run average of nearly 10 per cent.

That is no guarantee of a downturn, but it suggests the biggest debuts may be a warning sign for the wider market.

]]>Andrej Ivanov<![CDATA[It’s inflation, stupid: Trump faces the wrath of US voters ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/31/its-inflation-stupid-trump-faces-the-wrath-of-us-voters/https://www.irishtimes.com/opinion/2026/10/31/its-inflation-stupid-trump-faces-the-wrath-of-us-voters/Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:00:00 +0000On Tuesday the United States will hold a referendum on Donald Trump. The Republican Party has become the Trump Party, which means the careers of dozens of Republican politicians are tethered to him. The party of Abraham Lincoln depends on a man cut from very different clobber. If the polls are to be believed, “The Donald” is over, with ratings the lowest ever for a sitting president heading into the midterms. Across a whole host of economic and foreign policy matrices, Trump’s support is dwindling.

If he loses, US politics could become even more divided, which is almost impossible to imagine. The divisions will be most acute within the Republican Party, which would undergo its second civil war in a decade. The first war was fought to get Trump in; the next one will be fought to get him out.

No one said this was going to end well. Indeed, the party’s civil war is unlikely to end when Trump leaves office. His influence is likely to mutate into something possibly even more divisive as he tries to make sure that his chosen Make America Great Again (Maga) successor maintains his legacy and keeps his sons out of jail.

Meanwhile, the US will be left with the largest debt burden in its history, which is being added to every year with a huge budget deficit funded by issuing yet more debt. While not quite a Ponzi scheme, the US is moving in the Ponzi direction. By paying the interest on the debt by raising yet more debt, even Washington is vulnerable. What happens to the dollar if the foreigners who are buying this US debt, and in the process help keep the dollar pre-eminent, decide to cut their positions before those positions become losses?

Medium-term worries about US debt splurges are becoming more acute by the week. But for Tuesday’s plebiscite, the immediate issue is prices, particularly petrol prices. To paraphrase James Carville’s “it’s the economy, stupid” maxim from 1992, in 2026, “it’s inflation, stupid”. Inflation has been rising in the US, squeezing the car-driving suburban middle classes. At the same time, the one thing that really makes Americans feel wealthy – the price of their homes – has been going in the wrong direction.

The median house price dipped to $419,250 in September 2026 (down 1.2 per cent year-over-year), marking 11 consecutive months of declines as sellers slash asking prices. About one fifth of all houses listed on the market have seen their asking prices fall in the last year. This affects the perception of wealth among the 61 per cent of Americans who own their own homes. The fact that the Democrats – a party in disarray – hold a 9-point edge over the Republican Party among likely voters, with 53 per cent of them saying they are voting or leaning towards the Dems, tells you how far Trump has fallen.

What’s going on?

The US is experiencing what economists call a K-shaped economy: the gains of the growth are going to the richest people, while those at the bottom fall behind. The reasons are that the tax system has been changed to reward those at the top and the stock market, owned far more by the richest Americans, has been soaring.

For example, over the past four years since the end of the pandemic, house prices have flatlined but the Standard & Poor’s 500 index is up 131 per cent. The profits from the US tech boom have largely ended up in the pockets of the already wealthy, while real wages have fallen and tariffs imposed by Trump have increased the price of imported consumer goods, squeezing the middle earner that bit more.

What happens in Israeli and US elections may reshape the Middle East

A lot, but not all of this, is Trump’s fault.

His war in Iran was a turning point. The first thing to know is you have very robust rights as a consumer in Ireland, and indeed throughout the EU.

If a fault emerges with a product within 30 days of buying or receiving it, you are entitled to cancel your purchase. Under your “short-term right to terminate a sales contract”, you can opt for a repair or, if you prefer, a replacement.

Your legal position is particularly strong during the first year of ownership, but your rights in relation to faulty goods can extend for up to six years if the product – such as a washing machine or TV – could reasonably be expected to last that long.

It is important to note that your contract is with the retailer, not the manufacturer, and it is the retailer’s responsibility to remedy faulty products.

Consumer law does not, however, cover ordinary wear and tear, or products that were misused or accidentally damaged.

Serious problems, if they arise, still have to be dealt with. For the first year, the law is generally on your side and assumes the fault was already there when you bought the product.

After that, the onus shifts to you to show the problem was inherent in the product rather than caused by wear and tear, misuse or accidental damage.

And this is where extended warranties or appliance insurance might begin to offer something extra.

There are, broadly speaking, two types of cover you’re likely to be offered.

Extended warranties usually offer additional repair or replacement cover, sometimes extending beyond the manufacturer’s guarantee.

Insurance policies, on the other hand, offer wider protection and that can include things such as accidental damage. Naturally, this can be more expensive, and protections can vary hugely so pay close attention to the details.

For something more robust such as a washing machine, you might decide breakdown cover is enough if accidental damage is less of a concern.

Our €1,399 4K TV, though, can easily be knocked from its stand, or the screen could get a whack from a sweeping brush or two kids playing catch. This is where an insurance policy might be an option.

Retailer Currys offers “tech insurance” for TVs in different price categories, ranging from €200 to more than €3,000.

For our €1,399 TV the cost would be €180 for a three-year package, and €280 for five years. Monthly payment plans are also on offer if you prefer to spread the cost.

For that, Currys promises to fix the TV within 14 working days and if they don’t meet that deadline, or they’re unable to repair the item, they’ll offer a replacement.

Their website says there is no limit to repairs and if the TV suffers repeated problems, you can seek a new one.

Similar plans are in place for laptops, tablets, cameras, home-cinema set-ups and satellite equipment.

Harvey Norman’s Product Care offers similar cover in two-, three- and four-year plans. It includes things such as “food spoilage cover”, which pays for up to €500 worth of food if a fridge or freezer fails.

Similarly, it offers cover of up to €150 for laundry expenses if your washer or dryer is out of service for more than 10 days after you notify it of the fault.

Are these plans worth it? That’s probably a question only you can answer.

As with any type of insurance, some people are risk-averse and will draw comfort from knowing an unexpected fault or accident will be dealt with. Others might decide they are better off keeping the money in their pocket and taking on the risk themselves.

The price of the appliance matters, but so, too, does your ability to absorb the loss if forced to buy a new item.

Replacing a TV that cost less than €500 might be irritating but manageable, particularly with second-hand options available. Having to find €1,399 – or north of €2,000 for a super high-spec telly – is a completely different story.

You might also want to consider your own track record.

Are you very careful, or are you living in a busy household with children and pets where accidents are more likely to happen?

And before buying any extra protection, make sure to check what it covers.

Currys’ policy, for example, covers sudden accidental damage and mechanical or electrical breakdown. It does not, understandably, extend to cosmetic damage, misuse, neglect or damage during severe weather.

Ultimately, the decision whether to buy will be a combination of your risk appetite, how much the product costs and whether your household budget could absorb the sudden shock of a full replacement.

]]>Bryan O'Brien<![CDATA[Breaking down the bill: where does the money you pay for electricity actually go?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/breaking-down-the-bill-where-does-the-money-you-pay-for-electricity-actually-go/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/30/breaking-down-the-bill-where-does-the-money-you-pay-for-electricity-actually-go/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Irish people pay more for their power than most other Europeans. But no matter how you weigh it, the actual electricity accounts for a far smaller share of your electricity bill than you think.

All in, electricity here costs families around 40 cent a kilowatt hour, the unit in which it sells to domestic customers. That is roughly the energy needed for a typical load in your washing machine. The EU average is 29 cent. Germany is the nearest to us at more than 38 cent.

But that 40 cent ends up going in multiple directions. Energy think-tank Trifecta Ireland estimates that costs other than the actual electricity consume 55 per cent of what Irish homes and industries pay every year.

Those costs range from the money required to get that electricity from power plants to customers to incentives for businesses to build those generators in the first place.

Consultancy Aurora Energy Research calculates that of the €1,583 that an average urban household paid in the 12 months to October 2025, €597, or 32 per cent, covered the price of the electricity, with two-thirds of the total going on associated costs.

Aurora bases its assessment on a home consuming 4,200 kilowatt hours a year, which is what the industry says a typical household uses over 12 months. Those figures pre-date price increases of between 8 and 11 per cent, depending on the supplier, which began to bite this summer. They will have pushed that €1,583 average past €1,700.

Surges in the price of natural gas, which is used to generate half of our electricity, was responsible for those hikes. The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine has pushed gas prices higher as supply tightens.

But the other costs are creeping up also. Last year, regulators approved plans by national grid operator, Eirgrid, and ESB Networks to spend up to €18.9 billion between now and 2030 on improving the systems that get electricity from power plants to customers. That increase could add up to €1.75 a month to household bills.

More recently, industry watchdog, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilties (CRU), confirmed that emergency generators installed as a backstop against short-term electricity shortages would remain in place up to February 2029. Customers will pay €229 million for this. That scheme will have cost those bill payers €1.44 billion by 2029.

Liberalised

Over the last quarter of a century, the Republic has liberalised its electricity market, merged it with Northern Ireland’s, introduced increasing amounts of wind and solar as it shoulders a large part of meeting the State’s climate targets and shut ageing power plants, all while expecting it to meet increasing demand from economic and population growth.

The policies and strategies meant to deal with all of that have left the State with an increasingly complex system, says Conall Bolger, chief executive of Trifecta Ireland.

“The system we have now wasn’t planned, it sort of evolved rather than being planned, and it’s become unwieldy,” he explains. “We tried to make it do something that it wasn’t built to do.”

Part of the problem is the national grid itself. Stephanie Unsworth, Aurora analyst and author of the consultancy’s recent report on affordability, points out it was built “back in the sixties and seventies”. “Everything then ran on oil and gas,” she says.

At that time, it was a question of connecting power plants, that ran constantly, to where there was demand. It was not designed to link remotely located wind farms than run intermittently to distant cities and towns.

Alongside this, University College Cork academic Paul Deane told the launch of Trifecta’s report this month, electricity is distributed to customers through a large network of copper wire strung on timber poles. This is a legacy issue, according to Deane, who noted that there is enough copper wire in the Irish system to run four times around the globe.

The upshot is that national grid operator Eirgrid is often forced to tell power plants not to supply electricity, even when it is available, as bottlenecks in the system mean it cannot reach customers.

Wind farms, including those in Northern Ireland, are worst hit. This is a double whammy for consumers as alternative suppliers must switch on or increase output even though their power may be more expensive than that of the company unable to operate. Customers pay for this through something called “imperfection charges”, which the CRU says came to €790 million over the last 12 months.

Eirgrid says it is using new technologies to increase its use of renewables and to store power. Following initial trials, it has begun using “dynamic line rating” which allows more effective use of the grid. The State company points out that a planned €18.9 billion investment, approved last year, will tackle many of the problems.

Customers also face a bill of €550 million to support gas-fired power stations when they are on standby to back up renewables, but not supplying electricity, and so not earning money. These “capacity payments” are an incentive to encourage developers to build these plants in the first place.

Unsworth notes that many of the extra charges are the price customers pay as they foot the bill for integrating renewables into a system designed for fossil fuel. He does agree that the plans by Eirgrid and ESB Networks to invest in the system over the next four years should help.

Trifecta, funded by the family of industry veteran, Eddie O’Connor, focuses on providing affordable, secure and clean electricity. Its report, What Can Move the Needle on Bills Before 2030?, assesses ways of cutting costs to the consumer in the shorter term.

Its CEO, Bolger believes that we need to step back and look at all elements of the system in their entirety. He argues that the needs of consumers got lost while government and State agencies increasingly added complexity to the system. But cutting bills in the absence of a major overhaul remains challenging.

Deane told the Trifecta launch that, in some cases, cutting €10 from bills could require spending of €100 million on the system.

Trifecta proposes 17 smaller measures that it says should add up to greater savings. They focus on more efficient use of the grid that takes more account of customers’ needs. More electrification of heat and transport should help, the organisation says. This is because many of the “non-electric” costs are fixed, so spreading the burden across more customers cuts individual burdens.

Unsworth agrees that more electrification is part of the solution, but with a different emphasis. Instead of focusing on “crazy” renewables targets, she advocates building power plants to meet demand while incentivising electrification, which would still allow the Republic to meet its climate targets. Aurora calculates that taking this alternative approach would cost consumers 20 per cent less by 2035 than if we continue with our current mix of strategies.

How your electricity bill adds up

Generation: This is the cost of producing the electricity we use. It is generated by burning natural gas, or by wind and solar farms, along with contributions from other sources, including imports and hydroelectric power.

This amounts to a lower portion of bills than most people assume. A recent report by Trifecta Ireland calculates it at 45 per cent across the board. A breakdown of charges for a typical home by consultancy Aurora Energy Research shows it came to €597 out of a total annual average bill of €1,583, or around 38 per cent, in the 12 months to October 2025.

Network: This is the cost of getting electricity from power plants to homes and businesses. Basically, it goes through two stages. The national grid takes the electricity direct from power stations, and the distribution network takes it from the national grid and transmits it to customers’ premises. This cost is itemised as a standing charge on electricity bills, generally coming to around one-third of the total.

Aurora calculates that this cost its typical home €443 last year. Energy industry overseer, the Commission for the Regulation of Utilities (CRU) is currently reviewing how these costs are allocated across electricity customers.

Public Service Obligation (PSO): This pays for schemes that guarantee prices for power produced by renewable power plants. Two account for most of this charge. The first is the Renewable Energy Feed-in Tariff, which guarantees older onshore wind farms €72 or €75 per mega-watt hour for their electricity. If the market price falls below that figure, customers make up the difference through the PSO levy. If the market price is higher, the renewable power companies keep any surplus.

The second is the Renewable Energy Support Scheme, which pays wind and solar farms prices agreed at various auctions. Customers make up the difference if the market price falls short but get a rebate if the market price tops the guaranteed amounts.

The CRU recently set the PSO at €6.12 for each household in total for the coming 12 months, a sharp reduction on what they paid between October 2025 and this month. The charge is itemised on domestic bills.

Imperfection charge: This is one of two big items not set out on your bill. It is the cost of bottlenecks on the national grid that prevent it from transmitting electricity generated in one place to where the customers are located. In this situation, national grid operator, Eirgrid, instructs the power plant to reduce output. The market compensates the supplier for this. At the same time, the grid may have to instruct other companies whose electricity can reach those customers to step in. Those companies are also paid for their power.

Industry organisations have been highlighting this problem for a while. Most often, it hits wind farms in the west or other locations far from the greater Dublin area, where demand for electricity is greatest.

One significant bottleneck is the continued absence of a planned high-capacity power line between counties Meath and Tyrone. This prevents wind farms and other suppliers in the North from getting their electricity to the South. All electricity customers share this cost. Overall, CRU approved €790.24 million for imperfection charges over the last 12 months. Aurora calculates that it added €67 to individual bills last year.

Capacity payments: These are incentives to suppliers to build gas-fired power plants. Wind and solar power are not available all the time so our system needs gas plants that can be switched on or off quickly to back them up.

As these power stations do not run all the time, their owners cannot recover their costs simply by selling electricity, so they receive capacity payments for ensuring that they are available to supply power, even when they are not doing so. All electricity customers also share this cost. The CRU allowed €550 million in capacity payments over the last 12 months. Aurora says it cost the typical family €75 last year.

Bear markets usually stem from tightening monetary policy that triggers a financial crisis, which quickly morphs into an economywide credit crunch and a recession.

Admittedly, the US had a bear market in 2022 without a recession. It was relatively short and shallow, making it an excellent buying opportunity. First, the US midterm elections will be next week. We wouldn’t rule out the possibility that the Republicans will maintain their majorities in both houses of congress. However, various polls strongly suggest they will lose the House of Representatives and maybe even the Senate.

Stock investors tend to favour gridlock in Washington. This is a feature of the US constitutional system of checks and balances, designed to reduce legislative extremes and the risk of an authoritarian government.

Another risk is that the midterm results could increase policy uncertainty by unshackling president Donald Trump. With or without congressional gridlock, the midterms could clear the way for further policy-driven volatility.

Second, the AI investment boom faces three big constraints: financial, physical and political.

Financial constraints led the recent AI jitters, as investors increasingly questioned whether the returns on huge AI investments would justify the spending and whether enough capital would be available to finance it all. The risk is that another round of intense fighting could push oil prices past the $120 level reached at the start of the war. Higher-for-longer oil prices would mean stickier-for-longer inflation, forcing the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates higher.

In this scenario, synchronised global bond-yield rises would continue, raising the risk that something breaks in the financial system.

]]>gorodenkoff<![CDATA[The career costs of non-competes: ‘Your star striker is sitting on the bench’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/30/non-compete-clauses-employment-law-work-rival-employers-united-kingdom-andy-burnham/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/30/non-compete-clauses-employment-law-work-rival-employers-united-kingdom-andy-burnham/Fri, 30 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Damien Couture remembers going through “seven, eight months of hell” with his family after he was sued by his former hedge fund employer for allegedly breaching a non-compete agreement when he left to join a rival.

Despite his recent legal ordeal, the French quant trader still believes the British government is wrong to plan to end the use of non-competes, a move that is supported by tech companies but has sparked a backlash across the financial sector.

“I’ve been on the bad side of this litigation,” Couture says. “But I one-hundred-per-cent agree that there is a need for non-competes in companies to protect themselves.”

The issue of non-competes has shot to prominence in the United Kingdom after prime minister Andy Burnham this month pledged to introduce legislation to ensure such clauses could “no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising start-ups and scaling firms”.

More than five million British workers have non-competes in their employment contracts that prevent them moving to a competitor for a period after leaving their job.

The clauses, widely used among financial and professional services companies such as hedge funds and banks, as well as tech groups, are intended to protect intellectual property and the investment companies make in training and developing staff.

They are a key tool for City firms to stop star traders, money managers and dealmakers from taking their clients and trade secrets to a rival.

“Non-competes can give ... comfort that people are not just going to walk out the door and join or set up a rival using the intellectual property they have gained at the company,” says Amy Bird, a partner in the employment team of law firm Clifford Chance.

But their use has broadened significantly in recent years – spreading to lower-paid roles such as care staff and fast-food workers – while the time periods they cover have extended to sometimes more than a year.

Workplace conflict is said to be costing Irish firms €239m annually. What can be done about it?

Portfolio managers at top hedge funds in London often have non-compete clauses requiring them to sit out of the market for as long as 18 months to two years before they can join a rival, while an analyst might have to wait a year.

Citadel, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, successfully lobbied last year for legislation in its home state of Florida to allow non-compete agreements lasting up to four years.

While highly paid fund managers often appreciate the chance to take time off and travel or spend time with their family, such lengthy non-compete periods can make top performers less attractive to other employers, limiting the opportunities to seek out better and higher-paid roles.

Workers are usually unpaid during the period in the UK at least, and their skills may fall behind those of their peers, particularly in fast-growing sectors.

Burnham said the clauses “stunt innovation and trap workers” because these “prevent the best really being energised and bringing that dynamism to the economy”.

The UK’s tech sector has criticised non-competes for making it harder for them to hire. More than 20 start-up founders recently wrote to Burnham to ask him to “ban lengthy post-termination restrictions”.

Alan Chang, founder of the $5 billion (€4.5 billion) energy start-up Fuse and co-signatory of the letter, says his company’s progress has been slowed because of the delay in hiring caused by non-competes and other employment restrictions.

Chang says his chief technology officer, Greg Wilk, was originally subject to an 18-month non-compete clause. This was reduced to six months of gardening leave – which differs from a non-compete period as the person remains a paid employee – before he joined Fuse because he was changing industry.

But Chang says the wait was still too long. “Let’s say [Wilk joined in] one month rather than six ... I think our share price [would] be worth a lot more ... And rather than us being in two markets, we [would be] in four markets.”

Jacomo Corbo, founder of $2.4 billion start-up PhysicsX, says he is currently negotiating a 15-month non-compete agreement to hire an employee, an experience that has made him consider recruiting more in the US where restrictions are less prevalent.

“In Europe ... on the whole, you find that these long notice periods and gardening leave are very prevalent,” he says. “The lack of liquidity means you end up refocusing a lot of that hiring on US hires.”

Edward Hughes, who had a three-month gardening leave after leaving Google DeepMind to co-found London-based artificial intelligence (AI) start-up Inherent, which co-ordinated the letter to Burnham, says restrictions risk leaving fast-growing companies a “generation” behind their Californian competitors.

People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers. What makes a great one?

“It’s a little bit like you buy your great striker and the Premier League season starts and all the other teams are playing and ... your striker is sat on the bench instead,” he says.

Burnham did not give full details of the reform he is planning, but said the aim was to free up hiring for innovative companies, including in the AI sector.

The UK is an outlier in having relatively few constraints on employers’ use of non-competes, although they must show a clause is reasonable to enforce it in court. Elsewhere, efforts to curb the use of non-competes have had mixed results: a long-standing ban in California has not stopped some employers writing the clauses into contracts, even though these cannot be upheld by law.

Spain can fine employers that use them wrongly; France requires companies to continue paying staff part of their salary during non-compete periods. Australia plans to limit their use to high earners.

Shivchand Jhinku, an employment partner at law firm Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer in Sydney, says an unintended consequence of restricting non-competes in Australia may be to benefit bigger companies that have more ways to compete for staff, such as the ability to pay more and offer better perks.

“Smaller businesses and start-ups, which often rely on non-competes as the only practical mechanism to protect their investment in key employees, may be less able to compete for talent,” he says.

Lawyers predict the curbing of non-competes in the UK may lead employers to use other tools to protect their intellectual property and delay the departure of employees. In their letter to Burnham, the tech founders also argued for the restriction of “extended notice periods and gardening leave”.

Another downside to non-competes is that disputes over the terms often result in costly and stressful legal contests.

Citadel, for example, this year launched a lawsuit against its former portfolio manager Daniel Shatz, who left to join UK rival Marshall Wace.

London-based quant trader Couture was sued by Jump Trading in 2023 after telling the Chicago-headquartered firm he was joining rival Verition Fund Management. The 41-year-old reached a confidential settlement with Jump that allowed him to continue working at Verition, but only after he had spent almost £1 million (€1.2 million) on lawyers to defend himself in court. “It was a huge stress,” he says. “Anxiety for the whole family went through the roof.”

Couture still believes non-compete clauses can play a valuable role, but thinks they should have a time limit placed on them by law. “The fact that UK law does not express up to what point they are reasonable makes it a matter to be determined by a judge, where individuals have to face deep-pocketed companies,” he says.

That comes as the bank prepares for a new president, chief economist and an executive board member in charge of market operations in 2027.

Faced with increasing risks to the growth and inflation outlook, the ECB needs to ensure the smooth transmission of its monetary stance and a smooth transition in leadership.

The ECB has been in similar situations before, but this time looks different regarding the inflation outlook, geopolitical context and personnel dynamics.

Energy prices remain elevated and early signs of the second-round effects of that on consumer prices are emerging. While underlying inflationary and wage pressures have remained contained for now, they have not eased either.

Candidates to replace ECB president Christine Lagarde

The latest ECB bank lending survey suggests banks are already tightening lending standards, while demand for new loans is weakening.

Higher borrowing costs and tighter credit conditions should reduce the need for further increases in policy rates, all else equal, but the ECB is facing a bigger communication challenge.

On the one hand, it has the appropriate toolkit to address financial fragmentation across the euro zone member states. In particular, ECB staff must be squarely focused on the repo market, a key transmission channel of monetary policy to the real economy, ready to intervene in case of stress.

From a technical perspective, preventing a liquidity crisis is the easy part.

Tweaking the TPI conditionality to make France eligible may be politically toxic in other countries.

Ideally, verbal intervention would suffice. The question is whether proverbial constructive ambiguity can work in France’s case – a communication strategy the ECB has long relied on to signal willingness to intervene while preserving flexibility.

These trade-offs come at a time when heads of state and government will need to agree on a large package of nominations for the bank’s executive board in coming months.

Bank president Christine Lagarde has now announced her departure. This will allow governments to decide on all executive board replacements before the French election. The changeover will inevitably raise questions about the direction of policy under the next leadership.

France is likely heading towards ECB support and a Marine Le Pen presidency

In that context, Klaas Knot’s self-described approach of “principled pragmatism” looks particularly relevant. The former president of the Dutch central bank and a contender for the top job argued that the European Central Bank would need to keep acting decisively to preserve monetary transmission in the future without becoming a substitute for fiscal or political action.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, the former governor of the Bank of Spain, is another strong candidate with the credentials and experience to run the ECB.

Both have been in charge during previous economic and fiscal crises. Whoever gets the job will need to strike the right balance between principles and pragmatism in the next one. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

  • The writer is head of strategy and macro research at Pictet Wealth Management
]]>Raimund Linke<![CDATA[Government considers early repayment of €8bn in post-crash loans]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/29/state-could-reap-90m-saving-from-early-repayment-of-post-crash-loans/https://www.irishtimes.com/ireland/2026/10/29/state-could-reap-90m-saving-from-early-repayment-of-post-crash-loans/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 09:55:42 +0000The Government is considering the early repayment of about €8 billion in loans secured in the aftermath of the economic crash.

It has been calculated that any such move could generate savings of €90 million to the exchequer.

On Wednesday, the Cabinet is understood to have agreed to the option of repaying loans earlier than scheduled dates over the next decade.

However, no final decision has yet been taken, and will ultimately depend on whether it considered to be financially beneficial at the time.

The plan would involve the repayment of loans either partially or in full of €8 billion originally secured under the European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism (EFSM) next year and in 2028.

The EFSM provided financial assistance from the European Commission to Ireland and Portugal between 2011 and 2014. The money was conditional on implementation of economic reforms.

Short-term loans were also provided to Greece under the arrangement.

Ireland holds just over €15 billion in EFSM loans. Should it decide to go ahead with the move, it is understood the Government would issue new debt to pay them off.

The plan as envisaged would see repayments, either in whole or in part, of €3 billion due to mature in 2032, €2 billion scheduled to be paid back in 2035 and €3 billion due in 2036.

The Government would not repay the entire amount at one time but would look at exercising the option agreed by Cabinet at points in 2027 and 2028, if it was thought likely it would lead to savings for the State.

In a statement on Thursday, the Department of Finance said that its Minister and Tánaiste, Simon Harris, had brought a memo to Government regarding potential early repayment of certain European Financial Stabilisation Mechanism loans.

“The EFSM was used to provide financial assistance to Ireland between 2011 and 2014 in the context of the financial crisis. Any repayments would be subject to engagement with relevant European Institutions to finalise the process,” the statement said.

Ireland originally secured €67.5 billion in bailout support from the EU, the IMF, Britain, Denmark and Sweden in a deal agreed in December 2010. Under the terms of that deal, the State is subject to post-programme surveillance until at least 75 per cent of the financial support is repaid.

These biannual review missions assess the State’s economic, fiscal and financial situation, ultimately to measure Ireland’s capacity to repay its outstanding loans

“Ireland originally borrowed €22.5 billion under the EFSM, with €15.3 billion currently outstanding,” the department said. “The proposal is to allow Ireland to repay up to €8 billion of these loans.”

“Any repayments would take place during 2027 and 2028. This provides the National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) with greater flexibility in managing the overall debt profile and would involve replacing existing EFSM debt with Irish sovereign debt.

“The NTMA will determine whether individual repayments are beneficial in relation to its management of Irish debt. No repayments would be made that would result in a financial disadvantage to the State,” it said

]]>PeskyMonkey<![CDATA[ECB pauses rate hikes as Lagarde announces early exit]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/ecb-holds-rates-steady-as-lagardes-departure-overshadows-decision/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/ecb-holds-rates-steady-as-lagardes-departure-overshadows-decision/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 13:17:20 +0000The European Central Bank (ECB) paused its run of interest rate hikes on Thursday at a meeting overshadowed by president Christine Lagarde’s announcement earlier in the day that she will leave her post next February, nine months before her term ends.

Her departure comes as the ECB battles a renewed surge in energy prices and as bond-market turmoil, particularly in France, threatens to dampen growth.

According to one report, Lagarde’s early exit is intended to give EU leaders time to select her successor before France’s presidential elections in the spring, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading in the polls.

“I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” Lagarde told reporters in Frankfurt.

“We have an obligation of neutrality” and “I don’t think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality,” she said.

Her remarks heightened speculation that she may be considering a return to French politics where budgetary concerns and political gridlock have sparked a bond-market rout in the final months of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency.

Lagarde’s tenure in charge of the EU’s most powerful economic institution has been shaped by the worst pandemic in a century, the bloodiest war in Europe since 1945, the biggest inflation shock in a generation and a trade war with the US.

Her announcement immediately set off a succession race with former Dutch and Spanish central bank governors Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernández de Cos seen as the front-runners.

ECB executive board member Isabel Schnabel will also leave her role one year early in January to take up a position at the International Monetary Fund while ECB chief economist Philip Lane’s term will expire in May.

Lagarde’s retirement plan overshadowed the ECB’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged. Policymakers kept the bank’s main deposit rate at 2.5 per cent, a move that markets had anticipated.

The bank has raised rates twice in the last five months as it combats the surge in inflation from energy prices. While there is concern that euro zone inflation may soon climb above 4 per cent, double the ECB’s target rate, rising bond yields are acting as a counterweight, allowing the bank to pause its monetary tightening at least for now.

Markets are still pricing in another rate hike in December and potentially another in the first quarter of next year.

“Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook,” the ECB said in a statement accompanying Thursday’s decision.

Lagarde said the possibility of a rate hike was discussed this week before policymakers opted to leave the deposit rate at 2.5 per cent, the upper limit of a range within which monetary policy is deemed to have a neutral effect on the economy.

While she played down the risk that inflation was broadening beyond energy, she cautioned that risks were skewed to the upside. That stands in contrast to the economy with growth across the euro zone’s private sector slowing to its weakest pace in ‌four months in October amid the upsurge in energy costs.

“Lagarde will probably bring the current rate hiking cycle to an end in December. That may provide her successor with some breathing room before any interest-rate changes need to be made,” Bloomberg Economics analysts David Powell and Simona Delle Chiaie said.

]]>Ronald Wittek<![CDATA[Minister for Finance has put PTSB board in ‘straitjacket’, minority shareholder alleges]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/minister-for-finance-has-put-ptsb-board-in-straitjacket-says-minority-shareholder/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/minister-for-finance-has-put-ptsb-board-in-straitjacket-says-minority-shareholder/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 14:17:39 +0000Minister for Finance Simon Harris “unequivocally” controls PTSB and has put the bank’s board “in a straitjacket”, a minority shareholder who is fighting to stop the bank’s acquisition by Austrian lender Bawag has told the High Court.

The Minister, who currently holds a 57.5 per cent stake in PTSB on behalf of the State, has benefited from “special, incredible rights” since the State paid €4 billion in 2011 to acquire a 99.2 per cent stake in the bank, “disapplying any rule of law imaginable” in the process, Piotr Skoczylas told Judge Michael Quinn.

PTSB’s “board cannot move a muscle unless the Minister approves it”, Skoczylas told the court, although “he has graciously allowed day-to-day control” to be operated by the bank’s executives.

Skoczylas is one of four PTSB shareholders – who the court heard own a combined 0.00287 per cent share of the bank – objecting to a “scheme of arrangement” to sell PTSB (Ireland’s third largest domestic bank) to Bawag for €1.6 billion – or €2.97 a share.

Skoczylas briefly questioned the constitutionality of the Minister’s status as PTSB’s majority shareholder.

“Everybody is acting on the basis that he is selling his shares lawfully,” he told the court, but “the legality of the ownership of his shares is subject to ongoing litigation”.

That issue, he said, was currently being considered by the Court of Appeal and he indicated a possible intention to refer it to the Supreme Court.

“I’m aware of the existence of other litigation,” said Judge Quinn, “but I have plenty to focus on in this case alone.“

Skoczylas described the arguments made by Kelley Smith SC, for PTSB, as “incongruous and grotesque” and said she had “failed to deliver ... [a] certain amount of respect” towards him required, given he is a former director of the bank.

He said Smith’s comment that he and other litigating shareholders own a combined 0.002 per cent of PTSB was “an attempt to belittle us” and “completely irrelevant legally”.

He said he was once “one of the largest shareholders” of the bank, before “the Minister removed me as a director”.

He argued the Minister for Finance enjoys additional rights not held by ordinary shareholders because the State has entered into contractual agreements with the bank. This resulted in unequal access to information during the consultation process upon the announcement of Bawag’s offer, he argued, and therefore the scheme should not be sanctioned.

He further argued a deed of partial release related to the Minister’s shares must be taken into account when sanctioning the scheme of arrangement, as, under that, the shares were released on the same day (as the deal was approved by an egm of shareholders) and further demonstrate the Minister’s special status as PTSB’s majority shareholder.

“These special shareholder rights” must “play a critical role in the court’s decision”, Skoczylas said.

Later in proceedings, Skoczylas claimed “the minister is currently placing his shares with Bawag now”, prompting Lyndon MacCann SC, counsel for the Minister, to object, saying there “is not a scintilla of evidence” of this taking place.

Skoczylas subsequently noted that MacCann’s fees in this hearing “are paid by me as a shareholder”.

“I have no idea whether or not this [sale of shares] was invoked”, he said. However, addressing Judge Quinn, he added: “I don’t have to prove to you, or anyone else, that it was.

“The threshold is so low that I simply have to prove that the right [to do so] exists,” he said. “Irrespective of whether or not it was invoked, what matters is the right.”

The case continues.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[Irish economy grows by 5.5% in GDP terms despite inflation challenges]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/irish-economy-grows-by-55-in-gdp-terms-in-third-quarter/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/irish-economy-grows-by-55-in-gdp-terms-in-third-quarter/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 16:02:34 +0000The Irish economy grew by more than 5 per cent in the third quarter despite the inflation shock, according to the Central Statistics Office (CSO).

The agency said provisional estimates indicate that gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 5.5 per cent between July and September when compared with the previous quarter.

“The result was driven mainly by increases in the multinational-dominated sectors of industry and information and communication in Q3 2026,” it said.

The GDP metric is increasingly seen as a bad gauge of domestic activity because of contract manufacturing (where goods are produced abroad but included in Irish exports) and other multinational-led activities.

It is a better indicator of multinational exports.

AIB said in its latest bulletin that it expected the economy here to grow by 3.8 per cent this year using the CSO’s bespoke measure of growth, modified gross national income (GNI*).

It also noted that AI-related spending connected with the fit-out of data centres and general investment by Irish-based companies in the tech sector was fuelling this growth. It warned that inflation was likely to peak at 4-5 per cent.

Separate data published by the Central Bank indicated the net financial wealth of Irish households increased by €31.8 billion in the second quarter to reach €473 billion.

“Positive revaluations contributed €29.8 billion to this movement,” it said.

Net financial wealth excludes property and land assets. When they are included, household wealth is valued at €1.4 trillion.

This equates to approximately €268,000 per person in the State.

The increase in recent years has been driven by higher property values, which account for more than two-thirds of household wealth.

“Overall, the Irish economy remained a net lender vis-a-vis the rest of the world in the period, as net investment in financial assets exceeded the net incurrence of financial liabilities by €67.9 billion,” the Central Bank said in its latest quarterly financial accounts.

Government financial assets stood at €156.1 billion in the second quarter, while liabilities totalled €234 billion.

“At the end of the quarter, the government’s net financial wealth stood at -€77.9 billion, representing a continued improvement in its net financial position,” it said.

]]>KanawatTH<![CDATA[Energy costs force CRH to trim full-year earnings forecasts]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/crh-revenues-rise-in-third-quarter/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/29/crh-revenues-rise-in-third-quarter/Thu, 29 Oct 2026 12:04:32 +0000Building materials company CRH downgraded its full-year earnings guidance on Thursday, despite reporting a jump in revenues in the third quarter and what it described as good momentum going into the final stretch of the year.

The New York-listed, Dublin-headquartered group cited challenges posed by increasing costs and subdued residential activity.

Still, revenues rose 3 per cent to $11.4 billion (€10.2 billion), driven by pricing momentum, underlying demand and acquisitions. However, impairments weighed on net income, reducing it to $1.2 billion from $1.5 billion a year earlier.

The US-listed group said it expected net income for the year of between $3.1 billion and $3.3 billion, with adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the range of $7.8 billion to $8 billion. Previously, it had forecast earnings in the range of $8.1 billion to $8.5 billion.

The cut in guidance comes as the company noted a “sharp and sustained increase” in energy costs, particularly in diesel, and across haulage and distribution, chief executive Jim Mintern said.

“For us at this time of year, it is difficult to recover that kind of cost inflation late in the year, and also in what are some of our busiest activity months,” he said.

Residential demand in the US had also softened further, he said, as interest rates rose.

“Activity softened throughout the summer and impacted volumes across many of our markets.”

However, Mintern pointed to activity in some key infrastructure and non-residential markets, including in the roads business and re-industrialisation, particularly in data centre activity.

The group has also introduced a new transformation initiative, Velocity, that is expected to simplify the organisation’s structures, optimise processes and use AI to underpin growth objectives while enhancing operational efficiency and improving margins.

The two-year programme is expected to deliver annual run-rate benefits of approximately $400 million.

Mintern said Velocity was incremental to the 2030 targets the company gave last September. “We are raising our ambition for the company across the group,” he said.

Speaking to analysts, Mintern said the broader outlook for the company remained positive as it entered 2027, although residential business remained subdued. “CRH is in good shape,” he said. “We are building a better CRH, one that is going to have structurally higher margins. I am confident that the building blocks are in place to deliver another year of growth as we enter into 2027.”

CRH also announced a new share buyback programme of up to $6 billion, set to run until the end of 2030.

Reiterating the brokerage’s ‘outperform’ rating on the stock, Davy Stockbrokers analyst Colin Sheridan said CRH’s results were slightly ahead of expectations.

“The company has launched a new multiyear $6 billion buyback programme and a transformation initiative aimed at delivering $400 million in annual benefits by the end of 2028,” he said. “The stock remains cheap at current levels, and we reiterate our ‘outperform’ rating.”

CRH recently completed the earlier-than-expected closing of an $8.5 billion (€7.6 billion) deal to acquire US peer Arcosa.

The group’s focus is on four key areas: aggregates, cement and sustainable alternatives, roads and water. It sees these benefiting from three infrastructure megatrends: continuing investment in the transport system, from roads to airports; a need to develop water management; and the re-industrialisation of the US.

Mintern said the Arcosa transaction fed into these megatrends and increased CRH’s exposure to the utilities sector.

   <title>Machtkampf um Verfassungsgericht eskaliert</title>
   <description>In Polen eskaliert der Streit zwischen den beiden großen politischen Lagern des Landes um das Verfassungsgericht weiter. Die rechtskonservative PiS, die von 2015 bis 2023 regierte, hatte das Gericht mit ihr politisch nahestehenden Richtern und Richterinnen besetzt. Die seit 2023 amtierende Mitte-links-Regierung unter Ministerpräsident Donald Tusk machte die Besetzungen rückgängig, wogegen sich aber der rechtskonservative Staatspräsident Karol Nawrocki sperrte. Am Freitag wurde das Gelände um das Gericht zum Schauplatz des Disputs.</description>

   <title>Auch Votum zu Steuer und Stopfleber</title>
   <description>Am 3. November stehen in den USA nicht nur die Kongresswahlen und damit ein großer Stimmungstest für US-Präsident Donald Trump an.    <title>Viel Unzufriedenheit mit Klimagesetz</title>
   <description>Die Begutachtungsfrist für das Klimagesetz hat am Freitag geendet. Kritik gibt es vor allem bezüglich des Ziels der Klimaneutralität bis zum Jahr 2040. Die Wirtschaftskammer (WKO) etwa und einige Unternehmen zeigten sich nicht damit einverstanden, dass Österreich zehn Jahre vor der EU klimaneutral sein will. Diverse Organisationen vermissten hingegen die Verbindlichkeit, auch beim 2040-Ziel. Bis Donnerstag gab es über 330 Stellungnahmen.</description>

President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis.

However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters.

pic.twitter.com/Gk4bPH1pJU

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 31, 2026

On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw.

At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors.

The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her.

pic.twitter.com/sni7uvIVke

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 30, 2026

Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”.

Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”.

Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”.

⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal.

Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence.

At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker.

The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon.

There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice.

Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026

Leading figures from the right-wing and far-right opposition, with which Nawrocki is aligned, have indicated their willingness to engage in talks, as have two of Tusk’s junior coalition partners.

Szymon Hołownia, the founder of the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), confirmed on Saturday morning that his group would attend the talks. He also urged Tusk to sit down at the table with Nawrocki.

Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”.

On Saturday afternoon, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, leader of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and a deputy prime minister, also revealed that he would personally attend the consultations with Nawrocki.

@PL_2050 na wydarzenia dzisiejszej nocy patrzy z zaniepokojeniem. Przynoszą one Polsce wstyd. Nie przybliżają nas do naprawy tego, co zostało zepsute.

Jest dla nas jasne, że Bogdan Święczkowski, wraz z nominatami PiS-u, zrobił z TK karykaturę sądu konstytucyjnego. Sytuacja w…

— Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026

Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. His justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, announced on Friday evening that he was seeking to have Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution lifted.

On Saturday, speaking to broadcaster TVN, Żurek expressed support for the actions taken by Korwin-Piotrowska. He called Nawrocki’s behaviour at the TK “shameful” and said he “hoped prosecutors will take action, because it is unacceptable for someone protected by presidential immunity to behave in such a way”.

Meanwhile, Tusk’s other main coalition partner, The Left (Lewica), announced on Saturday afternoon that it would not attend the talks with Nawrocki.

“One cannot accept an invitation from someone who is himself responsible for the current situation regarding the Constitutional Tribunal,” wrote Anna-Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus. “The TK is in the hands of independent judges. Politicians should not tell them what to do.”

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki.

Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years.

Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”.

 

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.
