The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law.

Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled.

Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed.

Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners.

In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.

The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.

The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.

In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives.

The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city.

The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London.

While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice.

Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model.

The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users.

 

The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees.

Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains.

Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly.

An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public.

Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025

The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards.

The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves.

A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium.

I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️

Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸

Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem

— Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026

Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025.

Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula.

The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”.

Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months.

Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Tuesday, the Polish police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CBŚP) announced that anti-terrorism officers had detained the man, who can be named only as Artem S. under Polish privacy law, in Warsaw under a European Arrest Warrant issued by Romania.

In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company.

On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack.

The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.”

 

In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”.

Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania.

Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated.

Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.

Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026

In some cases, such operatives are amateurs – so-called “disposable agents” – recruited, coordinated and paid through messaging service Telegram. Some have also been pre-existing criminal groups hired by Russia to carry out such tasks.

In August, a drone production plant belonging to private Polish arms company WB Electronics was targeted in an arson attack that Poland has blamed on Russia.

The following month, a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was likewise hit by an arson attack that Poland blamed on Russia. Two Turkish men were later detained in Germany on suspicion of carrying out the attack.

Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”.

The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea.

The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership.

Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L

“Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw.

“The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added.

His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine.

 

Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies.

Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones.

The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems.

This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security.

Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year.

In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway.

Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries.

She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle.

Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year.

Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs.

Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe.

Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany, while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters.

The testimony was given after the president himself sued the owner of a website that, just before last year’s presidential election, published claims that Nawrocki had been involved in procuring prostitutes while working at the luxury Grand Hotel in the town of Sopot.

While the after-work crowd deserts the pub, weekday evening padel bookings are heading skywards, says Playtomic’s Alan Douglas.

Every town has one. The pub with a quiz and darts, the one with the best pint but the table by the fire is always taken. For generations, the local has been where Brits go to socialise, unwind and set the world to rights.

It’s an institution. But pubs are, sadly, in trouble. The British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) says 295 pubs closed in the first nine months of 2026. That’s roughly 5,000 jobs, most held by under-25s.

This raises a question: where is everyone going to socialise now? From where I sit, a growing number of them are playing padel.

Playtomic is the community platform for padel, running approximately 85 per cent of UK padel bookings, so I see the stats in real time and one specific trend strikes me: weekday evenings are booming.

In the first nine months of 2026, players made nearly 600,000 weekday bookings between 6pm and 9pm. That is twice as many as in the whole of 2025. September was the busiest month yet, touching 80,000 evening bookings.

Driving this trend are 25- to 44-year-olds, accounting for 63 per cent of these slots. These are working people, finishing their day and looking to socialise with friends. Not long ago, that meant the pub; now, it can mean padel.

Social padel is winning over Britons

Not every booking is pints lost, but habits are shifting for younger Brits. They are health-conscious and a round is not cheap.

Padel gives people much of what the pub once did. It’s played in groups of four, it’s sociable and fun for all abilities, and everyone leaves happy. Think of it like this: for the price of a couple of drinks you can have an hour’s good fun with your friends, with added cardio.

Increasingly, padel clubs are working out that cafes and courts go hand in hand. I walk into many busy padel clubs on weekday nights and see happy, sweaty groups, still in their kit, discussing great shots, often with a beer in hand. The social aspects of padel, on and off the court, are part of the reason why Brits have fallen for this sport.

The stats back up my anecdotal conclusions. The 2026 Playtomic and PwC Global Padel Report shows that UK padel has grown 86 per cent year-on-year since 2021, with many courts at 85 per cent occupancy or more and about half of UK players saying they struggle to book at peak times. 

Our own stats show that, on average in 2026, 62,000 people per month played padel for the first time. Over 60 per cent of them played again within four weeks. 

So, what does all this mean for the pub? The stats and stories suggest that the after-work social crowd hasn’t disappeared. Their want for routine, community and familiar faces hasn’t evaporated. They have simply found new pastures.

I hope the pub will always be part of British life, and I hope it gets the support it needs because it is one of our greatest exports. But if you want to know where a lot of Brits go at 7pm on a Tuesday night, increasingly, the answer is a glass and metal box with a net across the middle, four laughing, sweaty friends and a tipple afterwards.

Alan Douglas is Regional Manager UK and Ireland for Playtomic.

]]> 2473430Alan Douglas Alan Douglas McLaren Artura UK review: Brit supercar versus the Top Gear Test Track https://www.cityam.com/mclaren-artura-uk-review-brit-supercar-versus-the-top-gear-test-track/ Sat, 31 Oct 2026 06:04:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473144

I have always wanted to drive like The Stig, but not right here, not now. Twenty years ago, Ben Collins – the ‘tame racing driver’ behind the tinted visor – lost control of a Koenigsegg CCX on this very corner, crashing violently and expensively backwards through a tyre wall. Now it feels like the McLaren [...]]]>

I have always wanted to drive like The Stig, but not right here, not now. Twenty years ago, Ben Collins – the ‘tame racing driver’ behind the tinted visor – lost control of a Koenigsegg CCX on this very corner, crashing violently and expensively backwards through a tyre wall. Now it feels like the McLaren Artura and I might suffer the same fate.

The curve in question is the flat-out Follow Through, which slices across the centre of Dunsfold Aerodrome – better known as the Top Gear Test Track. I have already turned in, it’s too late to brake and I’m carrying way more speed than seems sensible. I feel the car go light and twitch slightly as it hits the destabilising hump near the apex, but try to ignore every instinct shouting at me to back off. Calmly, almost serenely, the Artura settles on its suspension, holds its line and accelerates away. Wow, that was fast. 

After Collins’ crash in 2006, Koenigsegg fitted the CCX with a new rear spoiler to boost downforce and stability. But as I push the McLaren to its limits – and a fraction beyond – around slower, less consequential corners such as Chicago, Hammerhead and Gambon, it’s clear this supercar is already well sorted. The Artura can make anyone drive like The Stig. Or feel as if they can, at least.

New era for McLaren Automotive

Like the Alpine A110 or just about any recent Aston Martin, the Artura is proof that critical acclaim doesn’t always translate into sales success. We gave the updated 2024 model a full five stars in our review, yet it remains a rarity, even by supercar standards. When did you last see one?

However, big changes are afoot in Woking, which has just received an investment of £500 million to create 1,000 jobs over the next six years, and develop a new range of cars – including the oh-so-inevitable SUV. There’s also a redesigned logo, a forthcoming new factory and the stunning McL 6GT concept, due to enter limited production in 2028.

All of which means McLaren’s current models are now living on borrowed time. The end of 750S production has already been marked by the special edition 788HS, while the GTS could be phased out in early 2027. The Artura likely won’t be far behind them. 

So, when an invitation arrived to revisit the Artura on UK roads, followed by a blast around the Top Gear Test Track, I jumped at the chance. Is McLaren’s ‘junior’ supercar really as good as I remembered?   

Petrol power with a hybrid punch

The day begins at the McLaren Technology Centre (MTC), where both the road car company and championship-winning Formula 1 team are based. Designed by Norman Foster, the glassy, clinically clean building resembles a space station that has landed in the Surrey countryside. For sheer wow-factor, no other car factory I have visited – including those in Maranello and Sant’Agata Bolognese – comes close. 

After a tour that takes in several McLaren F1s, classic race cars in various states of undress and the largest collection of motorsport trophies in the world, I’m introduced to Richard Jackson. As chief powertrain engineer, he is responsible for the Artura’s plug-in hybrid system, which combines a 3.0-litre turbocharged V6 with a 7.4kWh battery and axial flux electric motor.

“The Artura’s powertrain was born off the back of the Mclaren P1,” Jackson explains. “We wanted to prove that hybridisation is about more than just a Toyota Prius.” The 120-degree V6 has a low centre of gravity and is unusually compact, helping to save weight. “The engine is 40kg lighter than our V8, while the e-motor weighs just 15kg. Altogether, the hybrid hardware adds 80-100kg.”

The technology, since adapted for McLaren’s flagship £2 million W1, not only saves fuel, but allows the Artura to drive 21 miles in EV mode and – most importantly – gives it an almighty wallop of extra performance. “Engines are very important to us,” adds Jackson. “We talk a lot about the crescendo. You need to chase the revs to enjoy the car fully.” Duly noted.

On the road in the Artura Spider

The first part of my drive is a circuitous road route from the MTC to Dunsfold in the open-top Artura Spider. Its folding roof is made from carbon fibre composite and can disappear beneath the rear deck in 11 seconds. Alternatively, if the weather turns a bit ‘British’, you can simply lower the vertical rear window to turn up the V6 volume.  

The Spider’s carbon monocoque chassis makes it just as rigid as the coupe, which pays dividends on potholed rural roads that are, regrettably, also a bit British. I have to activate the hydraulic nose lift on the roughest sections of tarmac to avoid grinding the chin spoiler, but the Artura never feels jittery or discombobulated. It moves with deftness and precision, relaying messages to your fingers, feet and posterior with utter clarity. You feel hard-wired into the car, rather than like an adversary trying to tame it.    

As ever with McLarens, the hydraulic steering is a highlight. While its rivals all rely on electric assistance, Woking still does things the old-fashioned way – and the Artura is greater for it. Indeed, I’d say the steering’s perfect weighting and finely wrought feedback are the best of any new car on sale. Yep, that good.

A supercar for daily driving

Like any modern supercar, the Artura has more power than you can realistically deploy on the road – without getting locked up, at least. Yet the plug-in hybrid system also widens its breadth of abilities. 

Sometimes it’s nice to simply cruise in EV mode, for instance, enjoying the calm ride and crisp tactility in near-silence. The eager and ever-ready torque of the frisbee-sized electric motor also makes for safe and rapid overtakes when you aren’t minded to chase that high-rev crescendo. 

Equally, much as I love the (V8, non-hybrid) McLaren 750S, it’s quite a hardcore proposition for a motorway commute or popping to the shops. The Artura is more like a Porsche 911 Turbo: a supercar you could happily drive every day. Spec one in a subtle colour – i.e. not the signature Papaya orange – and it almost flies below the radar, helped by modest proportions and an absence of aero addenda. 

Taking it to the track

All that easygoing civility doesn’t mean the Artura can’t raise its game, though. Far from it. Some 700hp and 531lb ft of torque are force-fed to the rear wheels via a dual-clutch auto gearbox and electronic differential. Use launch control and you can blast to 62mph in 3.0 seconds. Maximum speed is 205mph. 

Arriving at Dunsfold, the track looks larger and more intimidating than on television. The wide tarmac makes picking the right line even more important, and there are places where the grass has been scuffed by skidding tyres. There’s also an elevated viewing area next to the tricky Hammerhead corner, just so everybody can witness your mistakes.

My ‘Stig’ is one of McLaren’s own tame racing drivers. He talks me through a safety briefing, helps adjust my driving position and gives a run-through of the car’s controls. The Artura’s standard Club Sport seats move through an elliptical arc to keep you tightly ensconced, while the steering wheel is devoid of any buttons at all. Instead, rocker switches on the instrument binnacle are within fingertip-reach, used to toggle the powertrain and chassis settings between Comfort, Sport and Track. 

How to slide a McLaren Artura

We start with a few warm-up exercises on-track, including a launch control getaway. Exposure to powerful EVs has made many spoiled car journalists, yours truly among them, rather numb to instant, violent acceleration. Yet the way the Artura takes off still elicits an involuntary “ooof”. Select launch mode, hold the brake with your left foot and then push your right sole to the floor. There’s no squirm from the chassis or scrabble from the rear Pirellis; the Artura simply grips and goes. 

Our next exercise uses the Variable Drift Control (VDC), which allows you to determine how much the car will slide before its stability system kicks in. The easiest way to test it is via a full-bore, tyre-smoking start while turning the front wheels – the ‘Ford Mustang exiting a car show’ manoeuvre, in other words. With VDC on, the Artura will execute a graceful slide, then gather itself up and blast away. With the software switched off, it’s a swift reminder of how 700hp can send you immediately and irretrievably sideways… 

The final warm-up is a slalom between white lines along the runway, switching between drive modes to experience the car’s behaviour. The adaptive dampers have notably more squish in Comfort mode, Sport feels exuberant and playful, while Track is ruthlessly focused on lap times. In all settings, however, the Artura’s modest inertia (kerb weight is 1,498kg for the coupe, 1,560kg for the Spider) and fundamental mid-engined balance shine through.

Time for a Top Gear power lap

Finally, it’s time to drive the circuit – thankfully without Jeremy Clarkson adding my name to the Power Lap leaderboard afterwards. Typically in such situations, your undivided attention is on the track itself, rather than on evaluating the car, but after a couple of laps – and a misspent youth watching golden era Top Gear – I’m pretty confident that I know where I’m going. 

As on the road, there’s a deep sense of connection between the car and driver. The Artura is on your side, fluid when you string a complex of corners together and forgiving when you don’t. It joins the dots around Dunsfold with athletic poise and expressive feedback, keeping it tight through Willson and Chicago, then sliding gleefully around Bacharach.

Electric ‘torque fill’ makes the car instantly responsive, but its engine also loves to rev, spinning towards its 8,500rpm limiter with reckless enthusiasm. Gearshifts are equally immediate, each new ratio banged home with a well-padded thump, plus occasional crackles from the twin tailpipes. Interestingly, the long, slender paddles behind the steering wheel operate on a rocker system, so you can pull or push on either side to shift up or down.

My only cause for complaint – and it’s a familiar one in Artura reviews – is that the engine could be more characterful. Like the hybridised V8 in a Lamborghini Temerario, McLaren’s V6 only really sounds exciting when you’re closing in on the redline. Perhaps in normal driving you will appreciate its civility, but I’d prefer Track mode to broaden the car’s vocal range. Still, it’s nothing that you couldn’t fix by bolting on an aftermarket exhaust.  

Verdict: McLaren Artura 2026

Priced from around £220,000, the McLaren occupies the middle ground between the much pricier Temerario and Ferrari 296 GTB and (relatively) more affordable supercars such as the 911 Turbo S, Aston Martin Vantage and Mercedes-AMG GT 63. 

Alternatively, you could find a three- or four-year-old Artura with less than 20,000 miles for around £125,000. In 2026, that is 911 Carrera S money – and it buys you a full-paid-up 700hp supercar. Makes you think doesn’t it?

The Artura has long felt overshadowed by McLaren’s faster and more visceral 750S, along with some of its showier, shoutier rivals from Italy. True, it takes a bit more time to appreciate its talents, but there’s a depth and maturity here that bodes well for McLaren’s next chapter. Whatever that may bring.

• Tim Pitt writes for Motoring Research

]]> 2473144Tim Pitt Tim Pitt Revealed: The luxury London pads getting Healey’s energy handout – while poorer areas miss out https://www.cityam.com/revealed-the-luxury-london-pads-getting-healeys-energy-handout-while-poorer-areas-miss-out/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 16:13:31 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2473338

John Healey’s energy bills support package was meant to be targeted. But a City AM analysis has found homes worth millions are in line for a handout, while others in poorer areas will get nothing. John Healey’s maiden fiscal event was nothing if not targeted. Painful tax rises – be they on banks or gambling [...]]]>

John Healey’s energy bills support package was meant to be targeted. But a City AM analysis has found homes worth millions are in line for a handout, while others in poorer areas will get nothing.

John Healey’s maiden fiscal event was nothing if not targeted. Painful tax rises – be they on banks or gambling firms – were “targeted” at industries the Chancellor deemed ripe for a raid.

The word “targeted” appeared as many as 30 times in the Budget document published to mark Healey’s big day, as officials sought to play down fiscal significance of their measures.

The biggest of those changes – a £2.4bn promise to bung £100 to households to help them with their higher energy bills – claimed to be focused on poorer households.

But a City AM analysis of council tax data revealed Healey’s reliance on the outdated property tax means his payment will land in the bank accounts of moneyed professionals and retirees in London and the South East. Meanwhile other, less affluent households from elsewhere will miss out.

Council tax bands have not been set nationwide since the early 1990s – meaning they often inaccurately represent current property prices. Some areas, such as in central and suburban London postcodes, have rocketed in value over the past 30 years – while homes in deindustrialised parts of the country have fallen in real terms.

That means million-pound homes in some of the swankiest London postcodes – including Notting Hill, leafy Twickenham and Primrose Hill – are in line for the energy handout, while homes in towns with much lower property prices, including Blackpool and Aberdeen, are not.

“Using 1991 house prices to target 2026 support was never going to be a good design,” Arun Advani, a director of the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation (Centax), says. “After the support during Covid and the 2022 energy crisis, it is a sad indictment of government that a more effective way to target relief still hasn’t been created.”

The City AM analysis found freehold properties with as many as five bedrooms – in areas like Peckham, Nunhead and Camberwell – will receive the targeted support. The pocket of south east London was among the most deprived parts of the capital when the government evaluated council tax bands 35 years ago. Since then, however, the area has enjoyed an influx of upwardly mobile professionals looking to snap up affordable large terraced homes within a stone’s throw of central London. 

In the 25 years to 2019, Peckham property prices rose by over 1,000 per cent, according Land Registry data. That means even the owners of the area’s largest properties will receive £100 from the taxpayer. Take 130 Ivydale Road, a five-bedroom home sandwiched between the picturesque Nunhead cemetery and a sports ground. Sold last year for £1.26m, it boasts three bathrooms, a well-kempt hydrangea-filled patio garden and a palatial open-plan kitchen. It will also get £100 from the government by January. 

Cast the net beyond London, and even properties situated in the more salubrious enclaves of the Cotswolds are in line for the bung.

Situated just five miles away from the picturesque market town of Burford, The Haven is on the market for £1.3m. Its estate agent describes it as a “superb home” in the “highly sought-after and quintessentially rural village” of Filkins. It “perfectly marries period charm with modern elegance”, according to Oxford estate agent Penny & Sinclair, with “a generous entrance hall, utility, sitting room with feature fireplace and log burner”. But with the extra £100 for heating, its prospective owner might not need to stock up on as much firewood as feared.

City AM even found smaller flats and homes in parts of prime central London – including Notting Hill and St John’s Wood – that are included in the scheme. Several band-D houses on the picturesque, cobbled St Petersberg Mews are now worth an estimated £1.6m.

That means that had John Healey ploughed ahead with a rumoured plan to reduce the mansion tax threshold to £1.5m, those homes would have been liable to both the impending ‘council tax surcharge’, and the ‘targeted’ energy support package.

“A hundred pounds is nice, but the point is it’s extremely badly targeted,” Greg Thwaites, interim chief economist at the Resolution Foundation, told the think tank’s post-Budget press conference.

“There are lots of people doing ok, who can probably manage without that money – and probably need to manage without that money – if we’re going to support the people we need to support.”

The scheme’s poor targeting means there are also plenty of losers. Those tend to be focused in Britain’s former industrial heartlands. Places like Aberdeen, Nottingham and Merthyr Tydfil, whose economies were thriving in the early 1990s thanks to Britain’s steel, oil and mining industries.

A two-bed semi on Aberdeen’s Cranford Road, pictured above, falls in council tax band E – and thus misses out on the payment. That’s despite the property being worth 89 per cent less than the mews houses in Notting Hill and 86 per cent less than the Ivydale Road five-bed.

See also, the band-E, £250,000 home in Methyr Tydfil (below), the south Wales town once known as ‘the iron capital of the world’. Now, nearly 30 per cent of its residents are listed as economically inactive, as deindustrialisation and economic dislocation robbed it of high-skilled jobs and led its property prices to stagnate.

John Healey, for his part, has defended the scheme’s structure, hailing it as “real help” when people “need it most”. He will be glad, no doubt, to have the strident support of Martin Lewis, too. The all-powerful Money Saving Expert boss was fast out of the traps to declare it the “least worst option” for a package of this kind. “If you’re going to do an intervention, I think the mechanism of the intervention is right,” he said after visiting Downing Street ahead of the Budget.

A look at predicted energy prices at the start of next year and the reasons to intervene are obvious. Household bills are expected to jump some 27 per cent in early 2027 – roughly £300 for the average home.

But it is also those bleak forecasts that help explain why economists who have run the rule over the scheme and who it will benefit are in an altogether less celebratory mood than Healey and his money saving acolyte.

“It means a lot of cash going going to people that don’t need it,” Centax’s Advani says, “and some people who do need the support completely missing out.”

The latest phase of the government’s workers rights overhaul may have “an adverse impact on the labour market”, experts have warned, as businesses deal with the costly implications of taking on new staff. Taking effect on Friday, the next stage of the overhaul comes as part of the government’s sweeping employment reforms in its landmark [...]]]>

The latest phase of the government’s workers rights overhaul may have “an adverse impact on the labour market”, experts have warned, as businesses deal with the costly implications of taking on new staff.

Taking effect on Friday, the next stage of the overhaul comes as part of the government’s sweeping employment reforms in its landmark Employment Rights Act (ERA), bringing tighter workplace protections for employees.

Businesses are set to be required legally grant trade unions greater access, be directly liable for staff harassment from third parties, such as clients or customers, as well as being required to take all the reasonable steps set out in the law to prevent against sexual harassment.

The new laws are due to be rolled out over the next two years, which have so far already reduced the qualifying period for unfair dismissal to six months, removed the compensation cap, and strengthened trade union rights.

However, Tania Goodman, partner and head of employment at Collyer Bristow, told City AM that although the laws “may be well-meaning”, they could negatively impact the labour market as employing staff could become more expensive and complex.

“Laws designed to enhance workers’ entitlements may be well-meaning, but if employing staff is perceived as becoming more costly, complex or uncertain, there is a risk this will have an adverse impact on the labour market,” Goodman said.

Goodman said employers are starting to “assess the implications of forthcoming reforms, including the move towards unfair dismissal protection arising at a much earlier stage of employment.”

She added: “As a result, some are reviewing their current workforce and future staffing requirements.

“The challenge for Government is ensuring that measures intended to support workers do not inadvertently discourage hiring or investment,” Goodman added. “The real test will be whether it can strike the right balance between supporting employees and maintaining the confidence employers need to invest, recruit and grow the economy.”

As of 30 October, independent trade unions will given new legal rights to be able to access workplaces both physically or digitally to support, meet, and recruit workers.

Richard Harvey, partner at Fisher Phillips, said businesses “should get their procedures in order now, including deciding who handles requests, how workplace access would operate and how confidentiality and data protection will be protected”.

“But they should also look at the underlying relationship with their workforce. Employers who communicate openly and deal with concerns early will be better placed to navigate these changes than those who only start thinking about employee relations when a union comes knocking,” Harvey added.

OBR warns reforms may have ‘negative impact’ on economy

Britain’s fiscal watchdog, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), said the changes are expected to hit growth in the economy as the cost to businesses will outstrip any boost to workers’ productivity.

In its economic and fiscal outlook, which was published alongside the Budget on 28 October, the OBR said Labour’s workers rights overhaul “will likely have a negative economic impact from negative impacts on businesses.”

Commenting on the OBR’s assessment, employment and recruitment body, the Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC), said this comes as a “fresh blow to UK growth.”

“The verdict from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is in, and it is clear they think NIC increases and the Employment Rights Act (ERA) changes are bad for jobs and bad for the economy,” Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the REC, said.

The St Paul’s ‘raves’ are an exquisite evening of culture: ★★★★★

There was the sound of cans being cracked open between songs, but those cans were filled with water… 

And beers had to be left at the door: about the most rebellious thing I saw at the St Paul’s Fabric ‘rave’ last night was two blokes sipping on craft ales in the queue – but they had to chuck those in the bin before they entered the hallowed building.

It was hardly a pulsating, thunderous clubnight, more a serene affair at the first of St Paul’s collaborations with the nightclub Fabric, the beginning of a four-year event series.

And despite tabloid murmurings of the show being the equivalent of a rave, everyone was sitting motionless in their chairs, the polite crowd silent throughout the hour-and-ten-minute-long show, watching the music respectfully from the pews.

Inside the St Paul’s ‘raves’

It was the controversial first night of the electronic music collaboration between the Cathedral and one of central London’s biggest nightclubs. Ahead of the night, the Daily Mail published criticism from the president of the Nelson Society (Lord Nelson is buried at the Cathedral), who expressed his unease that ticketholders would be “dancing on his [Nelson’s] grave,” and called the events a “sad reflection” on Christianity.

But – as I wrote in an op-ed earlier this autumn – this criticism derives from the snobbish perspective that all electronic music will induce antisocial behaviour.

The programmers of Fabric, it turns out, can also curate sophisticated evenings where sitting rather than dancing is the vibe. The musicians last night, who are members of The Cinematic Orchestra, were playing atmospheric, low-fi electronica, fused with soul and groove, featuring live singers. There was a drum kit, but it was never used heavily, and there was barely ever even a driving beat. This was modern classical music, composed with synthesisers, one of which was on stage, but the result was sophisticated, grown-up electronica: the sort of music that makes you sit and think, rather than the sort of music that makes you want to lose your mind.

Mesmeric

That said, I’d see no issue with bringing more danceable music into the St Paul’s pews.

It was a mesmeric evening. The music was wonderful, but it was equally special to see the Cathedral’s roof bathed in brown and red hues of light. And a privilege to sit and listen to such contemporary sounds and talented non-religious artists in such a historic setting. And it was wonderful to see hundreds of young, fashionable, City types in here, who’d swerved going to the pub for one Thirsty Thursdays to visit the Cathedral instead. 

I’m sure I’m representative of most who work in the City when I say I’ve come to an office in the neighbourhood most days for the past five years, but only twice been into St Paul’s. The reality is people like me need an event like this to bring us in. And once I’m inside, there are very few spaces as special to spend an evening with live music.

There is absolutely nothing controversial here, it is simply bringing in new audiences, and given how prominent the Cathedral is in the Square Mile, the local community engaging with it more fully can only be a good thing.

Other Cathedral ‘raves’ are taking place across the country. Martin Kemp from Spandau Ballet is performing his ‘Back to the 80s’ DJ sets in Bristol, Guildford and Peterborough Cathedrals, and the ‘Silent Discos in Incredible Places’ tour has seen Canterbury, Ely, Coventry, Manchester, Salisbury, Sheffield and Hereford Cathedral’s double as places to dance. 

Cathedrals like St Paul’s receive no state funding

Besides the current trend though, the acoustic attributes of these venues have long been recognised as ideal for clubbing – former churches in cities including Bournemouth and Leeds have been refashioned as late-night music venues. 

These events cook up cash for the venues. Cathedrals and other religious venues receive no direct state funding, and very little of the Church of England’s money goes into their maintenance. The costs of running these institutions is getting higher under cost of living constraints. These events – like the St Paul’s one which sold out – are bringing in decent cash. Tickets for the St Paul’s Fabric collaboration evenings cost between £25 and £35. Given the venue capacity is 3,500, back-of-fag-packet sums means the Cathedral might have brought in £87,500 from last night alone. 

It’s the sort of cash that I’d hope would have the Dean cutting shapes in the aisles. I might not have been dancing last night, but I’d hope with that kind of profit, he was once us punters were kicked out.

With the regular series returning in the new year, could The Traitors fall victim to reality TV fatigue, asks Dean Rodgers

Forget faithfuls and traitors, the real winner of The Celebrity Traitors is the BBC. 

As series two reaches its dramatic climax tonight, the broadcaster has plenty to celebrate. The opening episode attracted 15.7m viewers in its first seven days, making it the UK’s most-watched TV programme of 2026 so far.

Arguably the show’s crowning achievement, however, is the way it’s created a world that people are desperate to be a part of. Friendship groups are organising watch parties in a way we’ve not seen since The X Factor’s heyday. Immersive experiences offer fans the chance to don the infamous cloak themselves. 

Whether it’s Richard E Grant ‘accidentally’ revealing himself as a Traitor or Ross Kemp’s paranoia inadvertently turning him into a never-ending meme manufacturer, conversation surrounding the season has reached fever pitch. And in doing so, fans are effectively doing the show’s marketing pro bono. 

It helps that the celebrity edition comes with ready-made fandoms, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and her “Mixers” a prime example. Each famous face has brought their own community to the castle. And what makes The Celebrity Traitors truly unique is that unlike many reality shows, it’s still capable of attracting genuinely big names. Even Hollywood is queuing up for a go, with Andrew Garfield and Tom Hiddleston publicly expressing interest in taking part. 

Getting these celebrities through the portcullis is a great way to win the immediate battle for attention. But as we’ve seen from The Traitors’ original format, viewers stay long after their favourite castle resident is banished (or worse). 

Let this be a lesson to any business trying to capitalise on the fame and fortune of established IPs and celebrated A-listers. Sure, these partnerships can get your foot in the door and drive initial engagement. Lasting loyalty, however, has to be earned with the quality of the product you actually deliver, as the brilliance of The Traitors format itself attests to.

Will Traitors fatigue set in?

With the regular series returning in the new year, could The Traitors fall victim to reality TV fatigue? Personally, I find that hard to believe. It’s not just that it has a catalogue of brand assets a mile long, from the ever-looming castle and cloaks to more nuanced items like perfume bottles. It’s that these parts all come together to form a distinctive world, arguably as recognisable and important as the contestants that play the game.

I’ve seen how powerful this can be firsthand. Back in 2015, I co-founded The Crystal Maze Live Experience, bringing a much-loved 1990s game show into the real world. We even got the original host, Richard O’Brien, involved in a promotional shoot!

A decade later, people are still turning up to collect crystals and tackle the challenges. Although many weren’t even born when the original show first aired, the experience has outgrown nostalgia, attracting new generations and given the franchise a commercial life of its own.

That’s the beauty of what we call the ‘Live Layer’: giving people the chance to step inside a story rather than simply watch it.

In a similar vein, The Traitors: Live Experience gives fans the opportunity to take their own seats at the Round Table and play the game themselves. It turns passionate viewership into ticket sales and could reach people who might not have watched the show in the first place.

But the real secret to The Traitors’ success isn’t simply its potential for spin-offs. It’s that everyone can picture themselves in the castle. More than that, we’re all convinced we’d be rather good at it. We know who we’d trust, who we’d banish and how we’d outsmart the Traitors.

Business leaders can learn from this want to get involved, giving people a role to play in their offerings, and by extension giving them a reason to come back. Because, at the end of the day, the most important faithfuls aren’t just loyal customers, they’re the ones who recruit others. 

Dean Rodgers is experiential director at Studio Secret Cinema

The High Court has upheld the media watchdog Ofcom’s powers to harvest retroactive safety data from tech giants.

In February, Ofcom issued formal information notices to major tech platforms, including Meta, Tiktok, and X, requiring them to share detailed data on content and user exposure to harmful material under the Online Safety Act.

Meta, Tiktok, and X jointly challenged Ofcom with a judicial review case at London’s High Court.

The court rolled the platforms’ legal challenges into one case, in which they challenged the notices on several legal grounds, largely arguing the watchdog unlawfully circumvented the act’s specific transparency framework.

The Online Safety Act was designed to tackle the risks to users, including children, of encountering harmful content online. It provided Ofcom with extensive powers, including the ability to fine non-compliant platforms up to £18m or 10 per cent of their qualifying global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

On Friday, the High Court refused permission for the tech platforms’ claims, in the first judicial review proceedings to test Ofcom’s new powers.

Lord Justice Singh and Justice Collins Rice found that Ofcom’s information-gathering powers served a distinct regulatory purpose and that the individual notices did not legally trigger the threshold for an overarching impact assessment.

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “We welcome the High Court’s decision to dismiss the challenges brought by Meta, X and Tiktok against our efforts to gather information from them.

“Under the Online Safety Act, Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that’s been unaccountable for more than 20 years.

“Gathering information from companies is fundamental to our ability to do our job of assessing compliance with their duties, and we’ll continue to use our powers to create a safer life online for people in the UK,” they added.

A Tiktok spokesperson said: “We are considering this judgment.”

“We’re disappointed with the court’s decision, but we and others across industry pursued this challenge because information-gathering of this scale goes beyond what is necessary or proportionate. We remain committed to working with Ofcom and are reviewing the judgement in full,” a Meta spokesperson said.

X was also approached for comment.

Earlier this month, Meta appeared in the High Court, challenging how Ofcom calculates fees and fines under the UK’s online safety law, arguing the methods are disproportionate and unlawful. While in August, Tiktok lost in the Court of Appeal to overturn a £12.7m fine from the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) for illegally processing the data of over 1.4m children under the age of 13.

Fiat has taken the much-loved 1956 Multipla, squeezed it down to about the size of an original 500 and made it electric, and if the price lands where the early estimates point, it could be the cheapest way to get four people across town without waiting for a bus.

Fiat’s new Multiplina is a four-seat electric car about three metres long, with a claimed top speed of 55mph, and it’s due on sale in 2028. Fiat hasn’t put a price on it yet, but Auto Express reckons it’ll come in at around £14,000, which would slot it between the £8,995 Topolino and the £18,995 Fiat 500 Hybrid. The catch is that it’s classed as a heavy quadricycle, which comes with much lighter rules than a normal car, and Fiat hasn’t said whether it’ll build one with the steering wheel on the right for British buyers.

We’ll admit our first reaction was a grin, because it looks like something you’d see parked outside a café in Turin in 1960, but the more we read about it the more it looks like a clever bit of thinking from a brand that knows small cars better than almost anyone.

Fiat Multiplina price and specs

The £14,000 figure is an estimate, so treat it as a guide. Italy’s Il Sole 24 Ore thinks it could sit closer to Topolino money, with options taking it to about €12,000, so the real number could be lower still, and either way it would be one of the cheapest four-seaters you could buy new.

Underneath, it uses a stretched version of the Topolino’s platform with a bigger battery (Fiat hasn’t said how big). That’s what lets it move up a class to the heavy quadricycle rules, which cap top speed at the 55mph Fiat claims, against the Topolino’s 28mph. Fiat hasn’t given a range, but it should comfortably beat the 46 miles the Topolino manages, and the concept has two doors, four seats and little windows that hinge outwards.

What is the Fiat Multiplina based on?

The name and the shape come from the Fiat 600 Multipla of 1956, a tiny people carrier with a flat, upright nose that could seat six in about 3.5 metres and stayed in production until 1967, with around 240,000 sold, according to Autocar. The Multiplina borrows the vertical front, the round headlights and the bubble-shaped profile, and it was first shown as the Quattrolino earlier this year (it was renamed, Auto Express says, because Audi owns the rights to “quattro”).

Most people in Britain will think of a different Multipla, the bug-eyed 1998 MPV with three seats across the front that became a bit of a national joke. Fiat says this one draws on the 1950s original, so don’t expect any of that car’s odd styling, though we suspect the shared name will do Fiat no harm at all when it comes to getting people talking.

Fiat boss Olivier François calls it “the missing link” between the Topolino and a normal city car, speaking to CAR magazine, and that’s a fair way to describe it.

Is the Fiat Multiplina coming to the UK?

Nothing is confirmed yet. What we do know is that Fiat only opened UK orders for the Topolino this summer, at £8,995, which suggests it thinks there’s a market here for tiny electric cars, though it has also said some Topolino versions won’t come to Britain, so there are no guarantees.

Is the Fiat Multiplina a good city car?

Regit’s motoring reporter Tim Barnes-Clay hasn’t driven it (it’s still a concept), but he’s already sold on the idea.

​“I get excited about driving anything wacky and wonderful, and the Multiplina is both,” he says. “Fiat has always been at its best when it builds small cars with a sense of humour, and if this arrives at around £14,000 I’d happily have one as a London runabout, as long as Fiat can show me it’ll look after the people inside.”

For London, it makes a lot of sense on paper. You get four seats in something short enough to squeeze into the gaps that most hatchbacks drive straight past, and 55mph is plenty when so much of inner London is now limited to 20mph. Where we’d be less keen is on a fast dual carriageway with lorries thundering past, because a three-metre quadricycle is going to feel very small out there.

The bigger worry is safety. Quadricycles aren’t held to the same crash-test rules as normal cars, and Fiat hasn’t said anything yet about what protection the Multiplina will offer, which is the first thing we’d want to know before putting three passengers in it.

It also has a rival from France. Citroën’s revived 2CV is due around 2028 for similar money, and if that turns up as a full car you can take on the motorway, it’ll be the obvious one to compare this with.

What we like

●       Four seats in a car about three metres long

●       An expected price around £14,000, well under a Fiat 500 Hybrid

●       A top speed of 55mph, so it can keep up on faster town roads

●       Styling that will make people smile

What worries us

●       No UK plans or right-hand drive confirmed yet

●       Quadricycle crash-test rules are much lighter than a normal car’s

●       No range figure yet, and it’s two years away

Verdict

If Fiat brings the Multiplina to Britain at close to £14,000, it’ll be the most charming way we can think of to move four people around a city, and for a London household that wants a second car for the school run and the shops, we can see the appeal. But it’s a quadricycle, and until we know how it protects the people inside, and whether Citroën’s 2CV arrives as a proper car for similar money, we’d hold off getting excited and keep an eye on both.

If the Multiplina has you wondering whether the family’s second car is still earning its parking space, get a free valuation with Regit and see what it’s worth before 2028 comes round.

BMW’s facelifted i7 now goes up to 452 miles between charges and rides with all the calm you’d hope for at £109,320. Tim Barnes-Clay took it to Epsom Downs and calls it a heart-over-head choice, though the company car tax bill gives the head a surprisingly strong argument too.

The BMW i7 is a seriously luxurious electric saloon, but with the i7 50 xDrive M Sport costing £109,320, it needs to be more than a comfortable way to travel. The 2026 facelift brings a bigger battery, faster charging and a redesigned digital cockpit, lifting the range to as much as 452 miles (up from 388), while the ride remains exceptionally refined.

For me it’s worth the money because it makes you feel special behind the wheel, and as a BMW lover I’d call it a heart-over-head choice that says you’ve made it. The head gets a say too, though, because at 4% benefit-in-kind a higher-rate taxpayer pays about £1,750 a year to run one as a company car.

BMW i7 price and specs


The 2026 facelift is what BMW calls its most extensive model update ever, with new battery cells, faster charging, a new face and the iDrive X dashboard.

The fully electric i7 is the one to have if you want limousine comfort without a petrol or diesel engine. Prices start at £104,230 for the i7 50 xDrive, rising to £109,320 for the M Sport version I tested. The i7 60 xDrive (from £120,335) and the range-topping M70 xDrive (£164,420) sit higher in the line-up, with the M70 aimed at buyers who want a lot more performance.

Even the entry-level car comes generously equipped. Standard features include a 17.9-inch central touchscreen, a 14.6-inch screen for the front passenger, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, satellite navigation, heated seats, adaptive air suspension and four-zone climate control.

M Sport adds a more assertive body kit, darker exterior trim, an M steering wheel, upgraded brakes and 20-inch alloy wheels. Move further up the range and the equipment can include doors that open and close automatically, rear window blinds, a panoramic glass roof with illuminated details and rear-seat entertainment.

The options list can get expensive very quickly. My test car didn’t have any options fitted, but I can see the temptation, because once you’ve spent north of £100,000 another couple of thousand pounds doesn’t feel like much. Personally I think less is more, so I wouldn’t add anything.

BMW i7 design and dashboard

The i7 is enormous, and it looks it. The facelift brings a slimmer, more upright kidney grille, new vertical headlight units, a reshaped bonnet and longer tail-lights. I love the way it looks and think it’s an improvement on the last model, and if you want to make an impression in the company car park, its dignified presence will do the job.

The rear is more restrained, with longer tail-lights and a clean tailgate, but the overall effect is still imposing, which is part of the appeal if you want your luxury saloon to stand apart from more conventional executive cars.

Inside, BMW has created a cabin that feels suitably special. The materials and build quality impress, the seats give the sort of comfort you’d expect from a flagship, and there’s plenty of adjustment in the driving position, so longer journeys feel less demanding.

The updated infotainment system is responsive, with sharp graphics and a more modern interface. BMW’s Panoramic Vision display runs along the base of the windscreen from pillar to pillar, alongside a 3D head-up display, so you don’t have to rely on the central touchscreen for everything.

BMW’s decision to remove the iDrive rotary controller, which the 7 Series had until this facelift, is disappointing, though. The touchscreen is capable, but a physical controller is easier to use when you’re concentrating on the road. My hand reached for it briefly out of muscle memory, but I’d adapted within five minutes behind the wheel.

The optional rear theatre screen is one of the i7’s most extravagant features. At 31.3 inches, it folds down from the ceiling to entertain rear passengers, and other options include touch-sensitive controls in the rear doors, a Bowers & Wilkins sound system and lounge-style seating with a footrest. They’re impressive, but they only make sense if you regularly carry passengers who’ll use them.

BMW i7 performance and driving experience

The i7 has the sort of performance that makes a car weighing the best part of three tonnes feel surprisingly effortless.

The i7 50 xDrive produces 455hp and accelerates from 0 to 62mph in 5.5 seconds. The i7 60 xDrive raises output to 544hp and cuts that time to 4.8 seconds, while the 680hp M70 xDrive does the sprint in just 3.8 seconds.

The way it delivers that performance matters just as much as the figures. Acceleration is smooth and instant, with none of the gear changes you get with a combustion engine, and the i7 gathers speed without making a fuss, which suits its luxurious character.

Its size and weight mean it will never feel like a small sports saloon through tight corners, but the handling is more composed than you might expect. There’s plenty of grip, the body stays controlled and the steering gains useful weight as the road gets more demanding.

The real highlight, though, is the ride. Adaptive air suspension helps the i7 glide over uneven surfaces, and the cabin stays impressively quiet at motorway speeds. I drove it around Epsom Downs and the racecourse in Surrey, where it looked perfectly at home, and it wafted along beautifully, though like the horses up the road it could break into a gallop whenever I asked.

Optional active roll stabilisation improves body control further, but it’s frustrating that such a desirable feature isn’t standard across the range.

BMW has also worked on the smoothness of braking and energy recuperation. In a large electric car, the transition from regenerative braking to coming to a halt makes a noticeable difference to passenger comfort, and the i7’s refined behaviour helps keep the feeling that everything happens with minimal effort.

Driver assistance does a lot of the heavy lifting on long trips. Driving Assistant Plus is standard, and I particularly liked the way it keeps the car centred in its lane, which could make a real difference if your concentration dips for a second or two.

BMW i7 interior and boot space

Space is one of the i7’s strongest selling points. There’s loads of room in the front, rear passengers get generous legroom and headroom, and the electrically adjustable driving position makes it easy to get comfortable.

Rear-seat comfort is particularly impressive. Depending on the specification, the back can have reclining seats, a footrest and entertainment that turn it into a very relaxing place to spend time.

Visibility is reasonable for a car of this size, although the thick rear pillars restrict the view behind. Parking sensors and a 360-degree camera help when manoeuvring, but the i7’s sheer size still demands attention in multi-storey car parks and narrow streets.

The boot holds 500 litres, with extra storage under the floor. A ski hatch lets longer items through to the cabin, but the rear seats don’t fold, so if you regularly carry bulky things you’ll find that limiting.

Cabin storage is useful, with door bins, cupholders and a central storage compartment. A powered glovebox adds to the sense of occasion, and there’s an optional fridge if you want to take the luxury theme further.

BMW i7 range and charging

The 2026 i7 has a new battery built from BMW’s Gen6 round cells, with 112.5kWh of usable capacity. BMW quotes up to 452 miles of WLTP range for the i7 50 xDrive, up to 451 miles for the i7 60 xDrive and up to 426 miles for the M70 xDrive, against up to 388 miles before the facelift.

My drive was on a warm day on A and B roads, and although I didn’t go far, I was averaging 3.3 miles per kWh, which points to a more realistic 370 miles or so. That’s still a very usable range for a car of this size.

DC charging is rated at up to 250kW, up from 195kW before the facelift, and BMW quotes 28 minutes for a 10 to 80 per cent charge under the right conditions. That makes a big difference when you’re using a high-power public charger on a long trip.

At home, overnight charging is the most convenient option if you have off-street parking and can fit a wallbox. On a typical 7kW home charger, filling the battery from empty takes around 16 to 17 hours, so an overnight top-up is easy but a full charge from flat isn’t. The i7 can take up to 22kW on AC, which helps at faster workplace and destination chargers.

Home charging is generally much cheaper than relying on public rapid chargers, but tariffs vary, and a car of this size and weight uses a lot of energy over long distances.

BMW i7 as a company car

This is where the i7 makes most sense. Because it produces no tailpipe CO2, it sits in the 4% benefit-in-kind band for 2026/27, rising to 5% in 2027/28. On the £109,320 M Sport before options, that’s a taxable benefit of about £4,370, so a basic-rate taxpayer pays around £875 a year and a higher-rate taxpayer around £1,750. A petrol or diesel limousine at the same price would sit in the top 37% band, which would mean a bill of more than £16,000 a year for a higher-rate taxpayer.

That said, a BMW is a driver’s car, and I’d argue there’s little point having one as your company car if you only ever sit in the back. That would be like buying a mansion and never living in it, and anyone chauffeured around in an i7 would soon be jealous enough to want the wheel for themselves.

Private buyers have a different sum to do. Electric cars pay vehicle tax now, at £10 in the first year and £200 after that, and because the i7 costs more than £50,000 it also pays the £440 Expensive Car Supplement from its second year to its sixth, which makes £640 a year.

BMW’s warranty runs for three years with unlimited mileage, and the battery is covered separately for eight years or 100,000 miles.

What we like

1. Excellent ride comfort. The i7 feels calm and refined over long distances, with impressive isolation from road and wind noise.

2. A luxurious interior. Spacious seating, high-quality materials and clever technology make the cabin a lovely place to spend time.

3. Strong performance. Even the i7 50 xDrive has ample acceleration, and the more powerful versions are exceptionally quick.

4. Improved electric range. Up to 452 miles, up from 388 before the facelift, with 28-minute rapid charging.

5. Low company car tax. At 4% BIK it costs a higher-rate taxpayer about £1,750 a year.

What worries us

1. The price. The i7 costs more than £100,000 before you add any of the more extravagant options.

2. The missing rotary controller. The touchscreen works well, but losing a familiar physical control is a step backwards for some tasks.

3. Its size. The spacious cabin comes with considerable exterior dimensions, which make parking and manoeuvring harder work.

4. Real-world range. I was seeing about 370 miles on a warm day, well short of the official 452.

The i7’s six-figure price means it pays the Expensive Car Supplement for five years, and if you’d like to know what your own car costs to tax, Regit’s free car tax checker will tell you.

Is the BMW i7 worth it?

The BMW i7 is an exceptionally accomplished luxury electric saloon. It combines a refined ride, strong performance, generous passenger space and an interior packed with technology, and the 2026 facelift brings real improvements to its range and charging.

Its price is the biggest obstacle, especially when the options list can add so much to the bill. The loss of the iDrive rotary controller is another disappointment, and its imposing size won’t suit every driver.

If you want a luxurious electric car that covers long distances in comfort and looks after its passengers, the i7 deserves serious consideration, and the i7 50 xDrive M Sport is the one I’d buy, because it’s quick enough that you don’t need the much more expensive M70.

It’s best for the company car driver who wants a limousine but still wants to drive it, and for them it’s hard to think of a better place to spend £109,320, especially with a 4% tax bill to help justify it.

The Bank of England is expected to hike interest rates next week as policymakers battle to stamp on inflationary pressures building in the UK economy. 

City analysts have predicted that the Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee will vote to raise interest rates from 3.75 per cent to four per cent.

The Bank has been closely monitoring evidence for “second round effects”, where higher inflation could force workers to demand larger pay packets, with extra costs on firms thereby pushing inflation higher in a spiralling effect. 

Deutsche Bank is among a number of financial firms which has said the MPC will be split 6-3 in favour of tightening monetary policy due to growing concerns of these economic forces over the upcoming months.

Sanjay Raja, its chief UK economist, said governor Andrew Bailey would back a hike in interest rates as rising energy prices and stronger growth could prompt rate-setters to take “pre-emptive” action to prevent a higher spike in inflation over the next year. 

He said he expected “the MPC to emphasise that rate hikes are effectively an insurance policy on potential second-round effects”. 

Interest rate hike could be followed by another next year

The Bank is weighing up key data points showing stable private sector wage growth, high levels of spending, a declining number of job vacancies and inflation beating expectations as a result of elevated oil and gas prices feeding through into household bills. 

The Office for National Statistics said inflation in the year to September was 3.5 per cent, higher than the two per cent target set by the Bank. Threadneedle Street only briefly managed to get inflation to remain around two per cent in the middle of 2024. 

While larger settlements for public sector workers has kept wage growth well above three per cent, a rise in private sector wages, which are more closely watched by policymakers, has not yet shown clear signs of strengthening.

However, City economists have noted that a sustained rise in energy prices, which could take inflation far beyond four per cent, and growing momentum in the UK economy combined with a slight fall in unemployment could push the MPC to take immediate action to increase borrowing costs.

The Office for Budget Responsibility revised up its inflation forecasts for next year as price growth could average at about 3.4 per cent this week, sending a warning to John Healey and Andy Burnham on their mission to ease the cost of living.

Pantheon Macroeconomic analysts said a hike in interest rates was “nailed on”, predicting that just one member, Alan Taylor, would vote for no change to be made. 

Economists Rob Wood and Elliott Jordan-Doak said updated forecasts could be “consistent with” two interest rate hikes. 

“We expect the MPC to state that the size and duration of the energy shock are now large enough to require hikes in advance of evidence of second-round effects; in other words, justification for an insurance hike,” they said in a note to City traders.

It speaks to Prem Rugby’s ambition that its chief executive Simon Massie-Taylor is jetting off to the United States to drum up investment and sponsorship for the English game, as reported by City AM earlier this week.

It suggests the league – unlike many other top-flight union competitions – is actively seeking to go beyond its traditional market in order to attract financial support. Being backed by a major American insurance firm in Gallagher is one thing, but finding a US bank partner and further private investment into the league’s 10 teams would be a tonic for a sport still in need of as much help as it can get.

But I hope that Massie-Taylor, who was previously commercial chief at the Rugby Football Union, uses his trip to see just how US sports are able to commercialise, develop and sweat their assets, because that will be the difference between Prem Rugby truly turning a corner and repeating past mistakes.

Over 10 years ago the NFL launched an investment fund called 32 Equity, using a start-up contribution of $1m from each of the league’s main owners. By late 2026, it has raised more than $250m and had stakes in the likes of merchandise giant Fanatics – having purchased a three per cent stake at a $3bn valuation in 2017, the firm is now worth $30bn – and Genius Sports, the company behind VAR in the Premier League.

Stateside lessons

It is a smart way of keeping owners on the straight and narrow, incentivising them with investments into firms that directly work with the NFL, like Fanatics. Assuming you could persuade the Prem Rugby owners – whose wealth generally ranges from the billions at Bristol Bears and Newcastle Red Bulls down to the low tens of millions elsewhere in the league – to part with some cash, it could go into buying stakes in catering firms, sports AI organisations and kit/streetwear suppliers which could then service the league.

The NFL is a smart, rather large, cookie and Massie-Taylor should look beyond the bright lights of Manhattan’s banking district or the wider East Coast business front on his trip. US sports are great at turning their athletes into their own brands which transcend the field or the court and, while meetings with Matchroom suggest Prem Rugby is well on its way there, it is about getting players to invest and build portfolios. For all of the cheating that was revealed at Saracens at the end of the last decade, at least a number of players have gone on to have stakes in or ownership of successful businesses.

When David Beckham joined Jonny Wilkinson (or more likely the other way around) for an Adidas advert in 2003, the world was Wilko’s oyster. The star of England World Cup win could have gone on to be the most commercial figure the sport had ever seen, but he chose not to. Massie-Taylor must encourage his roster of players to build their appeal beyond the game; and that means more than Henry Pollock doing the cover of Men’s Health and being named one of Tatler’s 200 “hottest young eligibles”.

Play Video

Prem Rugby opportunities

Adidas once paid for the entire Newcastle team – including yours truly – to go on a pre-season tour to Japan because they wanted Wilkinson for brand promotion. Five weeks in the Far East was an incredible experience for me as a youngster, but there was one snag for the apparel brand, who undoubtedly forked out tens of thousands: Wilko got appendicitis on the first day and was forced to fly home.

Rugby needs brands – like Red Bull with, ironically, Newcastle again – to trust the growth potential in the sport and it looks like that may need to come from the US, given its own incentives to develop rugby ahead of their World Cup hosting duties in 2031 and 2033.

I commend Massie-Taylor on his growth agenda. But he needs to go beyond the surface and delve into just how sports Stateside have made themselves commercial, and fan-loved, behemoths.
