This will directly support companies across the space supply chain, from component manufacturers and launch technology developers to […]

The post European SpaceTech recieves a €560 million injection to promote European sovereignty appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> A new partnership between Deutsche Bank and the European Investment Bank (EIB) is set to mobilise a €560 million investment towards European SpaceTech, helping businesses scale, bring new tech to market, and strengthen Europe’s independent space capabilities.

This will directly support companies across the space supply chain, from component manufacturers and launch technology developers to satellite applications and in-orbit services.

“This new partnership between the EIB and Deutsche Bank will help unlock investment in Germany and across Europe – backing the companies, supply chains and technologies that will make Europe’s space sector stronger, more competitive and ready to scale,” said Nicola Beer, European Investment Bank Vice-President.

The agreement follows a series of SpaceTech financing announcements across Europe in 2026.

In Germany, Munich-based The Exploration Company secured €387 million, HyImpulse Technologies raised more than €50 million, ATMOS Space Cargo attracted €25.7 million and deltaVision received €10.2 million.

Elsewhere, Finland’s ICEYE raised €450 million in primary funding, Spain’s PLD Space extended its Series C to €288 million and France’s UNIVITY secured €27 million.

Alongside further announcements involving AIRMO, Hydrosat and Arkadia Space, these financings exceeded €1.3 billion, independently of the proposed Deutsche Bank–EIB investment mobilisation.

EU-Startups previously reported on the EIB’s separate €30 million venture-debt loan to PLD Space in April 2026.

“Europe has the engineering talent to lead in space. Our job is to help finance its next stage of growth,” added Marc Mueller, Global Head Trade Finance & Lending at Deutsche Bank. “Working with the EIB, we can offer space businesses the long-term financing they need to invest, expand production and compete internationally.”

Agreed ahead of the European Space Agency (ESA) Space Investor Forum in Munich, this operation also builds on cooperation between the EIB and European Space Agency to address the financing needs of Europe’s space sector. ESA provides market intelligence and sector expertise to support the development of financing solutions that reflect the needs of space SMEs and Mid-Caps and enable the space sector to access finance.

It also helps connect these financing opportunities with the European space ecosystem, raising awareness among eligible companies and facilitating outreach to potential beneficiaries.

The initiative will support investment in technologies including reusable launchers and spacecraft, advanced propulsion systems, satellite manufacturing and Earth observation. These technologies underpin services ranging from communications and navigation to wildfire detection, pollution monitoring and security.

The financing will have a pan-European reach, with around half of investment expected in Germany and the remainder elsewhere in the EU.

“This partnership with Deutsche Bank will help companies across Europe’s space sector invest in the technologies, production capacity and supply chains needed to scale up and compete globally. In doing so, we are strengthening Europe’s capacity to deliver essential space services more autonomously,” said Robert de Groot, European Investment Bank Vice-President.”

Space businesses often face long development cycles, complex technologies and uncertain commercial returns, making conventional bank lending harder to secure. The partnership aims to give Deutsche Bank long-term funding and flexible financing structures to support commercially viable companies investing in their next stage of growth.

The partnership forms part of Space TechEU, the EIB’s dedicated space financing programme launched in November 2025, designed to mobilise an estimated €1.4 billion in investment with commercial banking partners.

The idea is that this will compliment broader EIB Group support through direct investment loans, venture debt, equity investment and advisory services. By combining these instruments with commercial bank lending, the Group aims to help European space companies secure financing at successive stages of development – from innovation to industrial expansion.

“Europe has a growing number of space companies with outstanding technologies that are ready to scale,” said ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher. “The next step is ensuring they have access to the capital they need to grow. This initiative can help open that path, enabling European space companies to scale up, compete and succeed.”

The combined entity will span more than 5,000 members and partners across 25 countries on six continents. The network links climate investors, […]

The post Berlin’s Greentech Alliance to acquire Intermobility to connect mobility startups with investors and cities appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Greentech Alliance (GTA), a Berlin-based global connection network for sustainable technology businesses, has agreed to acquire Intermobility, a Paris-based transport and mobility network connecting more than 1,000 companies, public authorities, and ecosystem players.

The combined entity will span more than 5,000 members and partners across 25 countries on six continents. The network links climate investors, startups, corporates, and policymakers in one of Europe’s most challenging sectors to decarbonise.

“Europe does not have a mobility technology problem, it has a coordination problem. The capital, the startups and the cities are all there, but they rarely meet. Bringing Intermobility into Greentech Alliance puts the people who build, fund and buy mobility solutions in one network, and we are inviting investors and companies who want a seat at that table to join us,” said Charles Newton Price, CEO, Greentech Alliance.

The acquisition, whose financial terms were not disclosed, comes as Europe grapples with transport emissions that have remained stubbornly above 1990 levels and as startup funding continues to decline. According to the European Environment Agency, transport emissions were 25.3% above 1990 levels in 2023 and accounted for around 31% of total EU emissions. 

Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based clean-transport advocacy group, estimates the sector needs €310 billion in annual investment by 2030 to meet climate targets. However, data from Via ID and Dealroom show European mobility startups closed 654 funding rounds in 2025, down from 785 the year before, raising $10.1 billion in total private funding. Greentech Alliance says the acquisition is designed to bridge this gap.

Founded in Berlin in May 2020 by Lubomila Jordanova, Simon Thies, Hannah Kromminga, and Jan-Jaap Verhoeve, Greentech Alliance is a curated global network for ventures, investors, educators and partners building what it describes as a more regenerative economy. The organisation is incorporated as both a Canadian not-for-profit and a German for-profit company.

It currently counts more than 3,000 community members and partners across six continents, including more than 700 investor members, and has facilitated more than 2,000 introductions.

Intermobility was founded in 2022 by François Hoehlinger as a European network of transport and mobility players spanning private companies and public institutions. By bringing Intermobility’s operators, cities and public authorities into the same network as GTA’s climate investors, startups, and corporates, the deal paves the way for a mobility solution to mature from pilot to scale.

For investors, GTA membership will now offer curated access to mobility ventures from both communities, alongside introductions to co-investors, corporates and public buyers. For companies. It opens direct channels to customers, pilots and capital across Europe and beyond.

The two organisations will also explore joint ventures and financing projects, including work linked to GTA’s Climate Zero programmes, subject to separate approval. Hoehlinger will join GTA’s board to help shape the Alliance’s direction as it scales internationally.

“Mobility only changes when founders, investors, operators and public authorities move together. Intermobility built that table in Europe. Greentech Alliance gives it international reach and access to capital, while keeping a grounded European perspective at its heart,” said Hoehlinger, founder, Intermobility.

Since its inception, GTA has successfully connected members on its network and with the acquisition of Intermobility, it has an opportunity to move beyond connection. Using its proven model of trusted introductions and curated membership, the alliance will aim to bridge the gap between climate solutions and funding shortfall.

The post Berlin’s Greentech Alliance to acquire Intermobility to connect mobility startups with investors and cities appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> OPINION: You can’t scale with a startup mindset https://www.eu-startups.com/2026/10/opinion-you-cant-scale-with-a-startup-mindset/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 09:29:36 +0000 https://www.eu-startups.com/?p=373257 The best advice once your company achieves product-market fit? Don’t get stuck on things that got you there, keep adjusting your architecture and workflow to fit your new realities and sizes. Starting strong is one thing, but the real point is pushing past the growth ceiling without crashing: McKinsey found 78% of products launched successfully […]

The post OPINION: You can’t scale with a startup mindset appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> The best advice once your company achieves product-market fit? Don’t get stuck on things that got you there, keep adjusting your architecture and workflow to fit your new realities and sizes.

Starting strong is one thing, but the real point is pushing past the growth ceiling without crashing: McKinsey found 78% of products launched successfully only to fail later on. Having worked in international expansion, I have seen how the practices that help a startup gain traction can cause troubles as it grows. Here is my top-5 of what’s better to be changed once a company is too big for a startup mode, and what habits are worth keeping in mind.

Money moves faster than decisions

Congratulations, it’s been your big funding round. Having more capital can feel like you have almost unlimited freedom to chase everything at once. This money mostly goes to ideas that already work, more on tests, all at once. In a ten-person startup, the founder knows every ongoing experiment. In a 100-person company, nobody does. Tests overlap, compete for the same target audience, and rarely get switched off. Meanwhile, decision-making slows down as more people have something to say. More money won’t fix messy operations, it just makes the mistakes more expensive.

The Turkish quick-commerce company Getir expanded to nine countries by the end of 2021 and bought Berlin rival Gorillas for €1.13 billon ($1.2 billion) in December 2022. Yet, in a few years the company chose to exit Germany, the UK and the Netherlands to focus back on its core  Turkish business. Having enough money to go global doesn’t automatically mean it’s the right move. Sustainable scaling requires strong research: diving into local consumer behavior, understanding specific market nuances, and adapting your model to what local buyers actually want.

To grow without burning capital, build a fixed and transparent framework of your experiments: a single log where every project has one owner, a set budget, a clear deadline, and kill criteria agreed before launch. Each ongoing test should be backed by a specific hypothesis and (ideally) data. If an experiment went great in one market, don’t hurry to move forward –  assess whether the conditions that made it work still apply in other regions.

Customer behaviour, channel preferences, and acquisition costs vary from country to country, so goals need to be tailored to actual team capacity and adapted market by market.

Hiring and ownership need a system

In a startup mode, team members do everything at once, no matter the difficulty level. Quite often, juniors jump in wherever they’re needed, keep going, and naturally become team leads. Loyalty is important, but management requires a different skillset. Wharton professor Peter Cappelli points out that top individual contributors who get promoted often make the weakest managers. 

The same applies at the executive level. When founders are responsible for each new decision, they’re likely to slow down processes in their own business. Getting advice and seeing fresh perspectives from someone who has their own area of responsibility creates a clear structure with solid boundaries. 

Bringing in senior leadership only works if you fix how responsibility is assigned. As headcount grows, each person assumes someone else is handling it. Psychologists call this diffusion of responsibility. Every project needs one named owner with the authority to execute, and clear processes for who decides and who reports progress. If a project has two owners, in practice, it has none.

AI will not replace everyone

Every company that’s actively growing now feels pressure to automate more and hire less. But implementation itself is a huge project, and for plenty of everyday tasks, a skilled person is still faster, cheaper, and far less painful to manage.

In May 2025, Klarna backtracked their earlier beliefs that AI has a potential to replace human work. A bit more than a year earlier, the company paused hiring customer service agents in favour of their AI assistant. The bot took 75% of the company’s customer chats  in more than 35 languages. It sounded high-potential at first, but then there was: lower quality of support. Klarna began recruiting human agents again, while AI keeps handling simpler requests. 

The point is to define for your business when to use AI, and when human touch is a super power. Everything repetitive and predictable can go to the AI team, and situations that win from empathy and critical thinking, are better left for people. The next step is to start educating your team to make sure they’re staying flexible and are using modern solutions for the new way of living.

AI is way more than just right prompting. Show employees how they can make their own simple tools for their daily workflows – through online courses, internal bootcamps, hackathons, or any other solutions that work best for your business. Developers can then turn the most promising ideas into advanced solutions.

Plan beyond the next quarter

Startups live month-over-month. Meanwhile, scaling needs a longer horizon, with a solid six-month and a year plan, all while maintaining a flexible approach. Your core metrics have to evolve, too. 

A longer perspective also offers you a unique view of which temporary fixes no longer work and need to be redone in favour of a stronger infrastructure. Spreadsheets and manual workarounds are fine at a hundred orders a day, not at a hundred thousand. A McKinsey survey revealed that about 30% of CIOs said more than 20% of their new-product budget is diverted to fixing tech debt.

To keep everything aligned, run a strategy session every six months. On a more routine basis, make it a norm to have bi-weekly leadership syncs to review progress, track unit economics, and adjust tactics before small operational cracks can turn into a real problem.

Growth makes centralisation a necessity

As you grow, your operational architecture has to go through changes, including a call on what stays central and what lives in-market. Having worked in international expansion, I’ve seen how companies hit a ceiling when they try to manage global growth from two extreme ends: either micro-managing every local solution or letting regional teams operate like separate startups.

Core product decisions, CRM, brand guidelines, and customer support standards require consistency, so they are best managed centrally. Where you can really leave room for local teams is in what they know best: local landscape, relationships and competitors, regional traditions, preferences, and behaviors. The real challenge here is finding the right balance. Centralization cuts out messy duplication and keeps your brand cohesive, but excessive control from the top will blindside you to market-specific realities.

Scale up, but keep the best of the startup mindset. Stay adaptable. Keep testing (but make it wisely and don’t waste resources). Count money the way you did when there was very little of it, because the budget is never infinite, no matter how big the last round was.

“We believe the ability to verify digital information will become as natural a part of tomorrow’s infrastructure as cybersecurity is today. Founded in 2026 in Stockholm, Pixel develops proprietary technology to detect AI-generated and manipulated digital content. ]]> Air Canada published its third-quarter results on Thursday, demonstrating strong revenue growth across all business segments, as well as inflated costs driven by rising fuel prices.

In its subsequent earning call, the airline revealed it had taken several measures to mitigate some of the impact, banking on its new A321XLR fleet to bring about fuel efficiency savings, overall fare increases across the board and stronger performance on transborder flights to the United States.

The company registered a 21% increase in revenue, offset by a 22% increase in its operating expenses. Overall operating profit declined 8%. It saw fuel expenses rise 75%, representing nearly a third of all operating costs.

Fare hikes soften the blow of rising fuel costs, but only partially

Air Canada’s yields improved 11% over the quarter as fare increases sought to cover the impact of rising fuel prices. In its earnings call, Air Canada’s Chief Financial Officer (CFO) John Di Bert described fare increases as its “primary tool to offset a higher fuel environment.”

Its price rises followed earlier estimates for where the cost of fuel might be. However, its estimates fell short of reality.

“In all, we recovered 46% of incremental fuel expense, below our original expectation of 60%, primarily due to the significant increase in fuel prices experienced in September.,” Di Bert explained.

“We expect our recovery rate to improve to 70% in Q4. Fuel recovery remains a question of timing, not demand. When fuel spiked in September, approximately 50% of our fourth quarter bookings had already been sold, creating a natural lag before our pricing actions could be fully reflected in fares.”

Fuel cost recovery supported by growth in transborder revenue to the United States

Thanks to a closer booking revenue on its North America markets, the carrier was able to reflect part of the fuel price hikes into its fares, Chief Commercial Officer (CCO) Mark Galardo said. He described transborder results as “excellent” and complemented improvements in revenue, yields and sixth-freedom traffic growth.

Revenue on flights to the United States rose 27%, growing faster than any of its other markets. Cargo revenue to the US did not grow as much.

The CCO attributed its healthy US performance to the strength of the American dollar, a favourable supply-demand balance and higher margins relative to its domestic operations.

“As I look forward, I see much of the same for Q4 and for Q1. I’ve got no reason right now to be concerned about the state of the transborder market,” he concluded.

The Airbus A321XLR helps ease the pain through fuel efficiency advantage

Air Canada introduced its Airbus A321XLR into commercial service on 9 June with a flight linking its Toronto and Montréal hubs. Long-haul operations commenced a few days later, on its route to Toulouse, France. During the July quarter, it also introduced the type on flights to Nantes (France) and Berlin (Germany), as well as Lyon (France) and Porto (Portugal) in September according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Galardo said that the airline was “pleased” with the initial results of the type, praising its lower fuel burn per ASM compared to its widebodies, which is a “real advantage in this current fuel environment.”

“Supporting a better supply-demand balance in these markets, the XLR is delivering a more favourable margin profile than other aircraft types on comparable routes,” he continued.

The CFO also complemented the A321XLR’s fuel performance: “This is meaningful in any environment, but it matters even more in this current fuel environment.”

Elsewhere, the company admitted it was reevaluating some of its ultra-long-haul flights given the fuel environment. It already confirmed plans to cut service on some of its longer routes, including Vancouver-Singapore, Vancouver-Dubai, Calgary-London-Delhi and Toronto-London-Mumbai. Montréal-Algiers will also not be returning.

]]> What happens if no one shows up for a flight. Can a plane fly without passengers? https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/what-happens-if-nobody-shows-up-for-a-flight/ Sat, 31 Oct 2026 12:08:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54718 What happens when nobody books a flight or passengers fail to turn up? Airlines sometimes operate empty aircraft rather than cancel services. Here's why.

The post What happens if no one shows up for a flight. Can a plane fly without passengers? appeared first on AGN.

]]> An airline can operate a scheduled flight even when not a single passenger turns up. Whether the aircraft takes off depends on where it needs to be next, the airline’s schedule and the cost of cancelling the service.

Airlines plan their flights around more than passenger bookings. Aircraft must be in the right place for their next departure, crews have assigned duties, and some flights carry cargo or mail that must reach its destination.

An empty flight can still have a good reason to operate, though in some cases a cancellation will make more sense.

Can a commercial flight take off with no passengers?

Yes. There is no minimum passenger occupancy requirement for a commercial airline flight to depart.

An aircraft can operate with no passengers on board, provided it meets the applicable operational and safety requirements. Airlines routinely fly empty aircraft to move them between airports for maintenance, or reposition them for future services. These are called ferry or positioning flights.

A scheduled passenger flight that departs empty may still operate as part of the airline’s published schedule, even though nobody has checked in or boarded.

The airline must still meet flight planning, crew, fuel, weight and balance, and air traffic control requirements.

Why would an airline fly an empty plane?

Sometimes an outbound flight may have lower demand than the return or an onward flight. The same aircraft and crew would serve both legs on the schedule, and cancelling the first leg would disrupt the others.

For example, an aircraft scheduled to fly from London to Paris may have a lot of passengers waiting for the return flight from Paris to London. Even if no one books or shows up for the London–Paris service, cancelling the outbound flight could leave the aircraft in the wrong city and other passengers stranded at the destination.

The airline then faces a choice: fly the aircraft empty to Paris, rearrange its schedule or find another aircraft to operate the return flight.

Flying empty may be the least disruptive option.

These decisions depend on the airline’s network. A carrier operating several daily services between major hubs may have more flexibility than one serving a destination only a few times a week.

Would the airline cancel a flight if nobody booked it?

An airline could cancel a flight that no one has booked, but an empty booking list would not automatically trigger a cancellation.

Airlines monitor demand and booking levels well before departure. If a flight is selling poorly, the airline could reduce fares or consolidate services. 

For example, if two flights are scheduled to depart for the same city in a short time frame, they could combine them into a single operation, provided there is enough capacity on the aircraft to accommodate demand on the return leg. 

However, flight cancellations cost airlines. An aircraft may have to be repositioned, crews reassigned, and passengers on later services accommodated. Airlines must also consider their airport slot requirements, local operating restrictions for flight times, and the availability of alternate aircraft.

If cancelling the service costs more than operating it, the airline may decide to fly anyway.

What happens if passengers book a flight but nobody checks in?

A flight with no check-ins is different from one with no bookings. Airlines need to establish who is travelling before departure. Passengers who do not check in by the deadline are recorded as no-shows. 

Once the airline confirms that nobody is travelling, it can decide whether to operate the service empty or cancel the flight. The same decision factors apply: if the aircraft is needed at the arrival city for the return flight or an onward journey, the airline could operate the empty leg anyway. 

If the flight operates, the crew still completes the necessary departure checks and follows the applicable operating procedures.

Could a flight depart with just one passenger?

Yes. A commercial flight can depart with only one paying passenger onboard. Sometimes travellers find themselves flying alone in a cabin designed for hundreds of people. The full crew operates the flight, including the number of cabin crew required by regulations. 

For passengers, the experience may feel a bit like a private jet flight, but the service is still a commercial airline operation. 

Travellers must follow the airline’s safety instructions and keep to the seat they paid for. An empty cabin does not automatically entitle someone to move into business or first class, or even to change seats in economy class, without cabin crew permission.

What happens to passengers if the airline cancels the flight?

If a flight has bookings but the airline cancels it because of low demand, affected passengers may be entitled to a refund or alternative transport.

Under EU passenger rights rules, travellers covered by Regulation EC 261/2004 can choose between reimbursement and rerouting when their flight is cancelled.

Additional compensation may be payable depending on when the cancellation is announced and the alternative travel arrangements offered. 

The UK Civil Aviation Authority sets out similar protections for flights covered by UK passenger rights legislation. 

Rules differ in other countries, so passengers should check which regulations apply to their journey.

Are empty flights the same as ghost flights?

The term “ghost flight” sometimes describes an aircraft operating with very few passengers or none at all. The term has also been used in discussions about airport slot rules, when airlines operate services to keep their access to congested airports. But it’s not an operational classification.

An empty positioning flight may be intended, as airlines may need to move aircraft between airports regardless of passenger demand.

These are often classified as ferry flights—services used to return aircraft to base, deliver them between locations or move them for maintenance. These aircraft movements are a normal part of airline operations.

Is it cheaper for an airline to fly an empty plane?

An empty aircraft generally burns less fuel than the same aircraft carrying a full passenger load, because it weighs less. But flying without passengers is far from free.

The airline still has to pay for fuel, crew, airport services, catering, air navigation charges and other aircraft operation costs.

Cancelling a flight may save some of these expenses. However, if the aircraft needs to reach another airport, the airline may have to operate a positioning flight.

That is why airlines consider the cost of the entire aircraft rotation, not just one departure.

For passengers wondering whether their lightly booked flight will operate, the number of empty seats showing on the airline’s seat map on the booking platform is not a reliable indication. 

If you find yourself as the only passenger waiting at the gate, you may have the unique experience of flying solo on a commercial flight. You will likely fly in the seat you booked originally. 

For an airline, a flight with no passengers—or just one passenger—can still be worth operating if cancelling it would cause greater disruption or expense elsewhere in its network.

]]> This week in aviation history: 34 years since the Airbus A330’s first flight https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airbus-a330-first-flight-anniversary-guide/ Sat, 31 Oct 2026 09:51:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=54555 On 2 November 1992, an aircraft took to the skies for the first time that would go on to become one of the most versatile wide-body platforms in modern aviation.

The post This week in aviation history: 34 years since the Airbus A330’s first flight appeared first on AGN.

]]> The Airbus A330, developed to meet the demands of a changing airline industry, has spent the subsequent 34 years evolving far beyond its original purpose.

From carrying passengers across oceans to transporting time-critical freight and refuelling military aircraft in flight, the A330 has demonstrated an ability to adapt to different missions without abandoning the fundamentals of its original design.

First conceived when airlines were seeking more efficient long-haul aircraft, the A330 has endured through changing economic conditions, shifting passenger expectations and significant advances in aviation technology. Its longevity reflects not simply a successful airliner design, but the flexibility of a platform that Airbus has continually developed to meet new operational requirements.

Today, the A330 remains an important part of commercial aviation. Its evolution into dedicated freighters, next-generation passenger aircraft and military multi-role tanker transports illustrates how a single wide-body design can serve an increasingly diverse range of customers.

From a new-generation airliner to a global success

The A330’s origins date back to 1987, when Airbus launched its A330/A340 programme. The European manufacturer developed two complementary aircraft: the four-engine A340 for long-range operations and the twin-engine A330 for airlines seeking wide-body capacity with the operating economics of two engines.

The A330 made its first flight on 2 November 1992, beginning an extensive flight-test and certification programme. It subsequently entered commercial service in 1994, with French airline Air Inter becoming its launch operator.

The aircraft arrived as advances in engine reliability, fuel efficiency and aircraft systems were changing the economics of intercontinental flying. Rather than relying on four engines, airlines could operate a large-capacity aircraft with two powerful turbofans, potentially reducing fuel consumption, maintenance requirements and overall operating costs.

The original A330-300 was designed to carry substantial numbers of passengers on medium- and long-haul routes. Its twin-aisle cabin offered the space expected of a wide-body aircraft, while its flight deck incorporated Airbus’s digital flight-control technology and emphasis on cockpit commonality.

The shorter A330-200, introduced in 1998, broadened the family’s appeal. With a shorter fuselage and greater range, it gave airlines another option for routes where demand did not justify the capacity of the larger variant.

This ability to balance capacity and range became one of the defining characteristics of the A330 family. Airbus had established a foundation that could accommodate different missions without requiring an entirely new aircraft architecture.

Why the A330 has proved so adaptable

The A330’s success rests on several interconnected strengths: its wide-body airframe, twin-engine configuration, useful payload capacity, long-range performance and potential for further development.

The twin-engine arrangement is particularly significant. By combining wide-body capacity with two engines, the A330 offers airlines a balance between passenger numbers, fuel consumption, and operating costs. It can serve busy regional routes, connect major international hubs, and operate long-haul services where demand does not justify a larger aircraft.

That flexibility gives airlines options when building or adjusting their networks. Depending on the variant and operating conditions, the aircraft can serve shorter sectors or international routes, allowing carriers to match capacity to demand.

Its dimensions also contribute to its versatility. The wide fuselage provides room for passengers and luggage, while the airframe can be adapted to accommodate cargo containers, freight-handling equipment and specialised military systems. Its size offers a useful compromise between capacity and operating flexibility.

Another important factor is Airbus’s approach to incremental improvement. Rather than treating the original aircraft as a fixed product, the manufacturer has introduced changes to engines, aerodynamics, structural weights, avionics and cabin systems over successive decades.

These developments have helped keep the A330 competitive as technology and customer expectations have changed. Operators also benefit from an established aircraft family, supported by an extensive maintenance network and substantial operational experience.

Commonality across Airbus aircraft provides further advantages. Shared cockpit philosophies and similarities in operating procedures can simplify fleet management and help airlines integrate the A330 into wider Airbus operations.

The combination of a proven airframe and continuing technical development has therefore been central to the A330’s longevity. Its adaptability is not simply a matter of having space for different equipment; it is also the result of an aircraft with sufficient performance and development potential to support new roles.

Passenger operations: the foundation of the family

Commercial passenger services remain at the heart of the A330’s identity. The A330-300 established the family’s reputation for carrying large numbers of passengers over medium and long distances.

Airlines could use it to connect major cities, serve leisure destinations and provide additional capacity on established international routes.

The introduction of the A330-200 extended that versatility. Its shorter fuselage reduced passenger capacity but allowed the aircraft to serve longer routes with a different balance between payload and range. This made it attractive to airlines opening new long-haul services or operating routes where passenger demand varied throughout the year.

The A330 also suited different airline business models. Full-service carriers could configure it with business class, premium economy and economy seating, while leisure airlines could maximise passenger capacity for popular holiday routes.

Airbus continued developing the platform with the A330neo programme, launched in 2014. The family comprises the A330-800 and A330-900, which retain the fundamental architecture of the original aircraft while incorporating significant improvements.

The A330neo features Rolls-Royce Trent 7000 engines, aerodynamic refinements, redesigned wingtip devices, and updated aircraft systems. Its cabin incorporates Airbus’s Airspace design, with modern lighting, improved storage and other passenger-focused enhancements.

Airbus states that the A330neo delivers up to 25% lower fuel consumption and carbon dioxide emissions per seat compared with previous-generation competitor aircraft.

These improvements help the aircraft remain relevant in an industry increasingly focused on reducing operating costs and environmental impact.

The neo programme demonstrates how Airbus has built upon an established platform, updating its technology while preserving the characteristics that made it attractive to airlines in the first place.

From passengers to freight: a second life for the A330

The same characteristics that make the A330 suitable for passenger operations also provide a strong foundation for cargo transportation. Freight operators need aircraft capable of moving substantial payloads over long distances, accommodating standardised containers and operating efficiently across international networks.

The A330’s wide fuselage, payload capacity and twin-engine performance made it a natural candidate. Airbus launched the A330-200F dedicated freighter programme in 2007.

Designed specifically for cargo operations, the aircraft features a main-deck cargo door, a reinforced structure and a modified landing-gear arrangement to maintain an appropriate ground attitude.

The A330-200F entered service in 2010, providing cargo operators with a medium-sized, long-range freighter. With a maximum payload of approximately 70 tonnes, it could carry general freight, express parcels and specialised consignments.

Its capacity made it suitable for operators seeking to match aircraft size to demand rather than deploying larger freighters on every route.

Airbus also recognised that retired passenger aircraft represented a significant source of potential cargo capacity. As airlines replaced older aircraft with newer models, suitable airframes could be converted to carry freight rather than leaving commercial service entirely.

These passenger-to-freighter, or P2F, conversions involve substantial engineering work. Passenger interiors are removed, the structure is modified to accommodate cargo loads, a large main-deck freight door is installed, and cargo-handling systems are added.

Both A330-200 and A330-300 aircraft have been converted under these programmes, giving operators access to different freighter capacities while extending the useful commercial life of existing airframes.

This approach illustrates an important aspect of the A330’s success: adaptability does not always require a completely new production aircraft. Sometimes, the most valuable innovation lies in finding a new purpose for an aircraft that has already spent years carrying passengers.

A military transformation: the A330 MRTT

Perhaps the most striking evolution of the A330 is its transformation into a military multi-role tanker transport. Developed from the A330-200, the A330 MRTT combines air-to-air refuelling with strategic transport capabilities. It can transfer fuel to other aircraft, transport personnel and equipment, and support medical evacuation missions.

The aircraft’s commercial origins provided a useful foundation. Its range, payload capacity and established airframe design suited the demands of long-distance military operations.

However, the MRTT is far more than a passenger aircraft with additional fuel tanks. It incorporates structural modifications, specialised avionics, military communications equipment and dedicated refuelling systems.

The aircraft can carry approximately 111 tonnes of fuel without additional fuel tanks. Depending on the mission and configuration, it can transfer fuel through hose-and-drogue systems or a boom refuelling system. This capability allows fighter aircraft and other military platforms to remain airborne longer, extend their operational reach and reduce the need to land for fuel.

The MRTT’s versatility extends beyond refuelling. Its transport configuration can accommodate military personnel, cargo and medical evacuation equipment, allowing operators to use it for a range of strategic missions.

The Royal Air Force operates the aircraft as the Voyager. Its fleet supports air-to-air refuelling, troop movements and other military transport requirements. Other operators include Australia, France, Singapore, South Korea and Saudi Arabia, alongside European nations participating in NATO’s multinational tanker fleet.

The MRTT demonstrates how a commercial wide-body can be transformed into a sophisticated military asset.

Although the conversion requires substantial engineering, the use of an established airframe allows Airbus to build upon existing manufacturing knowledge and operational experience rather than developing an entirely new aircraft.

One platform, multiple futures

The A330’s evolution extends beyond passenger, cargo and military applications. The family has also supported corporate and government transport through Airbus Corporate Jets, with aircraft configured for private, executive and official travel.

Such specialised applications reinforce the principle that a successful aircraft platform can support very different missions when its fundamental characteristics suit the task.

The A330 has also benefited from continuous improvements in operating efficiency, cabin design and onboard technology. These developments have helped it remain competitive while allowing operators to retain the advantages of an established aircraft type.

Its enduring success reflects the interaction of sound engineering, commercial practicality and continuing development. The original passenger aircraft established the foundation; dedicated freighters and passenger-to-freighter conversions expanded its cargo capabilities; and the MRTT demonstrated its potential in military service.

The A330neo has carried that adaptability into another generation, introducing new engines, aerodynamic improvements and a modern passenger environment without abandoning the platform’s established strengths.

Celebrating 34 years of adaptability

Thirty-four years after its first flight, the Airbus A330 remains an instructive example of how thoughtful aircraft design can create opportunities far beyond an aircraft’s original purpose.

Its success has not depended on a single breakthrough or one particularly successful variant. Instead, it has emerged through a combination of sound engineering, operational flexibility and a willingness to develop the aircraft as customer requirements evolve.

For airlines, the A330 provides a versatile means of carrying passengers across a wide range of routes. For freight operators, it offers a platform capable of moving substantial payloads across international networks. For military customers, the MRTT demonstrates how a commercial aircraft can become a strategic asset with multiple operational capabilities.

These roles are different, but they share a common foundation: the A330’s balance of capacity, range, efficiency and adaptability. Few aircraft illustrate so clearly how one successful wide-body design can develop multiple lives in the skies.

In Brief 4 min read
  • Condor turned a major Lufthansa setback into growth, building its own feeder network to keep long-haul flights full.
  • CEO Peter Gerber says the airline’s new city routes are outperforming expectations and attracting lucrative corporate travellers.
  • With American Airlines, Alaska and JetBlue partnerships growing, Condor is positioning itself as a stronger independent competitor.

Condor has established a new European feeder network following the loss of its long-standing arrangement with Lufthansa, with load factors above 70% on its city routes as the German carrier seeks to strengthen its long-haul operation at Frankfurt.

Chief executive Peter Gerber said at Routes World 2026 – being hosted in the German financial capital – that the carrier had been forced to move quickly after a court decision meant it could no longer rely on Lufthansa’s network to supply connecting passengers for its long-haul flights.

Condor’s secret ‘Plan B’ after Lufthansa tie-up collapsed

The development had come as a surprise, he said, but Condor had already been preparing an alternative strategy in case its agreement with Lufthansa could not be extended.

“We worked secretly on a plan B, just in case it turned out like it did,” he said. “It was absolutely clear that we need to do something about it because if you have such a huge long haul fleet as Condor, and you have the geographic situation in Germany, obviously you can’t operate long haul fleets without a feed.”

Gerber said the airline initially concentrated on establishing connections within Germany and German-speaking markets before expanding into other destinations as airport slots became available.

The new network has also required Condor to re-establish itself as a different entity for passengers. While the airline has historically positioned itself as a leisure carrier, it is now seeking to attract passengers travelling between European cities, including corporate customers who can provide additional traffic for its long-haul services.

A return to the Lufthansa arrangement remains uncertain, Gerber said, with the outcome dependent on the courts and competition authorities. Condor is planning to operate without it, adding: “We have to plan on our own.”

Condor city network attracts corporate travellers

Gerber said the initial performance of the network had exceeded his expectations, with load factors above 70%.

Gerber said customer experience had been central to that effort, alongside advertising and the airline’s online presence. “People start to tell this to their friends, and we increasingly get more corporate contracts.”

Rather than attempting to replicate the breadth of Lufthansa’s domestic and European network, Gerber said Condor was concentrating on destinations that generate the most valuable connecting traffic.

“We will never be able to build up the broadness of the Lufthansa network,” he said. Instead, the airline is focusing on “the most important O&D destinations for our customers”, while adding the routes and slots needed to serve those markets.

He said the airline intends to continue developing Frankfurt as its principal hub, arguing that the economics and geography of Germany make it difficult to establish another comparable operation elsewhere in the country.

A second German hub would be harder to make work, Gerber said, because it depends on having enough customers nearby and on airport operating conditions. “The only second opportunity to run such a kind of a hub in Germany would be Dusseldorf,” he said, adding that the airport’s operating limits make it difficult.

American Airlines partnership opens new markets

Commercial partnerships are becoming increasingly important as Condor expands beyond its traditional leisure model.

Gerber highlighted the airline’s relationship with American Airlines, which he expects to support the development of services to Chicago by providing connecting traffic on both sides of the Atlantic.

He said this partnership worked for both parties. “We offer American a good opportunity to really be more present in Europe. So that’s a clear win-win situation.”

Condor also works with partners including Alaska Airlines and JetBlue, alongside carriers in South Africa and Asia. Gerber said these arrangements were helping passengers make more seamless connecting journeys while providing Condor with access to markets it could not serve as effectively on its own.

The airline is also considering whether joining an alliance could be a logical next step as its transformation progresses.

“I think it’s clear that we will look into that after we now more or less in principle completed our transformation, and so this could be a next logical step to expand the reach of Condor,” he told Routes delegates.

For the time being, the carrier intends to develop its existing partnerships without an alliance commitment.

Growth ambitions face pressure from costs

Despite the progress in rebuilding its network, Condor faces pressure from high operating costs in Germany and rising fuel prices.

Gerber said the airline remained ambitious about expanding both its long-haul and leisure operations, with winter demand for long-haul destinations performing particularly well. However, he warned that higher fares were becoming a constraint on some European routes.

The airline is also pursuing a €100m savings target, with Gerber saying it had reached agreements with employees and unions to support its expansion plans. 

Around two-thirds of the savings would come from contract management and efficiency measures.

Gerber said Condor had performed well operationally during the summer, particularly on routes to destinations including Bangkok and Phuket, but that higher fuel prices had impacted their financial results, especially compared with forecasts made at the beginning of the year.

In Brief 2 min read
  • The first M-346 built for Italy's Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team has completed its maiden flight, sporting a striking new tricolour livery.
  • The advanced twin-engine jet will replace the team's ageing MB-339 aircraft, marking a major fleet modernisation programme.
  • Operational deliveries are expected from 2027, with the Frecce Tricolori's first full display season on the M-346 planned for 2028.

Sporting the colours of the Italian flag, the first M-346 built for the Italian Air Force’s Frecce Tricolori aerobatic team made its maiden flight on 29 October.

Marking a milestone in the Frecce Tricolori’s transition to a new generation of aircraft, airframe manufacturer Leonardo rolled out the M-346 at its plant in Venengono near Varese on 16 October. Photos of the jet first emerged the following day and show it already carrying the new livery.

However, it still lacks its number and the Frecce Tricolori markings on its tail, according to The Aviationist.

The livery combines the three colours of the national flag with dark blue. It was designed by the Italian firm Pininfarina and first shown to the public in 2024. The Italian Air Force describes it as developing the theme of the “renaissance of the tricolor.”  

A new era for the Frecce Tricolori team

The M-346 will replace the MB-339s flown by the national aerobatic team since 1982. The decision to renew the fleet was announced in September 2024 at Istrana air base as the team returned from a display tour of the US. The twin-engine M-346 was chosen over an earlier plan to opt for the single-engine M-345.

According to the Aviationist, the Air Force plans to acquire 15 M-346s for its aerobatic team. Ten will be assigned to the main formation, one to the commander and four will be spares.  Another five will join the 18 already used for training by the 61st Wing and the International Flight Training School.

The M-346’s performance differs from that of the MB-339, so the team will need to adapt its display routine. With deliveries expected to begin in 2027, the first full display season on the new jet is currently pencilled in for 2028.

The M-346’s technical credentials

Leonardo, which manufactured the aircraft, describes the M-346 as “the backbone” of the International Flight Training School in Decimomannu in Sardinia.

The advanced flight training centre is used by military pilots from Air Forces around the world and was created through collaboration between the manufacturer itself and the Italian Air Force.

The jet is optimised for advanced military pilot training, offering a broad range of training capabilities and long-term reliability, according to Leonardo. It features a wingspan of 31.9 ft, and a maximum speed of 1,090km/h.

The twin-engine, tandem-seat aircraft is equipped with a fly-by-wire flight control system with quadruple redundancy. With its Auxiliary Power Unit (APU), it can also be operated in complete autonomy.

The type has a long track record. The first prototype flew in July 2004 and Leonardo says the M-346 has already logged more than 125,000 flight hours with 126 sold worldwide.

Air New Zealand has welcomed its first new Boeing 787 Dreamliner in seven years, with the aircraft arriving in Auckland on 29 October.

The Boeing 787-9, registered ZK-NZT, is the world’s first certified Dreamliner featuring increased maximum take-off weight capability, allowing greater flexibility to carry passengers, baggage and cargo on long-haul routes.

However, the airline has confirmed that its much-anticipated Skynest economy sleeping pods will not be introduced in December as planned. It says “regulatory certification is taking longer than anticipated”, and has pushed back the launch into next year.

Air New Zealand receives first higher-weight Boeing 787 Dreamliner

The new aircraft arrived in Auckland from San Antonio, Texas, marking Air New Zealand’s first new Dreamliner delivery since 2019.

Its increased maximum take-off weight capability is designed to provide additional flexibility on ultra-long-haul flights, particularly Air New Zealand’s nonstop Auckland–New York service.

Air New Zealand became the launch customer for the Boeing 787-9 in 2014 and has since made the type a central part of its long-haul fleet. A second new Dreamliner, registered ZK-NZS, is expected to arrive within days.

The newly delivered aircraft features Air New Zealand’s latest cabin interiors, with 219 seats comprising eight Business Premier Luxe, 34 Business Premier, 52 Premium Economy and 125 Economy seats.

The Economy cabin includes nine Skycouch seats and 24 Economy Stretch seats. Air New Zealand Chief Customer and Digital Officer Jeremy O’Brien said: “There’s something really special about welcoming a brand-new aircraft into the fleet, particularly one that’s been years in the making to design, test and refine with our customers. Now we’re getting to see all that work come to life.”

What are Air New Zealand’s Skynest economy sleeping pods?

First unveiled in 2020, Skynest is designed to offer Economy and Premium Economy passengers a lie-flat sleeping experience without upgrading to Business Class.

Skynest is a six-pod sleep zone arranged in a triple-tier bunk configuration, positioned between economy and premium economy cabins.

It is a radical rethink of how long-haul economy comfort is sold and experienced. Passengers will still sit in their economy seat, but they can book a four-hour sleep session in a dedicated bunk-style pod between meal services.

Each pod measures approximately 2.03 metres in length and includes a mattress, seatbelt and privacy curtain.

The pods are intended for selected ultra-long-haul flights, including services between Auckland and New York.

Skynest was initially expected to enter service in 2024, but its introduction was postponed following delays in the delivery of Air New Zealand’s new Dreamliners.

As Air New Zealand brings back berths on planes, here’s what to expect from its new economy Skynest As Air New Zealand brings back berths on planes, here’s what to expect from its new economy Skynest

Why have Air New Zealand’s Skynest sleeping pods been delayed?

The airline had planned to introduce its Skynest sleeping pods in December 2026, giving Economy and Premium Economy passengers the opportunity to lie flat during ultra-long-haul flights.

However, Air New Zealand has confirmed that two regulatory approvals remain outstanding.

According to the airline, an overseas certifying authority has been unable to complete its approval within the original timeframe because of resource constraints. A separate certification process involving a local regulator is progressing well.

Rather than delay the introduction of its new Dreamliners, Air New Zealand has decided to put the aircraft into service during the busy summer travel period and install Skynest afterwards.

O’Brien said: “We’ve got a fantastic new 787 Dreamliner ready to welcome customers, and with summer being our busiest time of year, we want it in the air doing what it was built to do.”

He added: “Rather than hold back a brand-new aircraft while the final approvals are completed, we’ve decided to get it flying and bring Skynest onboard after the summer peak.

“We’ll confirm the new launch date for the Skynest once the timeline is clear.”

Air New Zealand continues Boeing 787 cabin upgrades

While Skynest remains delayed, Air New Zealand is continuing its wider programme of long-haul cabin improvements.

The majority of the airline’s existing Boeing 787-9 aircraft have already received refurbished interiors, with the final upgraded aircraft expected to return to service before the end of 2026.

The programme includes new Business Premier Luxe seats alongside redesigned Business Premier, Premium Economy and Economy cabins.

Air New Zealand also plans to introduce new Business Premier and Economy cabins across its Boeing 777 fleet during 2027.

]]> NASA astronauts complete 100th US ISS spacewalk: Here’s how spacewalks work https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/100th-us-spacewalk-iss-solar-array-installation/ Fri, 30 Oct 2026 14:09:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55020 The landmark mission installed a new solar array, increased the station's power-generating capacity and highlighted the complex work astronauts carry out beyond the safety of the ISS.

The post NASA astronauts complete 100th US ISS spacewalk: Here’s how spacewalks work appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 7 min read
  • NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completed the 100th US spacewalk from the International Space Station.
  • The astronauts installed and deployed the ISS's seventh roll-out solar array, part of a programme to boost the station's power supply by up to 30%.
  • The mission also offers a closer look at how astronauts train for, prepare for and carry out spacewalks in the vacuum of space.

Two astronauts have completed a seven-hour spacewalk outside the International Space Station (ISS), installing and deploying a new solar array in a mission that marked the 100th US spacewalk from the orbiting laboratory.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent seven hours and 11 minutes working outside the station on 29 October. They returned to the Quest airlock at 3:08 p.m. Eastern Time after successfully installing the seventh of eight planned roll-out solar arrays.

Although it was the 100th US spacewalk conducted from the ISS without a visiting space shuttle docked to it, the mission was the 285th spacewalk overall in support of the station. The larger figure includes 66 spacewalks from the Russian segment and 119 carried out by visiting space shuttle crews.

The new equipment will help provide electricity for the station’s experiments, life-support systems and other operations. NASA says the additional power will also support the ISS’s eventual safe and controlled return to Earth.

The spacewalk was Menon’s fourth but Kutryk’s first. It was also the first by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019, when David Saint-Jacques ventured outside the station with NASA astronaut Anne McClain.

A seven-hour job outside the space station

Menon and Kutryk began their spacewalk at 7:57 a.m. Eastern Time, leaving the station through its Quest airlock.

Menon wore a spacesuit marked with red stripes, while Kutryk wore an unmarked white suit, allowing mission controllers and television viewers to distinguish between them.

Their principal task was to install an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array, known as an IROSA, on the station’s 2A electrical power channel.

The equipment had been delivered earlier in October aboard a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft. It was temporarily stored on a platform outside the ISS until the astronauts could install it.

The solar array weighs approximately 340 kg and measures about three metres long in its packed configuration.

After releasing it from its temporary mounting, Menon attached himself to the end of Canadarm2, the station’s Canadian-built robotic arm. Carrying the folded solar array, he travelled on the arm towards the installation site on the station’s port-side structure.

Kutryk made his way separately along the station’s framework, remaining secured by safety tethers.

Once together at the worksite, the astronauts mounted the equipment and connected it to the station’s electrical system.

Unlike conventional solar panels that require motors to unfold, the new array uses stored energy in flexible carbon-composite supports to unroll itself.

The panel extended to approximately 19 metres in length. It took about just over 11 minutes to deploy fully.

The astronauts also completed additional preparatory work for the next spacewalk, including tasks involving the mounting equipment for the eighth and final roll-out array.

Why the space station needs more electricity

The ISS has relied on large solar panels to generate electricity since its assembly began in orbit.

But the original arrays have exceeded their intended 15-year service life, and their power output has declined with age.

NASA has been adding smaller, more efficient roll-out arrays alongside the older panels rather than replacing the entire original system.

The new panels partly cover the existing arrays while generating additional electricity.

When all eight roll-out arrays are installed, NASA expects the station’s available power to increase by up to 30%, raising its generating capacity from approximately 160 kilowatts to 215 kilowatts.

The extra electricity will support scientific research, station equipment and essential operations during the remaining years of the ISS programme.

It will also help maintain the systems needed for the station’s planned controlled deorbit at the end of its operational life.

Menon and Kutryk are scheduled to conduct another spacewalk on 5 November to install the eighth and final roll-out array on the 3B electrical power channel.

That installation is expected to complete the station’s solar power upgrade programme.

How the astronauts prepared for the spacewalk

The work outside the ISS was the result of several days of preparation by the station’s Expedition 75 crew.

Earlier in the week, Menon and Kutryk rehearsed the movements needed to carry the solar array from its storage platform to the installation site.

Their colleagues, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, practised operating Canadarm2 and reviewed the camera positions and lighting conditions needed to monitor the work.

The two spacewalkers organised their tools inside the Quest airlock and prepared small checklists that could be attached to the cuffs of their spacesuits.

They also checked their suits’ oxygen, cooling, water and communications systems. Their emergency jetpacks were inspected to ensure that the batteries, fuel supplies and thrusters were working.

On Wednesday, the four astronauts held final discussions with specialists on Earth, reviewing the installation procedure and the robotic arm’s movements.

Watkins and Delaney remained inside the station during Thursday’s operation, helping the spacewalkers prepare and supporting the work outside.

What is a spacewalk and how is it done?

A spacewalk is any activity in which an astronaut leaves a spacecraft while in space. NASA calls it an extravehicular activity, or EVA.

Despite the name, astronauts do not actually walk. In the absence of normal gravity, they move by holding onto handrails, pulling themselves along structures or using equipment such as robotic arms.

Spacewalks allow astronauts to repair equipment, install new hardware and carry out experiments that cannot be performed inside a spacecraft.

Before leaving the station, astronauts put on specially designed spacesuits that function much like miniature spacecraft. They provide oxygen for breathing, regulate body temperature, maintain pressure and allow communication with the crew and mission controllers.

Preparation begins several hours before the astronauts go outside.

One important precaution is breathing pure oxygen to remove excess nitrogen from the body. Without this procedure, changes in pressure could cause nitrogen bubbles to form in the bloodstream and tissues, producing a painful condition known as decompression sickness, or the bends. Scuba divers face a similar risk.

Astronauts leave through an airlock, a small chamber with two doors. The inner door is closed before air is removed from the chamber, allowing the outer hatch to open without releasing the station’s atmosphere into space.

Once outside, astronauts remain attached to the station by safety tethers. Their tools are also secured to prevent them from floating away.

They carry an emergency device called SAFER, short for Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue. Worn like a backpack, it uses small thrusters that an astronaut can control with a hand-operated device to return to the station if accidentally separated from it.

A typical ISS spacewalk lasts between five and eight hours, depending on the work involved.

Training for work in the vacuum of space

Long before astronauts attempt these operations in orbit, they practise on Earth.

One of NASA’s main training facilities is the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory near Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

The enormous swimming pool contains approximately 6.2 million gallons of water and allows astronauts wearing training spacesuits to rehearse tasks around submerged replicas of spacecraft structures.

By carefully adjusting their buoyancy, instructors can recreate some of the difficulties of moving and handling equipment in weightlessness.

Astronauts also use virtual reality systems to practise working outside the station. Special headsets and gloves allow them to rehearse movements, become familiar with their surroundings and prepare for complicated operations.

These rehearsals are especially important because even simple tasks can become difficult in bulky, pressurised spacesuits.

From the first spacewalk in 1965 to the ISS’s 100th US excursion

The history of spacewalking began more than six decades ago.

On 18 March 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov became the first person to leave a spacecraft in orbit. His historic spacewalk lasted about ten minutes.

Less than three months later, on 3 June 1965, NASA astronaut Ed White became the first American to conduct a spacewalk during the Gemini 4 mission. He spent approximately 23 minutes outside his spacecraft.

Spacewalking later became essential to human space exploration, particularly during the construction of the ISS.

Astronauts helped assemble the station in orbit, connecting modules, installing equipment and carrying out repairs that could not be completed by robots alone.

The first US spacewalk from the station’s Quest airlock took place on 20 February 2002, when NASA astronauts Carl Walz and Daniel Bursch spent five hours and 47 minutes testing its systems and carrying out maintenance.

The record for the most spacewalks by an individual astronaut belongs to Russian cosmonaut Anatoly Solovyev, who completed 16 excursions totalling more than 82 hours.

  • NASA's X-59 is designed to make supersonic flight quieter for people on the ground.
  • The aircraft is testing technologies that could influence future aviation regulations.
  • Comparisons with Concorde highlight how supersonic ambitions have evolved over time.

At first glance, NASA‘s X-59 Quesst looks like a modern-day Concorde. Yet the experimental aircraft has been designed with a completely different objective in mind.

Here’s how NASA’s X-59 compares with Concorde across speed, altitude, design and supersonic noise.

X-59 vs Concorde: Which aircraft is faster?

The X-59 has reached Mach 1.53 during flight testing, faster than its planned cruising speed of Mach 1.4. But it still has some way to go to match Concorde.

The iconic Anglo-French airliner cruised at Mach 2.04, approximately 1,354 mph (2,179 km/h), carrying 100 passengers between Europe and the United States in around three and a half hours.

The X-59, developed by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works for NASA, has reached approximately 1,010 mph (1,625 km/h). Its usual operating speed will be around 925 mph (1,490 km/h).

Why sonic booms happen and how NASA’s X-59 Quesst plans to eliminate them Why sonic booms happen and how NASA’s X-59 Quesst plans to eliminate them

How do Concorde and the X-59 compare?

Concorde entered commercial service in 1976 with British Airways and Air France and retired in 2003. It remains the fastest passenger aircraft ever to have flown. 

The X-59, which first flew in October 2025, is an experimental aircraft with room for just one pilot.

Why was Concorde restricted in the United States?

Concorde’s sonic boom was loud enough to disturb people on the ground, which hampered supersonic operations.

The US Federal Aviation Administration introduced restrictions on civilian supersonic flights over land in 1973. Concorde could fly to New York JFK and Washington Dulles, but had to slow below the speed of sound when operating over US territory.

That kept airlines from taking advantage of its full performance on domestic transcontinental routes, limiting Concorde’s commercial appeal.

The X-59’s design prevents shockwaves from combining into the loud boom that Concorde produced. Its long, narrow nose separates the pressure waves generated at the front of the aircraft from those produced by the wings. NASA has also kept the underside of the aircraft smooth and mounted its engine above the fuselage, where the wings help shield the ground from the engine inlet’s shockwaves. 

The space agency expects people on the ground will only hear a quiet thump, more like a car door closing from about 20 feet away.

The noise-dampening design presents a challenge for piloting the aircraft. The X-59’s nose is so long that its pilot cannot see directly forward through a windscreen. Instead, pilots rely on camera images shown on a cockpit display to see what’s ahead.

NASA’s X-59 has already exceeded its target speed

The aircraft first broke the sound barrier on 5 June 2026, reaching approximately Mach 1.1.

A week later, on 12 June, it reached Mach 1.4 at 55,000 feet, the conditions NASA has planned for its future noise research flights.

During testing in September, NASA pushed the X-59 to Mach 1.53, its highest reported speed. By the first anniversary of its maiden flight on 28 October, it had completed 40 additional flights and reached altitudes above 56,000 feet.

NASA is now preparing for acoustic testing to measure the aircraft’s actual noise levels. Flights over selected US communities will follow, allowing researchers to record how residents respond.

NASA hopes the findings will give regulators the evidence they need to establish noise limits for future supersonic passenger aircraft. The FAA is already working to replace the longstanding US restrictions with noise-based standards, with rulemaking milestones planned for 2027.

In Brief 3 min read
  • Royal Navy F-35Bs from HMS Prince of Wales joined Norwegian F-35As to escort a USAF B-52 over the High North.
  • The sortie supported Global Thunder 27, USSTRATCOM’s annual strategic deterrence and nuclear command-and-control exercise.
  • The mission highlighted NATO integration between carrier-based fighters, land-based F-35s and US long-range bomber operations.

For the first time, British F-35B stealth fighters have escorted a US B-52 bomber in the High North

The F-35Bs took off from HMS Prince of Wales and were joined in the escort by Norwegian F-35As flying from the mainland.

Norwegian and British F-35s escort US B-52 in exercise

The Royal Navy’s HMS Prince of Wales, accompanied by HMS Dauntless, is currently taking part in Operation Firecrest as part of Neptune Strike 26-4. The group has been joined by Norway’s HNoMS Fridtjof Nansen.

On the 24th of October, the British F-35Bs from the embarked 617 Squadron joined Norwegian F-35As in escorting a US Air Force B-52. An RAF Voyager tanker (Airbus A330 MRTT) also took part.

Images released show the bomber flanked by six F-35 fighter jets with three on each side in close formation.

A second B-52 had been expected to take part (callsign HUSH 12), but it suffered a technical issue and did not make it, according to the media reports. The lone B-52 took off from Minot Air Base in North Dakota with the callsign HUSH 11 and was refuelled by multiple aerial refuelling tankers en-route.

Phase two of Operation Firecrest

Operation Firecrest is the second phase of the 2026 UK Carrier Strike Group deployment to the High North and involves Norwegian, Danish, and German forces.

The Royal Navy has repeatedly mentioned Operation Firecrest and other multinational efforts in the High North in the context of increased Russian aggression in the region and safeguarding strategic infrastructure such as sub-sea cables.

The British carrier strike group posted, “For the first time, an American B-52 was escorted by British F-35s, whilst working alongside Norwegian F-35s. A milestone for the UK, USA and Norway, and another example of what can be achieved when allies work as one.”

The Royal Navy stated the carrier strike group demonstrated the “operational effectiveness of Carrier Strike, launching UK F-35s, to escort a US B-52 along with Norwegian F-35s…”

Norway is notable for being the first country to officially complete its F-35 programme of record, having received all of its 52 planned fighter jets. It has divested of its legacy F-16 fighter jets to Romania and Ukraine.

UK criticized for sending F-35s to the Middle East without enough spare parts UK criticized for sending F-35s to the Middle East without enough spare parts

The US’s Global Thunder 27

Global Thunder exercises are large-scale training programmes that see US strategic forces and supporting units, alongside invited allied forces, simulate the build-up to and execution of a nuclear war scenario.

USSTRATCOM announced US Strategic Command began its annual Global Thunder nuclear command and control exercise on 22nd of October. USSTRATCOM states its purpose is to “enhance nuclear readiness and ensure a safe, secure, effective and credible strategic deterrent force.”

The US stated that the exercise is not in response to actions by any nation or current world events. The exercise can see an increase in bomber and other aircraft flights.

USSTRATCOM posted that the joint operation with British and Norwegian forces visibly demonstrated a “shared commitment to global security and stability.”

An official NATO statement noted it demonstrated the ability of British, US, and Norwegian forces to “integrate strategic airpower with advanced fighter capability across the High North.”
